# Specification and user API audit 004: Claude Fable report

[Audit 004](README.md) · [Audit directory format](../README.md)

- **Auditor:** Claude Fable 5.2, orchestrating Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude
  Sonnet 5.5 agents.
- **Date:** 2026-11-10.
- **Audited commit:** `931cfb596`, read as a frozen export. Main moved while
  the audit ran. [Section 17](#17-after-the-baseline) covers the first three
  commits, up to `aa46736e7`, and names two later ones that were not read.
- **Scope:** the written contracts of the repository: every page under
  `specs/`, the skills and agent instructions, the operator documentation and
  the tracked examples. The Go package map, the API types, the command catalog
  and the Ansible collection layout were read as evidence of how the contracts
  materialize, not reviewed as code.
- **Result:** 637 verified findings: 1 Blocking, 30
  High, 182 Medium and 424 Low. A further 3 were confirmed
  and are already recorded as open work, 11 candidates are settled by
  a recorded decision, and 21 were refuted. A separate pass read three commits that landed while the audit ran. They resolve, partly resolve or change 7 of these findings, and the text they added has 20 further findings (1 High, 5 Medium and 14 Low), reported apart in section 17.

The report changes no product code, specification, milestone or decision, and
it authorizes no implementation and no command with effects. Every
recommendation in it is a proposal for the owner.

## How to read it

- [Section 2](#2-executive-assessment) gives the verdict: what is good, what
  needs improvement, what is bad, a scorecard and the five actions that matter
  most.
- [Section 15](#15-ordered-remediation-roadmap) orders the work and lists the
  decisions only the owner can take.
- Sections 3 to 11 take one subject each: scope, concepts and names, the
  desired-state API, the CLI, the architecture, language responsibility, the
  reconciliation rules, the corpus as an agent harness, and the skills.
- [Section 12](#12-findings-catalog) is the catalog: every finding with its
  evidence, recommendation and verification. Any id in the text, such as
  [REC-01](#rec-01), links to its entry.
- [Section 16](#16-method-and-verification-record) says how the audit was run
  and what it did not do.
- [Section 17](#17-after-the-baseline) covers the first three commits that
  landed while the audit ran: which findings they resolve or change, and what
  a reading of the text they added found. Read it before acting on a finding
  about client releases, download mirrors, acquisition origins or the
  operator guide's setup sections.

## 1. The audit request

The owner asked for an audit of the repository's specifications and user API,
to find where they are not yet as good as they can be, and supplied the prompt
of the previous specification audit with leave to improve it. The text below
is the prompt this audit ran on. What it changes from the previous prompt is
listed after it.

### 1.1 The prompt as run

#### Role

Act as a principal architect who has shipped declarative infrastructure
products (Kubernetes-style APIs, installers, reconcilers), designed plugin and
adapter architectures for multi-vendor platforms, reviewed safety-critical
automation against physical hardware, and operates AI coding agents (Claude
Code and OpenAI Codex) on large repositories. You audit the written contracts
of this repository, not its line-level code. You judge by evidence, state the
standard you judge against, and separate confirmed defects from improvements
and from matters of taste.

#### What Bootwright is

Bootwright is a declarative day-0 orchestrator: an operator authors a set of
Kubernetes-style YAML objects (`apiVersion: bootwright.io/v1alpha1`; the kind
catalog in `specs/api.md` owns the list of kinds) describing one complete
environment (substrate providers and machines, operating systems,
infrastructure services, container clusters, storage clusters, cluster
add-ons). Bootwright admits and freezes that input into a context, compiles
it, plans an immutable operation of blocks, drives qualified native tools
(openshift-install, cephadm, Redfish, libvirt, oc, OLM) through Ansible
adapters, verifies each outcome and records durable evidence, until GitOps can
take over. It is not a continuously reconciling controller and has no day-2
scope beyond what `specs/project.md` admits.

The owner's immediate support portfolio is: libvirt with sushy-tools emulated
BMCs; bare metal through vendor BMCs; OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt)
machines; OpenShift clusters; IBM Storage Ceph; IBM Fusion Data Foundation as
a cluster add-on; NTP and proxy services either provisioned by Bootwright or
external; networking that already exists (provided, not managed). The owner
intends later additions with low code impact: other substrates (VMware, public
clouds), other cluster types (vanilla Kubernetes, Rancher, managed
Kubernetes), other storage (other Ceph distributions, external arrays) and
other infrastructure component types. The specs need not name these; they must
guarantee that the general code flow is generic, that specifics live behind
interfaces, adapters or registries selected by the operator's input, and that
general code never knows which implementation runs.

The project is pre-1.0 and carries no backward compatibility
(`specs/project.md`): a rename or a reshape is cheap now and expensive later.
A naming or shape improvement that is real is therefore worth reporting; a
cosmetic preference is not.

#### Material in scope

Every file under `specs/` (core specs, `specs/api/`, `specs/cli/`,
`specs/contexts/`, `specs/deferred/`, `specs/milestones/` including
`delivered.md` and `backlog.md`), every skill file (`.agents/skills/**`, the
`.claude/skills/**` wrappers, `.agents/skills/index.md`), the agent
entrypoints and rules (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/*.md`, the
hooks and permission rules in `.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json`,
`scripts/hooks/`), the knowledge index and its conventions
(`.agents/knowledge/index.md`; sample pages as evidence of the convention),
`docs/*.md`, `README.md`, `examples/README.md` and the tracked example inputs
under `examples/` (excluding `examples/wip/`). The Go package map
(`internal/**` directories, `contracts.go` files, `cmd/bootwright/wiring_*.go`,
`test/architecture/*.go`), the Ansible collection layout
(`ansible/collections/ansible_collections/bootwright/core/{roles,plugins,playbooks}`),
`api/v1alpha1/*.go`, `internal/cli/catalog.go`, the `Makefile` and `scripts/`
are in scope only as evidence of how concepts materialize at the package,
port, registry, role and tooling level.

Out of scope: low- and medium-level code review (function bodies, tests, error
handling), running any Bootwright command with effects, and any change to the
repository other than the report.

#### Questions the audit must answer

1. **Objectives, scope and domain.** Are purpose, scope, non-goals and domain
   boundaries stated once, consistently and testably? Is the immediate
   portfolio distinguishable from the intended family scope, and does the gap
   distort any design? Is the day-0/GitOps-handoff boundary coherent with
   everything the specs promise?
2. **Concept model and nomenclature.** Are the core concepts (environment,
   context, controller, operation, attempt, block, stage, wave, slice,
   substrate, provider, machine, realized target, reservation, implementation,
   variant, specialization, adapter, driver, package, profile, binding,
   export, custody, evidence, receipt, refusal) defined once, named
   consistently across API kinds, CLI nouns and verbs, specs and code, and
   free of overloads? Propose a normative vocabulary, a rename table where
   names should change, and naming rules for future kinds and fields.
3. **Desired-state API as an operator language.** Judge the authoring grammar
   (envelope, references, unions, collections, enablement, defaults, effective
   state, native fields, the environment directory and selection) and each
   kind's field design against the standard of the best declarative platform
   APIs: intuitive for a platform operator, minimal, composable, unambiguous
   on omission, null and empty, stable, provider-neutral where intent is
   shared and explicitly provider-shaped where it is not, and truthful about
   what is supported. Identify where the API leaks implementation, where it
   forces operators to repeat facts, where kinds should merge or split, and
   where a field name misleads. Give concrete recommended shapes.
4. **The CLI and its output as the second user API.** Judge the command tree
   (nouns, verbs, flags, scope), the lifecycle journey an operator walks, the
   inspection and access utilities, and the output contract (streams, exit
   statuses, JSON documents, the diagnostic taxonomy, logs) against the best
   infrastructure CLIs: a consistent grammar, safe defaults, scriptability,
   discoverability, and one answer per question between the command catalog,
   the prose, the help rules and the operator guide.
5. **Concept interaction and architecture.** Are the interactions between
   concepts (environment, machines, operating systems, services, clusters,
   storage, add-ons; context, operation, evidence; implementation selection,
   frozen request, continuation) specified as complete contracts? Does the
   architecture spec (bounded contexts, ports, dependency direction,
   composition root, registries, version specialization) guarantee a generic
   general flow with specialization only behind ports and registries chosen by
   input? What exactly would adding a new substrate, cluster type, storage
   type or infrastructure component touch today, and is that the minimum?
   Evaluate how the spec's promises materialize in the package map, ports,
   wiring, Ansible roles and action-plugin protocols, at the architectural
   level only.
6. **Reconciliation rules: security, safety, reliability.** Review every rule
   governing apply, destroy, plan, continuation, attempts and unknown
   outcomes, convergence, block transitions, state precedence, dependency
   safety during recovery, desired-versus-real comparison, GitOps readiness,
   mutation safety (quiescence, physical disk safety, opt-in overwrite,
   controller-host protection), confirmation and authorization, ownership and
   identity proofs, locking and reservations, secrets custody and the trust
   model. For each rule judge: sound, ambiguous, contradicted elsewhere,
   unsafe, or unimplementable as written; name the failure scenario and the
   smallest correction.
7. **Language responsibility.** Is it clear which logic belongs in Go,
   Ansible, Python and shell, and why? Where is the boundary violated or
   unspecified (Python action plugins and module utilities, shell wrappers,
   Makefile, completion scripts)? Propose a decision matrix with rules and
   prohibited uses.
8. **Spec corpus as an agent harness.** Is the one-owner-per-fact model, the
   index, the milestone and ID scheme, the "Not yet met" convention and the
   knowledge split effective for coding agents? Quantify the retrieval path a
   typical task forces an agent through (tokens) and identify duplication,
   drift between pages, pages that are too large or badly placed, and
   conventions that cost tokens without buying precision. Take the checks the
   fitness suite already runs over the corpus as given, and judge whether they
   are the right checks. Propose restructuring that preserves precision.
9. **Skills and agent instructions.** Review every skill, reference, wrapper,
   rule file, hook and entrypoint for correctness, discoverability (Claude
   Code and Codex), contradiction, duplication, procedural completeness,
   placement of vendor- or model-specific guidance, and total accepted-task
   token cost. Propose an explicit keep, modify, remove, add portfolio with
   the purpose, trigger description, body outline and size budget of each
   skill, a common contract that works in both runtimes, and the measurements
   that would show the portfolio works.

#### Method and evidence standard

- Audit a frozen export of one commit, so that every citation resolves and no
  concurrent change moves a line. The export omits `audits/`, `examples/wip/`
  and the local-only override file, so no auditor can read them.
- Read the owning sections for each question fully; do not sample a page you
  make a claim about. Record every file and range read, with its depth.
- Cover the corpus more than one way, because one reading finds one kind of
  defect: page by page, rule by rule; by failure scenario across pages
  (crash, unknown outcome, concurrency, removal, skew, secrets, physical
  hardware, authority, handoff, ordering); by cold-read authoring of the
  portfolio's scenarios from the operator-facing material alone; by a dry run
  of each extension the owner intends; by a benchmark against the reference
  APIs operators already know; by schema-to-page parity; and by drift sweeps
  between pages that cover one subject.
- Every finding carries: a stable id, a title, the area, a severity
  (Blocking: an unsafe or contradictory rule on a destructive, security or
  state-integrity path, or a design that blocks the stated goals; High: an
  operator- or agent-visible defect of the contract; Medium: a gap or
  ambiguity that will produce divergent implementations; Low: clarity, naming
  or cost with a concrete, cheap fix), the kind (contradiction, gap,
  ambiguity, unsafe-rule, design, naming, duplication, process, cost),
  evidence as `path:line-range` plus a quote of at most 25 words per cited
  passage, the consequence (a concrete failure scenario or cost), the smallest
  recommendation, acceptance criteria that a reviewer can check, the surface
  the change touches and its size, and the result of checking the
  recommendation against the recorded owner decisions
  (`specs/milestones/backlog.md`, D1 to D249) and the stated project
  principles.
- Prefer the finding that changes what the owner will do. Do not report style.
  Do not restate a "Not yet met" line, an unrealized-declaration row or a
  deferred page as a defect unless the rule itself is wrong. A specified
  capability that is not implemented is not a defect; a specified rule that
  cannot be implemented safely is.
- Record what is right as well as what is wrong: a restructuring must not
  destroy what works.
- Each finding is verified independently before it enters the report: one
  verifier tries to refute it from the cited text and the rest of the corpus,
  one checks impact, severity and the recommendation against decisions and
  principles. A split vote is arbitrated on evidence, never on rank. A finding
  rated High or Blocking gets one more independent reading. Every citation is
  checked mechanically against the export. Refuted findings are not reported
  as findings; a refuted candidate that an operator would plausibly also raise
  is listed as considered and refuted, and one that an open item or a recorded
  decision already covers is listed as tracked or decided.
- Treat `AGENTS.override.md` as a local-only override file: never quote or
  paraphrase its content, and never place environment-specific facts (host
  names, addresses, credentials, organization names, private branch names) or
  anything from `examples/wip/` in any output. Refer to that file only as "the
  local-only override file".
- Do not read `audits/` during the finding phases. A separate cross-check
  against the earlier audits, and against a sibling report of this audit if
  one exists, happens after verification and is reported in its own section.
- Never modify, create or delete a file in the repository other than the
  report and its navigation. Write intermediate material only under the
  scratch directory named in your instructions.

#### Report structure

1. The audit request (this text).
2. Executive assessment: what is good, what needs improvement, what is bad; a
   scorecard by dimension; the five actions that matter most.
3. Objectives, scope and domain.
4. Concept model and nomenclature: normative vocabulary, rename table, naming
   rules.
5. Desired-state API: grammar verdict, per-kind verdicts, recommended shapes,
   authoring friction, benchmark.
6. The CLI and its output contract.
7. Architecture: generic flow and specialization; extension scenarios with the
   exact impact of adding a substrate, cluster type, storage type and
   infrastructure component; code materialization map; the immediate
   portfolio.
8. Language responsibility matrix.
9. Reconciliation rule audit: rule-by-rule table, scenarios walked and
   findings.
10. Spec corpus structure and maintenance for agent efficiency.
11. Skills and agent harness: current state, proposed portfolio with drafts,
    Claude Code and Codex contract, token budget model.
12. Findings catalog, most severe first, with verification verdicts; then the
    tracked, decided and refuted candidates.
13. Per-file coverage ledger for every spec, skill, wrapper, rule, hook and
    entrypoint file.
14. Cross-check against the earlier audits.
15. Ordered remediation roadmap.
16. Method and verification record.

### 1.2 What changed from the previous prompt

- **The CLI is a question of its own (4).** The request is about the specs and
  the user API, and an operator meets two APIs: the YAML kinds and the command
  line with its output. The previous prompt judged the second only in passing.
- **Coverage by more than one reading.** The previous prompt asked for pages
  to be read fully. This one adds five other readings (failure scenarios,
  cold-read authoring, extension dry runs, a benchmark against reference APIs,
  parity and drift sweeps), because a page read alone cannot show a rule that
  two pages state differently, a field an operator cannot guess, or a general
  section that an extension would have to edit.
- **A frozen export.** Citations are to one commit, and the exclusions
  (`audits/`, `examples/wip/`, the local-only override file) are enforced by
  absence rather than by instruction.
- **Facts corrected.** The decision log now runs to D249, not D173. The count
  of kinds is gone, because `specs/api.md` forbids any page to state one. The
  portfolio names OpenShift clusters, which the previous list implied.
  `.codex/hooks.json`, `scripts/hooks/`, the command catalog, the `Makefile`
  and `scripts/` are named as evidence.
- **Strengths are recorded.** Each auditor reports what its slice gets right,
  so the assessment can say what must survive.
- **Each finding says what it would cost.** The surface a change touches and
  its size sit beside the recommendation, and the pre-1.0 policy is stated, so
  cheap-now renames are separated from cosmetic ones.
- **Verification is stricter.** High and Blocking findings get a third
  independent reading; arbitration must cite evidence; every citation is
  checked mechanically; candidates that an item or a decision already covers
  are reported apart from refuted ones.
- **The existing checks are taken as given.** The fitness suite already holds
  much of the corpus convention (byte budgets, section budgets, reachability,
  the "Not yet met" format). Question 8 asks whether those are the right
  checks instead of proposing them again.
- **The cross-check has a defined target.** No sibling report of this audit
  existed when it ran, so section 14 compares against the earlier audits.

## 2. Executive assessment

The specifications and the user API are strong, and they are not yet as good as they can be. The audit verified 637 findings: 1 Blocking, 30 High, 182 Medium and 424 Low. Nothing in them asks for a change of direction. What needs work is a small set of rules that are unsafe as written on destructive paths, and the way the text is kept: about half of the High findings are a stale copy of a rule that an owner decision had already changed on its owning page. Fix the unsafe rules first, then remove the two causes of drift named in section 2.3, and most of the rest becomes a cleanup list.

### 2.1 What is good

The design holds up. The defects below are in how the text is kept, plus a few rules on destructive paths. These passages are right and should stay:

- **Unknown is never success.** Only positive evidence moves an effect state off `unknown`, and a direct positive no-effect is a typed failure (specs/state-reconciliation.md:1428-1439).
- **Strict, credential-safe decoding.** Duplicates, aliases, merge keys, tags, nulls and octal-looking integers are refused. Unknown fields are refused at every typed level, and an open native map never opens its container (specs/api.md:110-122, 154-170).
- **One output envelope.** `ok` is true exactly when `exitCode` is 0, and exit 3 belongs only to `diff --exit-code` (specs/cli/output.md:238-244). An existing diagnostic code keeps its meaning (specs/cli/output.md:1106-1108).
- **Refusal tables held by tests.** Each row's reason and remedy is the diagnostic text, a named test holds the table equal to `Unsupported`, and a row lifts only in the commit that delivers what it refuses (specs/openshift-clusters.md:106-112, 157-166).
- **Proof on the destructive path.** A physical target must match an exact ComputerSystem and its complete MAC set (specs/substrates.md:774-782). Every physical proof, the installer's included, uses that one MAC-set predicate (specs/state-reconciliation.md:2446-2450).
- **Secret classes.** Effect material, access credentials and trust anchors are separate classes with immutable binding. Only access credentials can be rebound (specs/secrets.md:315-335).
- **Supply-chain trust stated honestly.** dnf never gets `--nogpgcheck` or `--allowerasing` (specs/controller.md:293-303). The target-tool trust gap is named rather than hidden (specs/security.md:775-783).
- **Exact selection and the seam rule.** Selection yields exactly one implementation, with no fallback. An edit to the general flow counts as a missing seam (specs/architecture.md:1166-1176, 498-502).
- **The language table.** Each language has a Holds cell, a Never cell and a placement question (specs/architecture.md:766-778).
- **A bounded day-0 scope.** Handoff transfers no ownership (specs/project.md:90-101). Utilities register no operation (specs/project.md:174-180). Only a recorded `uid` proves add-on ownership outright; the mark is a recovery rule (specs/add-ons.md:261-272).

### 2.2 What needs improvement

Each class below is real, bounded and fixable in the text. Most fixes are spec edits.

- **The journey after a completed apply gives four answers.** `plan`, `status`, `context update` and `diff` disagree about an edited or drifted context: [CLI-01](#cli-01), [CLI-09](#cli-09), [REC-03](#rec-03), [CLI-37](#cli-37), [CLI-39](#cli-39), [CLI-10](#cli-10), [REC-63](#rec-63), [REC-64](#rec-64).
- **Root-disk and erase rules disagree.** D239's forms did not reach the managed-OS and disk-safety owners, and the WWN spelling differs between consumers: [API-03](#api-03), [API-08](#api-08), [REC-02](#rec-02), [API-38](#api-38), [API-121](#api-121), [REC-15](#rec-15).
- **Admitted input that nothing reads.** Fields are admitted and frozen, but have no consumer or always refuse at plan, and some have no tracking item: [API-07](#api-07), [API-30](#api-30), [API-34](#api-34), [API-35](#api-35), [API-21](#api-21), [API-75](#api-75).
- **Recovery exits that are too wide or lead nowhere.** Some remedies roll back every context ([REC-32](#rec-32)), leave only orphaning ([REC-62](#rec-62)) or discard state on a read error ([REC-72](#rec-72)). A lost keyring reads as uninitialized ([REC-65](#rec-65)). Others name an exit that fails: [REC-15](#rec-15), [CLI-23](#cli-23), [REC-120](#rec-120).
- **Implementation names in general text, and incomplete touch lists.** Adding a second implementation would mean editing general code, or the text reads as if it would, and the guard checks less than the spec says it does: [ARC-07](#arc-07), [ARC-28](#arc-28), [ARC-26](#arc-26), [ARC-10](#arc-10), [ARC-21](#arc-21), [CLI-25](#cli-25), [ARC-32](#arc-32).
- **Glossary and naming.** Some "always" sets are false, the realized target has drifting field lists, and some names say the opposite of what they do: [CON-06](#con-06), [CON-04](#con-04), [CLI-08](#cli-08), [CLI-29](#cli-29), [CLI-07](#cli-07), [CLI-57](#cli-57), [API-140](#api-140).
- **Authoring repeats facts.** One fact is authored in two places, and a default can never match: [API-06](#api-06), [API-54](#api-54), [API-99](#api-99), [API-37](#api-37), [API-41](#api-41), [API-131](#api-131).
- **Retrieval cost.** Index rows route whole pages, the milestone read rule is unbounded, and budget exceptions never expire: [COR-26](#cor-26), [COR-30](#cor-30), [COR-28](#cor-28), [COR-13](#cor-13).

### 2.3 What is bad

Four groups of rules are unsafe as written. Two root causes will keep producing defects until they are removed.

- **Missing evidence read as "nothing happened" (unsafe).** OpenShift reads a powered-off installed cluster as positive no effect, and the retry reinstalls over it ([REC-01](#rec-01), Blocking). Managed OS has the same window earlier in its sequence ([REC-11](#rec-11)). Another managed-OS window reinstalls over a finished installation, which is safe but is described as "never installed" ([REC-46](#rec-46)). A loosened ownership observation reaches removal unchecked ([REC-07](#rec-07)).
- **Exclusivity is defined by one mechanism's records, not by the resource (unsafe).** An SSH-placed emulated BMC's key never meets a physical claim. Another context's power command can drive a server that is held: [REC-09](#rec-09), [REC-10](#rec-10), [REC-06](#rec-06), [REC-74](#rec-74). Two contexts of one controller store can install one server whose BMC reports no UUID, because only a UUID-keyed claim catches a second spelling of the BMC address ([REC-41](#rec-41)).
- **Promises that nothing enforces (unsafe).** An unnamed renew can orphan the only copy of a disk recovery passphrase ([REC-12](#rec-12), [CLI-22](#cli-22)). Uninstall can remove packages that were there before Bootwright ([REC-08](#rec-08)). An approved upgrade decays to a destroy remedy ([REC-13](#rec-13)).
- **The agent effect ban works in one runtime only (unsafe for agents).** The inline list omits commands and Codex has no guard: [COR-01](#cor-01), [SKL-01](#skl-01), [COR-36](#cor-36). The git deny patterns also miss variants, which then prompt instead of being refused ([SKL-02](#skl-02)).
- **Root cause: rules are restated instead of linked.** No rule says the owner page wins ([COR-85](#cor-85)). When a decision lands, only the pages its slice touched change, so stale copies remain on safety and operator pages: [REC-03](#rec-03), [REC-04](#rec-04), [REC-05](#rec-05), [DOC-01](#doc-01), [DOC-02](#doc-02), [SCO-01](#sco-01), [SCO-02](#sco-02), [API-04](#api-04).
- **Root cause: closed lists are typed by hand, and delivery state has a second home.** Registries and touch sets are copied with no derivation or test: [CLI-16](#cli-16), [CLI-20](#cli-20), [API-44](#api-44), [API-46](#api-46), [ARC-07](#arc-07). "Not yet met" lines stay after delivery ([COR-02](#cor-02)), are missing where they are needed ([COR-03](#cor-03)), and the test proves only that the linked item exists and is open ([COR-05](#cor-05)).

### 2.4 Scorecard

Scores run from 1 to 5. 5: sound, with only Low defects. 4: sound, with defects that mislead a reader but change no destructive or extension outcome. 3: a sound core, with defects that change what an operator, an agent or an extender does. 2: a Blocking finding on a destructive path. 1: the design itself must change. Counts are the verified findings of each area as Blocking/High/Medium/Low.

| Dimension | Score | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Objectives, scope and domain | 4 | project.md is short and testable; the coverage pages lag owner decisions ([SCO-01](#sco-01), [SCO-02](#sco-02)). 0/2/0/8 |
| Concept model and nomenclature | 4 | The one-meaning rule is right; core terms are missing ([CON-18](#con-18)) and some names mislead ([CLI-08](#cli-08)). 0/0/6/27 |
| Desired-state API | 3 | The grammar is strict and sound; disk rules contradict each other ([API-03](#api-03), [API-08](#api-08)) and inert fields stay admitted ([API-07](#api-07), [API-30](#api-30)). 0/8/39/99 |
| CLI and output contract | 3 | The safety rules and envelope are strong; the post-apply journey ([CLI-01](#cli-01), [REC-03](#rec-03)) and the guide ([DOC-03](#doc-03)) disagree. cli 0/1/30/31; operator docs 0/3/6/19 |
| Architecture and extension | 3 | The seams exist; none of the four extension scenarios is additive today ([ARC-28](#arc-28), [ARC-07](#arc-07), [ARC-21](#arc-21), [ARC-26](#arc-26)). 0/0/33/55 |
| Reconciliation rules | 2 | The engine core is sound; one Blocking ([REC-01](#rec-01)) and several unsafe High rules sit on destructive paths. 1/13/53/79 |
| Language responsibility | 4 | A clear table backed by tests; a few zones are uncovered ([LNG-01](#lng-01)). 0/0/1/12 |
| Spec corpus as an agent harness | 3 | Routing and budgets work; delivery state drifts ([COR-02](#cor-02), [COR-03](#cor-03)) and no rule says the owner wins over a disagreeing copy ([COR-85](#cor-85)). 0/3/13/76 |
| Skills and agent instructions | 3 | Small and mostly tested; the effect guard is incomplete ([SKL-01](#skl-01), [SKL-02](#skl-02); [COR-01](#cor-01) is counted under corpus). 0/0/1/18 |

### 2.5 The five actions that matter most

These are the audit's proposals. They follow the order of section 15.

1. **Require a durable before-state for positive no effect (package 1).** No effect may be read where a work-area mark or recorded identity exists, and the before-state is recorded when the marker is first proved. Loosened ownership must move the request version. This resolves [REC-01](#rec-01), [REC-11](#rec-11), [REC-45](#rec-45) and [REC-07](#rec-07), and it comes first because [REC-01](#rec-01) reinstalls over a live cluster. [REC-46](#rec-46) needs only corrected "never installed" wording and a new interruption row, and a recorded before-state is optional for it.
2. **Make the stated safety promises enforceable (packages 2 to 4).** Define exclusivity over the server and host, and make power commands refuse `controller.conflict` ([REC-09](#rec-09), [REC-10](#rec-10), [REC-06](#rec-06), [REC-74](#rec-74), [REC-41](#rec-41)). Refuse renewal of bound effect material ([REC-12](#rec-12), [CLI-22](#cli-22), [REC-76](#rec-76)). Record what each install transaction added, so uninstall proves what it removes ([REC-08](#rec-08), [REC-72](#rec-72), [REC-37](#rec-37), [REC-05](#rec-05), [REC-04](#rec-04)). Each package closes a High rule on a path that cannot be undone.
3. **One root-disk and erase rule, owned by machines.md (package 5).** Every other page then links to that rule, after the owner settles 15.3 (1) and (2). This resolves [API-03](#api-03), [API-08](#api-08), [REC-02](#rec-02), [API-38](#api-38), [API-121](#api-121) and [REC-15](#rec-15). It is the main contradiction on the physical destructive path.
4. **Guard agent effects by effect class in both runtimes (package 6).** AGENTS.md points to the catalog's Effects column, and the ask-rule test also checks the Codex rules. This resolves [COR-01](#cor-01), [SKL-01](#skl-01), [SKL-02](#skl-02) and [COR-36](#cor-36). It is small, and until it lands an agent can run an irreversible local command, such as an orphan-acknowledged context deletion, without being asked, and a Codex session has no tracked guard at all.
5. **Remove the cause of drift (packages 9 and 12).** Correct the stale copies or replace them with links ([SCO-01](#sco-01), [SCO-02](#sco-02), [DOC-01](#doc-01), [DOC-02](#doc-02), [DOC-03](#doc-03), [API-01](#api-01), [API-02](#api-02), [API-04](#api-04), [API-05](#api-05)). Derive or test the closed lists, and make delivering a decision include finding every copy ([CLI-16](#cli-16), [CLI-20](#cli-20), [API-44](#api-44), [API-46](#api-46), [CON-04](#con-04), [ARC-07](#arc-07), [ARC-28](#arc-28)). Section 15 places the completed-apply and handoff packages (7, 8) before these. This action matters because stale copies of this kind produced most of the High contradictions above.

### 2.6 After the baseline

Main moved while the audit ran. A separate pass read the first three commits,
the last of them a breaking change to the Environment API
([section 17](#17-after-the-baseline)). They do not change the verdict above. Of the 27 findings that cite text
or a subject they changed, 2 are resolved, 5 are partly resolved and 20 stand as stated. The text they added has
20 findings of its own (1 High, 5 Medium and 14 Low), whose ids begin
with NEW and which the counts above leave out.

One of them matters now. The new text promises that once a build raises a
client's minimum or default release, the next apply acquires the new release.
Under the lifecycle rule, an apply of a completed environment settles and
changes nothing, so the old client stays and nothing reports it ([NEW-01](#new-01)). The
fix is spec text plus one question for the owner, and it belongs with the
completed-apply rule, package 7 of section 15.

The three commits also test this section's first root cause on fresh text. The
slice that removed `latest` reached every live page that offered it. Within the
day it still left copies of its own new rules that disagree: three statements
of the advisory rule ([NEW-04](#new-04)), a delivery record and a design that misstate
which releases read a publisher's checksum ([NEW-14](#new-14)), a guide that calls the
delivered pins planned ([NEW-19](#new-19)) and a decision that claims a mirror route one
pinned client lacks ([NEW-17](#new-17)). Restating a rule on several pages produces this
on the day the rule lands, which is the case for linking to its owner instead.

## 3. Objectives, scope and domain

### 3.1 Verdict

`specs/project.md` states purpose, scope, non-goals and domain boundaries in one short page, and most of it can be tested. The committed portfolio is kept apart from the extension envelope, and only the owner may promote an envelope entry (specs/project.md:20-49). The fabric boundary (specs/project.md:51-61) and the handoff ownership rule (specs/project.md:90-101) are precise. The weak points are hand-copied lists and broad wording:

- The portfolio list leaves out M7 ([SCO-08](#sco-08)).
- The operator-utility list leaves out `machine cp` ([SCO-03](#sco-03)).
- The GitOps-boundary sentence is broader than D246 ([SCO-07](#sco-07)).
- The non-goal on running operator-authored code reads as permanent, while a reserved journey is kept open ([SCO-06](#sco-06)).

The coverage pages are where scope turns into evidence, and they lag behind owner decisions. Two High findings come from that lag: D224 ([SCO-01](#sco-01)) and D235 ([SCO-02](#sco-02)). The ledger rule also disagrees with the rows the owner accepted ([DOC-11](#doc-11)). None of this distorts the design. It does make the coverage pages an unreliable record of what is qualified.

The "Qualified tier" column is lane S02's own reading of the coverage pages and the ledger. It was not independently verified.

| KubeVirt machines | yes | committed | yes | in-tree; unrun | none |
| vSphere | no | committed | arm carried, refused | none | [SCO-05](#sco-05) |
| RHEL via Anaconda | implied | committed ("first") | yes | emulated, accepted | [SCO-08](#sco-08) |

OKD, other Ceph distributions and other operating systems sit in the envelope (specs/project.md:40-46) and show no mismatch.

The gap does not distort the general flow. Substrate selection is frozen once and dispatched through one port table (specs/substrates.md:41-56). Profiles are samples, not limits (specs/openshift-coverage.md:65-68). One defect sits at that seam: the three passages that say what a new arm touches disagree ([ARC-07](#arc-07)). vSphere, ACM, GitOps and GitLab are committed beyond the immediate portfolio by an owner decision, so they are not defects. The real cost is that coverage pages still describe tiers and gates the owner has already changed ([SCO-01](#sco-01), [SCO-02](#sco-02), [API-32](#api-32), [DOC-08](#doc-08)).

### 3.4 The day-0 and GitOps-handoff boundary

- **Additive apply (D211):** principled and bounded as a linked operation. The text around it erodes:
  - `context update` warns that apply refuses additive changes ([REC-03](#rec-03)).
  - `plan` previews a destroy over a completed apply ([CLI-01](#cli-01)).
  - A failed addition forces a full destroy, and nothing discloses this ([REC-63](#rec-63)).
  - The same-blocks proof for continuing an addition is undefined ([REC-64](#rec-64)).
  - The refusal wording disagrees with the changed-input refusal ([REC-91](#rec-91)).
- **Operator utilities:** principled. Each registers no operation, publishes no ownership and never repairs drift (specs/project.md:174-180). The list itself has drifted ([SCO-03](#sco-03)).
- **`diff`:** bounded, because it reads and never repairs. Its drift promise is wider than what it compares:
  - `diff --exit-code` misses add-on drift ([CLI-10](#cli-10)).
  - Some Ceph pool fields are never compared ([REC-77](#rec-77)).
  - The output points to `status`, which offers nothing for drift ([CLI-39](#cli-39)).
  - The lock table has no row for it ([REC-17](#rec-17)).
- **Update within release:** principled and bounded. It is installation work and never runs again after it completes (specs/managed-os.md:1603-1611). No finding.
- **Upgrade approval:** the approval is tolerated, never performed, through a proven replacement chain (specs/add-ons.md:471-489). It erodes in two places:
  - An approved upgrade decays to unknown, and the remedy offered is destroy ([REC-13](#rec-13)).
  - The GitLab package owns a chart version that an upgrade invalidates ([REC-14](#rec-14)).
  - The approver's name is also ambiguous ([SCO-09](#sco-09)).
- **Power commands:** bounded as operations that register no lifecycle operation and freeze no plan (specs/cli.md:1540-1545). The boundary leaks in four places:
  - The text says a stopped Machine "will reconcile" ([REC-81](#rec-81), against specs/cli.md:1542-1545).
  - Power may interrupt native effects of an incomplete operation ([CLI-55](#cli-55)).
  - Another context can drive a server held by a `bmc` reservation ([REC-10](#rec-10)).
  - The failure shape depends on how many Machines were named ([CLI-17](#cli-17)).

### 3.5 What to change

These are the audit's proposals. Each is the smallest change for the findings it names.

1. Bring coverage pages in line with owner decisions:
   - Physical rows say real hardware only (D224) ([SCO-01](#sco-01)).
   - The lab-physical shape and the kubevirt gate move to B730 ([SCO-02](#sco-02)).
   - Retire B776 ([API-32](#api-32)).
   - Replace the open OD21 and OD22 wording on the Ceph page with the D160 answers and the items that own the work ([DOC-08](#doc-08)).
2. Replace the B615-only exception in docs/acceptance.md with a general "Owner, by exception: &lt;unmet conditions>" form. Relabel the X290, X294 and X302 cells to it ([DOC-11](#doc-11)).
3. Reword specs/project.md:63-76 so that:
   - Bootwright installs the selected operators and sets up only what GitOps cannot do (D246 clause 1) ([SCO-07](#sco-07)).
   - The pools stay with Bootwright, as applied ([SCO-10](#sco-10)).
   - specs/add-ons.md says when a package owns an operand ([SCO-04](#sco-04)).
4. Fix the hand-copied lists:
   - Add `machine cp` to the utilities ([SCO-03](#sco-03)).
   - Add an M7 portfolio bullet and drop "first" from "first RHEL" ([SCO-08](#sco-08)).
5. Reword the code-runner non-goal to name the reserved CustomPlaybook shape and B102. Track realization items for the three "none tracked" rows ([SCO-06](#sco-06), [API-34](#api-34)).
6. Make the additive-apply wording agree with D211 in contexts.md and cli.md. Disclose that a failed addition cannot be fixed by editing input ([REC-03](#rec-03), [CLI-01](#cli-01), [REC-63](#rec-63), [REC-64](#rec-64)).
7. Bound the diff and upgrade promises to what is actually compared and proved ([CLI-10](#cli-10), [REC-77](#rec-77), [REC-13](#rec-13), [REC-14](#rec-14)).
8. Narrow vSphere in specs/substrates.md:58 to "refused until B99", and give the refusal its own item ([SCO-05](#sco-05)).
9. Name the upgrade approver without the word "owner". Replace "will reconcile" in the power section ([SCO-09](#sco-09), [REC-81](#rec-81)). Make a power command refuse a Machine whose `bmc:` key another context holds ([REC-10](#rec-10)).

## 4. Concept model and nomenclature

### 4.1 Verdict

The vocabulary is governed correctly and has drifted in places. The rule of one meaning, one owner page and a required qualifier is right (specs/glossary.md:3-4). The structural entries hold: block and step (specs/glossary.md:26-32), implementation and arm (specs/glossary.md:90-93), segment and Network (specs/glossary.md:61-66), and controller (specs/glossary.md:11-15). This section rests on 29 verified findings: 4 Medium and 25 Low. The Medium ones are the most serious. The glossary's Receipt entry asserts a closed "always" set that its owner pages contradict, and its Evidence entry links block evidence to a section that never defines it ([CON-06](#con-06)). The realized target contradicts itself ([CON-04](#con-04)). A Ceph node's site is authored in two places ([API-54](#api-54)). A security flag's name says the opposite of what it does ([CLI-08](#cli-08)). The rest are missing qualified entries and synonym clusters. Nearly every fix is a text edit or a rename, which costs little before 1.0.

### 4.2 Normative vocabulary

| Term | Definition (one normative sentence) | Owner page | Not to be confused with | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Context | A named, durable store of one lifecycle unit's frozen input, secrets and operation records (proposed). | contexts.md | bounded context; Go `context.Context` | fix [CON-19](#con-19) |
| Lifecycle unit | One context's complete validated Environment selection; the source directory is provenance only (proposed). | state-reconciliation.md:8-9 | input directory | fix [CON-15](#con-15) |
| Environment | The root object that selects a context's desired state; its name is a label, not an identity. | api/environment.md:3-6 | context; process environment | sound |
| Controller | The host that runs Bootwright, named in desired state by `spec.controller.machineRef`. | glossary.md:11-13 | management controller | sound |
| Management controller | A Machine's out-of-band endpoint: a BMC, or on an API-managed arm, the arm's management API endpoint and credential (proposed). | substrates.md | controller | fix [CON-04](#con-04) |
| Operation | Always qualified: a lifecycle operation is one registered apply or destroy; a port operation is one Go port method and the playbook it binds (proposed). | state-reconciliation.md; architecture.md | power or identity operation | fix [CON-18](#con-18) |
| Plan | The frozen block DAG that `plan.json` holds; `plan` is also the preview verb. | state-reconciliation.md:915-935 | in-memory operation plan | sound |
| Block | One frozen node of the plan DAG. | glossary.md:26-28 | step; block device | sound |
| Step | A block as a preview or result presents it; a status next step is a command, never a block (proposed). | glossary.md:26-32 | add-on step; `nextSteps` | fix [CON-16](#con-16) |

| Custody | The context keyring's holding of Secret versions and produced material (proposed). | secrets.md | retention | fix [CON-30](#con-30) |
| Native-side retention | Material a native side keeps, with what may reach it and what removes it. | secrets.md:413-442 | custody | sound |

The lanes also recorded the following terms as undefined or overloaded, but no verified finding backs them: Machine, node, host, provider host and the Ceph "runtime" and "core" profiles (lane S04); registry, port, role, adapter and protocol plugin (lane S05); refusal, proof, identity, lock, keyring and advisory (lane S06). The audit proposes adding qualified entries for these terms in the same glossary pass.

The realized target's placement does not become "reach Machine" ([CON-21](#con-21)). The Go package `clusterobjects/driver` keeps its name ([CON-28](#con-28)). The Ceph refusal codes are split into new codes, not renamed ([REC-126](#rec-126)).

### 4.4 Naming rules for future kinds and fields

1. Each term has one meaning and one owner page. A word with several senses takes its qualifier wherever two senses meet. A new term enters the glossary with its owner link in the same change. Stated at specs/glossary.md:3-4.
2. An "always" list in the glossary names every sense the owner pages use, each with an owner link. A new sense is added to the list in the same change. New ([CON-06](#con-06), [CON-24](#con-24)).
3. A kind name is a PascalCase noun that abbreviates only an established acronym. Stated at specs/api.md:370-371.
4. Fields, arms and Bootwright enum values are lowerCamel. Native values keep their spelling. Stated at specs/api.md:372-375.
5. A field naming a Bootwright object ends in `Ref` or `Refs`. Stated at specs/api.md:376-378. A nested reference names its target class, as in `secondaryNetworkRef`. New ([API-81](#api-81)).
6. `management: managed|external` says who operates a shared service. Stated at specs/api.md:379-381. `provided` says who realizes an object, and api.md lists every `provided` field by name. New ([API-141](#api-141)).
7. A fact has one authored field, and other objects show it only in effective state. New ([API-54](#api-54)).
8. A union selects by presence arm or enum, and "variant" names either kind of alternative. Stated at specs/api.md:309-346; the definition is new ([CON-26](#con-26)).
9. A flag that plays one role has one spelling across commands. Stated at specs/cli/commands.md:73-75. A selector of the command's own sub-parts stays singular. New ([CLI-58](#cli-58)). `-f` always means desired-state input. New ([CLI-07](#cli-07)).
10. A flag or member name states what it does. New ([CLI-08](#cli-08), [CLI-57](#cli-57)).
11. A name does not borrow a native or industry term with a different meaning, such as IPI, TOFU or OLM's `spec.name`; a kind that keeps such a name says how it differs. New ([ARC-84](#arc-84), [CLI-08](#cli-08), [API-108](#api-108), [API-68](#api-68)).
12. A vendor is a distribution, never a provider. New ([CON-23](#con-23)).
13. A playbook is named `<domain>/<capability>_<operation>.yml`, and a role `<domain>_[<implementation>_]<capability>`. Stated at specs/architecture.md:818-819. The playbook's capability token equals its role's, and a second implementation adds the implementation token. New ([ARC-65](#arc-65), [ARC-47](#arc-47)).
14. A name in a general position (registry accessor, port argument) names a domain fact, never an installer or a single arm's protocol. New ([ARC-58](#arc-58), [ARC-51](#arc-51)).
15. A new diagnostic code may be added, and an existing code keeps its meaning. Stated at specs/cli/output.md:1106-1108.

## 5. Desired-state API

### 5.1 Grammar verdict

The authoring grammar is sound. Decoding is strict, null is never a fallback, and explicit empties survive into effective state. The catalog, naming and family registry each have one owner and a test. Omission, null and empty have one meaning each.

It falls short in three places:

- **Rules and tests out of step.** The reference test cannot see two untyped references ([API-10](#api-10)). The union rule's wording covers more than its test checks ([API-09](#api-09)). The reference rule calls one external reference the sole one, but there are two ([API-11](#api-11)).
- **Truthfulness.** Some admitted fields always refuse at plan with no tracking item ([API-07](#api-07), [API-30](#api-30), [API-34](#api-34)), and the unrealized warning fires when no refusal would follow ([API-35](#api-35)).
- **Rule text duplicated across pages.** Field-level parity between schema and page is nearly clean. The prose rules around the fields are restated on two or three pages, and the copies drift ([REC-02](#rec-02), [API-17](#api-17), [API-42](#api-42)).

None of these defects needs a new abstraction. Each fix is a rename, a sentence or a reshape, and before 1.0 a rename costs little.

| Element | Verdict | What is right | What to fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Envelope and metadata | adequate | One version, closed metadata, one name rule for every kind (specs/api.md:232-257) | [API-60](#api-60) |
| YAML decoding | good | Refuses duplicates, aliases, tags and nulls with stable codes; null is always `api.type` (specs/api.md:110-118, 144-149) | [API-58](#api-58) |
| References | needs work | Typed classes held by a suffix test (specs/api.md:293-300) | [API-10](#api-10), [API-11](#api-11), [API-56](#api-56) |
| Unions | needs work | One rule decides arm or enum, with a named test (specs/api.md:311-318) | [API-09](#api-09), [CON-26](#con-26) |
| Collections and enablement | good | Named sets are `[]{name}`; `enabled` only where omission differs from false; `management` fixed (specs/api.md:348-364) | none |
| Naming rules | good | lowerCamel, native spellings exempt and tested, one-value fields need a consumer (specs/api.md:366-383) | [API-64](#api-64) |
| Kind catalog and family registry | adequate | Catalog row, order and page row tested; selection fields named by category (specs/api.md:385-391, 407-420) | [API-59](#api-59) |
| Graph validation | adequate | On a name collision no value wins and every side is diagnosed (specs/api.md:473-475) | [API-59](#api-59) |
| Defaults, normalization, effective state | adequate | Whole-value lists, arm protection, no I/O (specs/api/environment.md:259-325); empties preserved (specs/api.md:530-536); canonical order (specs/api.md:573-599) | [API-56](#api-56), [API-61](#api-61), [API-63](#api-63), [API-113](#api-113), [API-115](#api-115) |
| Native and implementation-shaped fields | adequate | Exact open points, integers kept exact, an open field never opens its container (specs/api.md:601-617) | [API-07](#api-07), [API-62](#api-62), [API-118](#api-118), [ARC-39](#arc-39), [ARC-44](#arc-44) |
| Input discovery and selection | adequate | Fixed inclusive ceilings, deterministic counting (specs/api/input.md:93-152) | [API-12](#api-12), [API-13](#api-13), [API-57](#api-57) |
| Unrealized and reserved surface | adequate | Rows are data in `api/v1alpha1`, held to warning and plan refusal by a test (specs/api.md:39-48) | [API-30](#api-30), [API-34](#api-34), [API-35](#api-35), [API-96](#api-96), [API-97](#api-97), [API-114](#api-114), [REC-80](#rec-80) |
| Schema-to-page parity | adequate | Field names, types and enums match (specs/api/environment.md:23-34; specs/ceph-resources.md:317-329); emit order stated (specs/api/infrastructure-services.md:65-74) | [REC-02](#rec-02), [API-16](#api-16), [API-17](#api-17), [API-25](#api-25), [API-26](#api-26), [API-31](#api-31), [API-42](#api-42), [API-43](#api-43), [API-44](#api-44), [API-116](#api-116), [API-117](#api-117), [API-119](#api-119) |

Lane D01a compared every field of seven Go files with their four pages and found no field-level mismatch. Lane D01b found the same for services, clusters and add-ons. These are the auditors' own counts. Most parity defects listed above concern rules and prose. The exceptions are CephCluster paths with no row on their page ([API-26](#api-26)) and a schema range the page omits ([API-116](#api-116)). The two High findings sit in this layer:

- **[API-07](#api-07).** A custom CRUSH device class is documented and validated, yet always refused at plan.
- **[REC-02](#rec-02).** The pages disagree on whether erase must list the root disk. X320 under D239 made the root optional, so the passages that require it are stale and no item tracks them.

#### Grammar changes that matter most

These are the audit's proposals. Each one is the smallest change that resolves the findings it names.

**1. Make the union and reference rules say what their tests enforce ([API-09](#api-09), [API-10](#api-10), [API-11](#api-11), [CON-26](#con-26)).**

- **Unions.** The smallest fix is wording: make rule 1 say "a block of its own", and add a sentence stating that an enum may gate scalar fields ([API-09](#api-09)). Align the glossary's definition of a variant with that rule ([CON-26](#con-26)). Both schemas and the union test stay unchanged, because the enum pattern is documented and admission-enforced. A presence-union reshape of the two schemas is only an owner preference, sketched below, and the audit does not recommend it.
- **References.** Type the untyped references, and list the external ones in `specs/api.md` instead of calling one the "sole" external reference.

```text
# optional reshape (BMC virtual media)
tls:
  trust: importCertificate
  removeCertificateAfterBoot: true
# after
tls:
  trust:
    importCertificate:
      removeAfterBoot: true      # omission selects importCertificate

# optional reshape (endpoint source)
source: {type: loadBalancer, loadBalancerRef: edge-lb}
# after (address stays an endpoint field)
source: {loadBalancer: {loadBalancerRef: edge-lb}}

# before (CephNFSExport, stretch tiebreaker)
serviceID: files
tiebreaker: {node: n3, site: c}
# after
serviceRef: files                # bare ID, type fixed by the field
tiebreaker: {nodeRef: n3, site: c}
```

The site fields are not part of this fix, because api.md never classes site names as references ([API-10](#api-10)).

**2. Make every admitted field truthful about plan ([API-07](#api-07), [API-30](#api-30), [API-34](#api-34), [API-35](#api-35)).**

- Every unrealized row names an item, and the test fails on an empty item.
- A conditional refusal says when it applies.
- A field that validates but always refuses gets a Not yet met line and an item. [API-07](#api-07) is the case: `crush_device_class` at spec or path level.
- D183 keeps `spec.steps` as validated surface. The owner decides whether `spec.inputs` and `addonConfigs` leave v1alpha1 or refuse at admission ([API-30](#api-30)).

```text
# before (unrealized row, as data)
- kind: ClusterAddon
  path: $.spec.inputs              # item: none tracked
# after
- kind: ClusterAddon
  path: $.spec.inputs
  item: B<parked>                  # required, non-empty
  # no new field: the warning text states the condition
```

The warning text changes from "so plan refuses it" to "so plan refuses it where it is selected" ([API-35](#api-35)).

**3. Never rewrite authored input, and keep one home for each default ([API-56](#api-56), [API-63](#api-63), [API-61](#api-61)).**

- A sole data pool with `default: false` refuses instead of being silently flipped to `true`.
- `defaults.Environment` goes away. It is a second home for every field of a singleton.
- The repeated bypass list becomes a fact of the Proxy service, not of each consumer.

```text
# before
dataPoolRefs: [{name: files-data, default: false}]   # becomes true
spec:
  defaults:
    Environment: {controller: {machineRef: controller}}
# after
dataPoolRefs: [{name: files-data, default: false}]   # api.invariant
spec:
  controller: {machineRef: controller}               # defaults.Environment: unknown key
# Proxy (API-61)
kind: Proxy
spec: {noProxy: [<bypass entries>]}                  # consumers inherit it whole
```

The recommendation for [API-61](#api-61) rejects a general `spec.fleet` block. That block would cut across per-consumer applicability rules.

**4. State each cross-page rule once and link to it ([REC-02](#rec-02), [API-17](#api-17), [API-42](#api-42), [API-43](#api-43), [API-44](#api-44), [API-16](#api-16)).**

| Rule | Proposed owner | Resolves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Erase lists the root disk only when the policy names it (D239, X320) | `specs/state-reconciliation.md`, the named owner; align `ceph.md`, `m2.md` | [REC-02](#rec-02) |
| Disk serial-number grammar | `specs/api/machines.md#bmc-and-root-device-shape` | [API-17](#api-17) |
| SSH credential pairs, including `nodeSSH` | one matrix with refusal codes in `specs/secrets.md` or the environment access section | [API-42](#api-42) |
| Install-gateway prefix and equality checks | `specs/api/machines.md` | [API-43](#api-43) |
| Native listener list, adding NVMe-oF | `specs/api/ceph.md` | [API-44](#api-44) |
| KubeVirt arm field table | `specs/api/machines.md`, out of `deferred/` | [API-16](#api-16) |

Smaller fixes need no grammar change:

- Give metadata labels one stated planning effect, or remove them until a consumer exists ([API-60](#api-60), P19).
- Add a one-sentence remedy for the `%YAML` directive ([API-58](#api-58)).
- Fix the scope wording "Environment's directory" ([API-57](#api-57)).
- Name which "selected" each condition means ([API-12](#api-12)).
- Extend the omitted-root refusal to `hostClusterRef` and `CephReplication` ends ([API-13](#api-13)).

### 5.2 Kinds: environment, secrets, machines, networks, operating systems and services

Verdict: the core of these kinds is sound. The weak point is drift around one physical disk. Secret, NetworkConfig and the destructive-path rules on Machine are specified rigorously. Four High findings sit here. Three are about disks or provider names on Machine and InfraProvider ([API-02](#api-02), [API-03](#api-03), [API-08](#api-08)), and one is the Entitlement registration scope ([API-01](#api-01)). Two more High findings fall on these kinds' consumers: the erase-root rule ([REC-02](#rec-02)) and SSH-arm coordination ([REC-06](#rec-06)). Five of the six are spec text that lags a decision already delivered or made (D239/X320, X48, D183/D186/D188); [API-01](#api-01) is a kind page that lags the managed-OS registration rule. All six are fixed by spec text alone. The services share one good flat pattern, but at the access surface it splits into five external shapes ([ARC-41](#arc-41)). They also carry several fields that can only hold their default or that do nothing ([API-21](#api-21), [API-75](#api-75), [API-80](#api-80)).

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

Two findings have no single row. [ARC-02](#arc-02) covers the missing Implementations part of the services selection section. [REC-22](#rec-22) covers loopback SSH placement. One shared role realizes Proxy, DNSServer and NTPServer from a fixed table (specs/infrastructure-services.md:590-593), which keeps a new daemon kind cheap.

#### Recommended shapes

These are the audit's proposals, most valuable first. Each one follows the final recommendation of the findings it resolves and is kept to the smallest change.

**1. One root-disk rule, owned by the Machine page.** Five passages on four pages still allow only two forms for a physical root. D239 admitted a third form, a proved logical volume with `bootVolume` as the default. The erase owner also still requires the root to be listed, which D239/X320 made optional ([API-03](#api-03), [API-08](#api-08), [REC-02](#rec-02)). The serial-declared root target is keyed by serial and size on two pages and by serial alone on a third, which is a wording gap ([API-121](#api-121)). The WWN form is spelled one way for the managed OS and another for the agent installer ([API-38](#api-38)). The serial grammar is stated in four places, and the API page says only "non-empty" ([API-17](#api-17)).

```text
# before: machines.md:661, managed-os.md:1257, :1996, openshift-clusters.md:43,
#         state-reconciliation.md:2440 each restate:
root = deviceName /dev/disk/by-id/wwn-0x...  |  serialNumber + sizeBytes
erase policy: the approved root disk must be listed
# after: machines.md#bmc-and-root-device-shape alone states it; others link
substrate.baremetal.rootDevice:
  wwn: "0x<16|32 hex>"             # one WWN form; managed OS derives the by-id path
  | serialNumber: <1-256 of A-Za-z0-9._:+/=->  + sizeBytes
  | volumeRef: {...}  | bootVolume: {}   # default when no hint is given
eraseOnRemoval: root kept unless the policy names it
```

What it breaks: `hardware.rootDevice.deviceName` refuses on an installed physical Machine, so the physical Ceph example changes. The managed-OS `%pre` and the disk-safety rule gain the NAA arm. Moving the disk policies under `substrate.baremetal` is left as an owner question ([API-107](#api-107)).

**2. One endpoint concept for every service, in both modes.** External DNSServer and NTPServer use a scalar `address`, Registry a `url`, Proxy `connection.*`, and LoadBalancer `bindAddresses`. Every consumer therefore branches on management mode ([ARC-41](#arc-41)). The URL a consumer derives from a managed Proxy is stated only in a milestone item, not in the owning specs ([API-20](#api-20)). DNS and NTP `port` fields admit one value only ([API-80](#api-80)).

```text
# before
kind: Proxy        spec: {management: external,
                          connection: {httpProxy: http://p:3128, httpsProxy: http://p:3128}}
kind: DNSServer    spec: {management: external, address: 192.0.2.53, port: 53}
# after
kind: Proxy
spec:
  management: external
  endpoints: [{name: primary, url: http://p:3128}]
  connection: {trustBundleRef: proxy-ca}     # auth and trust stay service facts
kind: DNSServer
spec: {management: external, endpoints: [{name: primary, address: 192.0.2.53}]}
# consumer: {proxyRef: p, endpointRef: primary}  (normalizes when single)
# managed Proxy consumer URL: http://<endpoint address>:<port>, IPv6 bracketed
```

What it breaks: every authored external service object. `port` is no longer accepted on DNSServer and NTPServer. Rename LoadBalancer `bindAddresses` to `addresses`, not `endpoints`, because its values are literal VIPs ([API-78](#api-78)).

**3. The Proxy owns its bypass list.** A fleet proxy and its `noProxy` are restated in up to three places: two kind defaults and the controller Machine ([API-61](#api-61)). The bypass grammar also has circular owners ([API-49](#api-49)). The final recommendation rejects a generic `spec.fleet` block because it would cut across per-consumer applicability rules.

```text
# before: same list under defaults.OpenShiftCluster.install.proxy,
#         defaults.MachineInstallProfile.proxy and the controller Machine
proxy: {proxyRef: default, noProxy: [.example.com, 192.0.2.0/24]}
# after
kind: Proxy
spec: {management: external, ..., noProxy: [.example.com, 192.0.2.0/24]}
# consumer
proxy: {proxyRef: default}            # inherits noProxy as a whole value
proxy: {proxyRef: default, noProxy: [...]}   # an explicit list replaces it
```

What it breaks: nothing that is authored today. The multidc example shrinks to one list. Proxy-choice becomes the single owner of the entry kinds, and an OpenShift `host:port` entry refuses at validate ([API-49](#api-49)).

**4. Point the registration row at its repositories.** The repositories a registration applies are authored under `customizations`, away from `spec.subscription`, and the `entitlementRef` row does not point to them ([API-74](#api-74)). The final recommendation adds one clause to that row and leaves the field placement unchanged. The Entitlement page also says managed registration covers only virtual Machines, and the profile row omits the Satellite route ([API-01](#api-01)).

```text
# before
spec:
  subscription: {entitlementRef: rhel-sat}
  customizations:
    repositories:
      subscription: {enable: [rhel-9-baseos], disable: ["*"]}
# after
spec:
  subscription:
    entitlementRef: rhel-sat   # the row now names customizations.repositories.subscription
  customizations:
    repositories:
      subscription: {enable: [rhel-9-baseos], disable: ["*"]}
```

What it breaks: nothing, because the field placement is unchanged and only the `entitlementRef` row gains a clause. [API-01](#api-01) needs text only, in two sentences.

**5. Remove fields that can only hold their default or do nothing.** Each of these costs schema, validation and documentation and offers no choice. `additionalIngressHosts` is frozen and inert, with no `api.deferred` warning ([API-21](#api-21)). `ssh.passwordAuthentication` and `rhsm.connectToInsights` admit only `false` ([API-75](#api-75)). External ArtifactServer is refused dead surface ([API-77](#api-77)). `defaults.Environment` is a second home for the singleton's fields ([API-63](#api-63)).

```text
# before (all admitted)
kind: DNSServer  spec: {..., additionalIngressHosts: [a.example]}
customizations: {ssh: {passwordAuthentication: false}}
rhsm: {management: managed, connectToInsights: false}
kind: ArtifactServer  spec: {management: external, ...}
spec.defaults: {Environment: {controller: {machineRef: c}}}
# after: each refused as an unknown field or value, with a remedy;
#        a future journey re-adds its field under its own contract
```

What it breaks: examples and e2e templates that write `false`. The `api.unrealized` row for `connectToInsights` and the kind-default fragment rule for ArtifactServer go away. This is cheap before 1.0 (D169 precedent).

**6. Inject the default-route next hop from the Network.** The gateway is written in both the Network and every NetworkConfig template, and admission only cross-checks the two copies ([API-70](#api-70)). Every copy fails closed, so the cost is authoring effort, not divergent behaviour.

```text
# before
routes:
  config:
    - {destination: 0.0.0.0/0, next-hop-interface: nic0.120,
       next-hop-address: 198.51.100.65}
# after: an omitted next hop is injected from the assigned Network's gateway
routes:
  config:
    - {destination: 0.0.0.0/0, next-hop-interface: nic0.120}
```

What it breaks: nothing, because an authored value stays admitted and checked. `vlan.id` stays authored, since the interface name restates it anyway.

**7. Let the hosted-tree DVD be pinned.** The boot image can carry a checksum, but the DVD that supplies the installed packages cannot ([API-19](#api-19)).

```text
# before
packageSource:
  hostedTree: {fromMedia: local-media:rhel-9.8-dvd.iso, artifactServerEndpoint: {...}}
# after
packageSource:
  hostedTree:
    fromMedia: local-media:rhel-9.8-dvd.iso
    checksum: sha256:<digest>      # same grammar as MachineImage.spec.checksum
    artifactServerEndpoint: {...}
```

What it breaks: nothing. The field is optional, and the plan refuses a DVD whose record digest differs from the declared one.

**8. Give one meaning one name and one place.** Several names and placements mislead. The fleet key is named "remote machines access", and its heading promises install defaults it does not hold ([API-64](#api-64)). The third OS lifecycle has two names ([API-72](#api-72)). The libvirt arm still states a provider-name collision refusal that X48 retired ([API-02](#api-02)). The realized KubeVirt arm is documented on the "Refused machine arms" page ([API-16](#api-16)).

```text
# before
spec.remoteMachinesAccessKey: {keyRef: k}       # heading "...and install defaults"
"installer-provisioned" | "downstream-installed"  # one lifecycle, two names
api/machines.md -> deferred/machine-arms.md      # realized KubeVirt fields
# after
spec.fleetKey: {keyRef: k}                       # heading "Fleet key"
"installer-provisioned"                          # one name, machines.md:246-258
api/machines.md "### KubeVirt arm"               # beside "### Libvirt arm"
```

What it breaks: the field path wherever it is cited. The rename is cheap before 1.0. The `os.provided` boolean stays as it is, and a union waits for an owner decision on D240 clause 12.

### 5.3 Kinds: container clusters, storage, add-ons and reserved automation

The verdict: the safety contracts of these kinds are sound, and most of the defects are in their text. Refusal tables, ownership proofs, credential custody and exact OLM approval are written precisely and hold up. Three things fail. Passages left from earlier slices contradict delivered work ([DOC-01](#doc-01), [API-04](#api-04), [API-47](#api-47), [API-32](#api-32)). The Ceph admission page restates native vocabulary and has fallen behind it ([API-05](#api-05), [API-44](#api-44), [API-46](#api-46)). The admitted surface includes fields that have no consumer, or only one legal value ([API-30](#api-30), [API-86](#api-86), [API-88](#api-88)). Only four proposals change the input shape (shapes 1, 4, 5 and 7). Pre-1.0, each one is cheap.

| Kind | Verdict | Keep | Change (finding ids) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenShiftCluster | adequate | Refusal table tied to code by a named test (specs/openshift-clusters.md:106-112); `spec.nodes` is the only roster (specs/api/openshift-clusters.md:494-501) | [DOC-01](#doc-01), [API-04](#api-04), [API-22](#api-22), [API-23](#api-23), [API-24](#api-24), [ARC-03](#arc-03), [API-81](#api-81), [API-82](#api-82), [API-106](#api-106), [ARC-46](#arc-46), [REC-16](#rec-16), [CLI-02](#cli-02), [CLI-30](#cli-30) |
| CephCluster | needs work | Qualified native service identity; fixed secret-leaf registry (specs/ceph-native-api.md:768-785) | [API-05](#api-05), [API-25](#api-25), [API-26](#api-26), [ARC-04](#arc-04), [ARC-01](#arc-01), [API-44](#api-44), [API-46](#api-46), [API-83](#api-83), [API-84](#api-84), [API-10](#api-10), [API-45](#api-45), [API-123](#api-123), [API-124](#api-124), [API-125](#api-125), [DOC-08](#doc-08) |
