### 15.5 What the audit does not recommend

- Treating a channel change on an owned Subscription as an upgrade (L26-3). A change to an owned object is a destroy and a fresh apply (D153, D155). [REC-13](#rec-13) covers only an owner-approved upgrade on the declared chain.
- Adding a storage object to a completed environment without a destroy (A10-5). Day-0 scope keeps this out (D153, D211), and a new scenario is its own slice.
- A firmware default or a bare-metal profile (A05-4). D191 keeps firmware on the Machine, and the other shared fields already take kind defaults.
- Withdrawing private material after a failed physical install (L16-2, L17-2). D122 keeps it published until the next apply or a destroy.
- A narrower exit than the orphan-acknowledged delete for a lost target (X04-5). D38 settles this, and the decommissioned-tiebreaker case is tracked as B938.
- Storage-generic names for the Ceph consumer effect and field (R09-4, A11-7). D185 fixed the names, and generality waits for a second consumer (specs/architecture.md:37-43).
- A per-kind managed-service request, or a service-kind registry (R10-1, R10-3). D142 and D241 accept the version-move cost, and tests already fail on a missing kind.
- An installer port beyond Anaconda, or image boot in the machine port (A06-1, R07-1). Both are outside committed scope; the image paths are B99 and B1166.
- A registry-keyed `dependencyVersions` (R05-4). The closed schema rejects unknown tools.
- Moving the release-specific stretch commands out of ceph.md (L22-4). D196 and D200 chose them, and the version-specialization seam already exists.
- Gating M3 and M4 only on the immediate portfolio (S02-5). D183 answered Q89 with (a).
- From the findings' own recommendations: no `spec.fleet` block ([API-61](#api-61)); no admission refusal for missing erase coverage ([REC-15](#rec-15), D177); no rename of `--stage`, `--node` or `Network.spec.provided` (D151, D243, D240 clause 12); and no registry or port before a consumer exists (section 7.3).

## 16. Method and verification record

### 16.1 Baseline and material

The audit read a frozen export of commit `931cfb596`, so every citation
resolves to one text and no concurrent change could move a line. The export
left out `audits/`; `examples/wip/` and the local-only override file are
untracked and were therefore absent. Auditors read only the export and a set
of lookup aids built mechanically from it: an outline of every heading, the
size of every section, an index of the 247 decisions and of the 490 item
sections, every "Not yet met" line, and statistics over the tracked examples.
Lane records and finders' checks call the export SNAP and the aids AIDS.

Two registers were written first and used by every later judge: a one-line
register of each owner decision from D1 to D249 (seven extractors, one per
chunk of the decision log, with the count and the ids checked mechanically),
and a digest of 45 stated project principles with their citations.

### 16.2 The lanes

150 lanes read the material, each with ranges to read in full, one
lens, a cap on the candidates it could file, and the duty to try to refute its
own candidates before filing them. Each lane also recorded what its slice gets
right, a working table, every file and range it read, and the findings it
named and had no room to pursue.

| Group | Lanes | Model | What the lanes did |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| L | 26 | Opus | Read the reconciliation, safety and security pages section by section and judged every rule |
| X | 10 | Opus | Attacked the same rules by failure scenario across pages |
| A | 20 | Opus | The grammar, each family of kinds, four cold-read authoring tests, two benchmarks against reference APIs |
| C | 6 | Opus | The command tree, the lifecycle commands, the access utilities, the output contract, the documented operator journey |
| S | 7 | Opus | Scope and portfolio, a census of about sixty terms, names across surfaces |
| R | 12 | Opus | The architecture spec, leak hunts in the general specs and the general code, four extension dry runs, language responsibility |
| H | 4 | Opus, one Sonnet | Routing, retrieval paths, the "Not yet met" convention, the knowledge base |
| D | 14 | Opus, three Sonnet | Schema-to-page parity and drift sweeps between pages on one subject |
| G | 3 | Opus | Skills, runtime parity for Claude Code and Codex, the skill portfolio |
| E | 1 | Opus | The tracked examples |
| M | 32 | Sonnet | The milestone pages, chunk by chunk |
| Z | 15 | Opus | The second round ([section 16.5](#165-the-second-round)) |

The cap was eight candidates for most lanes, six for the scope and concept
lanes, three for the milestone chunks and ten for the lanes that pursued
findings left over from the first round.

### 16.3 Verification

Each candidate went to two agents that had not seen each other's work. A
refuter (Sonnet at high effort; Opus when the candidate claimed High or
Blocking) opened every citation, read the enclosing section, searched the
corpus for a passage that resolved the claim and ruled confirmed, narrowed or
refuted. A judge (Opus) read the decisions and tracked items that bear on the
subject, applied the principles digest, rated the severity by the definitions
of section 1, not by the finder's claim, and accepted, amended or rejected the
recommendation. Candidates their finder rated Low were verified in batches of
up to three. A split vote went to an arbiter (Opus at high effort; Fable where
either side rated High or Blocking), who had to cite the passages that decided
it.

| Outcome | Candidates |
| --- | ---: |
| Filed by the lanes | 869 |
| Confirmed by both verifiers | 795 |
| Split, then arbitrated | 50 |
| Confirmed in the end | 834 |
| Confirmed, and already recorded by an open item | 3 |
| Settled by a recorded decision | 11 |
| Refuted | 21 |
| Left unverified | 0 |

Verification changed more than it removed. Of the confirmed candidates, the
judges rated 364 lower than their finder had and 3 higher,
amended 686 recommendations and rejected 5. For
655 of them a verifier or an arbiter wrote a narrower claim than the
finder's, and section 12 prints that claim, except where the extent step of
section 16.4 restored the finder's.

### 16.4 Consolidation

**Duplicates.** Several lanes often found one defect: the same contradiction
reached from the API page, from the safety page, from a failure scenario and
from a cold read. Confirmed candidates were grouped by the file they cite, one
reader per group marked the candidates that state the same defect, and the
marks were merged across groups. 197 candidates were merged into
others, leaving 637 distinct findings; a merged entry lists the
candidates it absorbs. How often a finding was reached independently is in the
index of section 12.2.

**Third reading.** Every finding that stood at High or Blocking after merging
was read a third time, by an agent that had to re-derive it from the text and
demonstrate it: both sides of a contradiction, each step of an unsafe path,
the two readings of an ambiguity. Of 37 read, 31 held
as rated, 6 were lowered after arbitration and
0 were dropped.

**Extent.** The first verification counted a candidate as confirmed when the
refuter narrowed its claim and the judge confirmed it as its finder stated it,
and merging joined candidates whose judges had rated one defect differently.
Such an entry would print one verifier's claim under another's rating, beside
the finder's title and consequence. Each of the 95 Medium
findings in that state, or whose claim carried a verifier's remark, therefore
went to an arbiter (Opus at high effort). The arbiter decided from the text
which statement of the defect holds, rewrote the entry's title, claim,
consequence, recommendation and acceptance to fit it, and rated it.
32 kept the finder's claim in full and 63 took
a narrower one; 57 stayed Medium, 37 were lowered
to Low, one ([REC-41](#rec-41)) was raised to High and none was dropped. A ruling that
dropped a finding or raised it to High needed a final arbiter (Fable) to
agree; only [REC-41](#rec-41) came to that, and the final arbiter agreed. The claims of
21 Low findings that carried a verifier's remark were restated
(Sonnet at high effort) with their rating unchanged. A finding lowered in
this step keeps its id, so within an area the ids no longer follow severity
exactly. An entry settled in this step prints the passages its arbiter cited
first. The counts of this report are those after this step.

**Citations.** Every citation of every confirmed candidate was checked
mechanically against the export: 3263 citations, of which
2120 matched word for word at the cited lines, 1106
matched once Markdown markup, punctuation and line wrapping were ignored,
27 were found at other lines of the file and corrected, and
10 were not found and were dropped as evidence. No finding lost
all its citations. Quotes longer than 25 words were cut to their first 25, and
a link inside a quote keeps its text and loses its target.

### 16.5 The second round

**Findings named and not pursued.** The lanes named 451 further points their
caps left no room for. Four lanes went through that list, pursued the points
that looked Medium or higher as candidates of their own, and left the rest;
the list itself is not in this report, and the points not pursued were not
verified.

**Critics.** Two critics then read across all lanes. One compared the coverage
ledger and the verified findings with the nine questions; the other read every
lane's assessment for causes no single slice could see. They proposed eleven
further examinations, and all eleven ran as lanes: the propagation of
decisions D235 to D249; observation and completion predicates across every
capability; exclusivity between contexts at every entry point; an inventory of
produced and retained secret material; the owner map for rule classes that
span pages; whether the guards the specs name prove the invariants they are
said to hold; the procedures agents follow outside the skills; refusal codes
as one registry; the traceability of two kinds from field to diff; time and
bounds across domains; and the site topology end to end.

The second round filed 75 candidates, verified and merged like
the first; 56 of the findings in section 12 come from it alone.
The critics' themes are the basis of section 2.3.

### 16.6 Writing the report

Sections 3 to 11 and section 15 were each drafted by one writer from the
verified findings of its subject and the lane records, under the rule that a
statement of a defect must name a verified finding. An independent reviewer
then checked each draft against the findings and corrected it. Section 2 was
drafted the same way after the others and edited by the orchestrating session.
The catalog of section 12, the ledger of section 13, the tables of section 14
and Appendix A were rendered mechanically from the verified data. Section 1,
this section and the introductions were written by the orchestrating session.
Section 17 was rendered from the data of its own pass, except its opening and
sections 17.1, 17.6 and 17.7, which the orchestrating session wrote, as it
wrote section 2.6.

The sections were drafted before the extent step of section 16.4. Afterwards
each section that cites a restated finding was compared with the new entries
by an editor (Sonnet at high effort; Opus for sections 2 and 15) and by an
independent reviewer (Opus), and only the sentences that the new entries no
longer supported were replaced: 64 replacements in
16 parts of the report.

### 16.7 After the baseline

Main moved while the audit ran. The audit proper was not run again. A separate
pass covered the first three commits, `53da37dcc`, `a7fee546c` and `aa46736e7`
([section 17.1](#171-the-three-commits)). It did three things, and section 17
reports its results apart from the findings of the audited commit.

- **Citations.** Every citation of every finding was checked mechanically
  against `aa46736e7`: 11 quotes of 5
  findings are no longer in their files.
- **Status.** 27 findings were read against the later text:
  those with a quote gone, those with a citation inside or within two lines of
  a changed hunk, and those that cite a changed file and name a subject the
  commits changed. One verifier (Opus) placed each finding as resolved, partly
  resolved, partly resolved, changed or standing, with citations of the later
  commit. A second (Sonnet at high effort; Opus for a High finding) tried to
  refute the result. An arbiter was to decide any disagreement, and none
  arose.
- **New text.** Five lanes (Opus) read the text the commits added or changed,
  as it stands at `aa46736e7`, with the lookup aids rebuilt for that commit
  and the decision register extended to D251. Their 31
  candidates went through the verification of section 16.3; one reader marked
  the duplicates among them and against the catalog; and each finding that
  stood at High or Blocking was read a third time. 20 findings
  resulted.

The pass read the changed text and what it depends on, not the corpus again. A
finding that cites no changed text was not re-read, and a passage the commits
left stale far from the text they changed can only have been found by the one
lane that swept for stale copies. Commits after `aa46736e7` were not read;
[section 17.7](#177-limits-of-this-pass) names the two that landed while the
pass ran.

### 16.8 Limits

- **Text against text.** The audit judged the contracts as written. Code was
  opened as evidence of how a concept materializes and to check a specific
  claim; no function body was reviewed, and no build, test or Bootwright
  command was run by an auditor. Whether the code does what a sound rule says,
  or avoids what an unsound rule permits, is outside this audit; code audit 003
  covers that ground.
- **One lane left its read-only bounds.** Lane E01 wrote a list of checksums
  of the tracked example files to a temporary file outside the export, against
  its instructions. The file held only the paths and checksums of tracked
  files, and it was removed. The lane also noted that the export held the
  untracked examples directory. It did not: the lane's commands, checked
  afterwards, ran inside the export and only excluded that path. A mechanical
  check found in this report none of the names that exist only in that
  directory.
- **Working tables are not verified.** Only candidates went through
  verification. A row of a lane's working table that names no finding id, and
  the counts taken from those tables in sections 7 to 11, are the auditors'
  own.
- **Severity is a judgment.** It was assigned by one judge per candidate under
  written definitions. It was re-read for every High and Blocking finding and
  for the Medium findings whose verifiers disagreed about extent. The other
  Medium ratings and the Low ratings were not re-read.
- **Counts depend on merging.** Two readers could draw the line between one
  defect with several instances and several defects differently. The catalog
  lists the candidates each entry absorbs.
- **Samples.** The knowledge base and the tracked examples were sampled, as
  section 13 states. Claims about them are limited to the pages read.
- **External systems.** Three lanes consulted public documentation of
  reference APIs and of the two agent runtimes. Statements about those systems
  are marked as verified on a named page or as unverified, and nothing in the
  report rests on an unverified one.
- **Token figures are estimates.** They are bytes divided by four.
- **Earlier audits.** The cross-check of section 14 read the consolidated
  reports of audits 001 to 003, not their source reports. No sibling report of
  audit 004 existed.

finding, judging, merging, writing and reviewing on Opus; and Fable only to
arbitrate a disagreement about a High or Blocking finding. The table counts
the agents' tokens, not those of the orchestrating session.

### 16.10 Checks on this report

The assembled report was validated mechanically before it was committed: 489 headings and 1301 anchors, every internal link resolves, every table row has as many cells as its header, every finding id cited in the text exists in the catalog or in section 17.3, no code fence is left open, no local path appears, and none of the names that exist only in the untracked examples directory appears. YAML sketches are fenced as text, because the repository's style test parses every YAML fence it tracks.

The repository's gates ran on the commit that adds this report, and their commands and results are recorded in that commit's message, as the commit convention requires.

### 17.3 Findings in the text the later commits added

Five lanes read the text the three commits added or changed, as it stands at `aa46736e7`: N01, client releases after X342: the Environment API and the controller stage; N02, acquisition origins and the controlled-network design; N03, operator and developer documentation after the three commits; N04, propagation: what the three commits left stale, and their milestone records; N05, attack: the pinned client table over time and under failure. Each could file a defect in that text, or a passage elsewhere that the commits made false or left stale; a defect that already stood at the audited commit in untouched text was outside the pass. <a id="new-01"></a>

#### NEW-01 Next apply after a table refresh settles; it does not acquire the new default

High; contradiction; changes spec-text; effort M; source N05-1.

**Claim.** environment.md:110-111 and controller.md:815-818 (delivered in X342), along with D250 (17) and the deferred design, say that a later build's next apply picks up the new default client release. Under the lifecycle unit, an apply over a completed apply's unchanged input settles: it plans nothing and reaches no host, and nothing exempts a tool-table move. An earlier build's incomplete apply also cannot be continued once the default moves. So the new default or a raised minimum reaches a completed environment only through a destroy followed by a fresh apply. No page says so, and no status or tracked item reports a proved client below the build's minimum.

**Evidence.**

- `specs/controller.md:816-818`: "an apply of a context that retained an older release acquires the new default, because a different release is a different request."
- `specs/api/environment.md:110-111`: "a later build's new default is a new release its next apply acquires."
- `specs/state-reconciliation.md:571-571`: "an 'apply' of the unchanged input settles without effect"
- `specs/state-reconciliation.md:53-54`: "an 'apply' repeated over the unchanged input its completed apply froze, while every block of that apply's plan is 'done'"
- `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:141-142`: "a new build raises both, and the next apply replaces a retained release below the new minimum."
- `specs/milestones/backlog.md:7879-7879`: "'latest' goes; the next apply replaces a retained release below a raised"

**Consequence.** Scenario: build A installs Helm 4.3.1 and the OpenShift environment completes. An advisory reaches 4.3.1, and build B raises the minimum and default to 4.3.2. The operator runs `bootwright apply` with build B, as the spec promises will replace the client. The apply reports `done`, changes nothing, and 4.3.1 stays the client every later block runs. A destroy under B runs the same 4.3.1, because it is located from the apply's proof and the minimum is checked only when an apply plans.

**Recommendation.** Rewrite controller.md:815-818, environment.md:110-111 and deferred/controlled-network.md:140-142 to say: the tool table governs only the plan of a fresh apply. A settling apply and a removal run the release the completed apply proved, even when it is below this build's minimum. A continuation registered by an earlier build refuses. A retained release therefore moves only after a destroy and a fresh apply. Leave D250 (17) as the owner wrote it. Add a parked item, or an owner question that cites D250 (17), covering two things: how a running environment takes a raised minimum without a destroy, and a status/diff report of each proved client below the build's minimum.

**Acceptance.** No passage says a next apply acquires or replaces a retained client without saying it is a fresh apply after a removal. controller.md states what a settling apply, a destroy and an earlier build's continuation each do with a below-minimum retained client. A backlog item or decision tracks reporting or replacing it.

**Decisions and principles.** Decisions read by the judge: D250, D251. Principles applied: none recorded. Finder's check: Read D250 (12), (17) and D251 at backlog.md:7796-7901. (17) asserts the replacement but does not address the settle rule. Read the lifecycle unit at state-reconciliation.md:25-75 and row 571: a completed apply's unchanged input settles, and nothing exempts a tool-table move. The table is not desired-state input, so the input is unchanged.

**Verification.** refuter narrowed; judge confirmed at High; recommendation amended by the judge; third reading: holds.

**Demonstration (third reading).** Build A installs Helm at its default, and the environment's apply completes. An advisory reaches that release, so build B raises the minimum and the default. The Environment omits the release, and the table is not desired-state input, so the input is unchanged. environment.md says B's "next apply acquires" the new default. Under the settled-verb rule (state-reconciliation.md:51-58, row 571), B's apply reports `done` without planning, registering or reaching a host. Every later block keeps running the proved old client (controller.md:736-742). The operator guide's path (794-799) is destroy, then a fresh apply. So one state, B applying a completed context, gets two answers: "acquires" and "settles". diff --observe marks the controller block "plans differently" and names the old build as the remedy, but nothing names a client below the minimum.

<a id="new-02"></a>

#### NEW-02 Mirror ordering is cyclic for a mirror on a Bootwright-installed Machine

Medium; contradiction; changes spec-text; effort M; source N02-1; related [NEW-13](#new-13).

**Claim.** In 'Filling the mirror', the controller block waits for the mirror's blocks, and every other block still waits for the controller block. A mirror on a Machine whose operating system Bootwright installs waits for that installation, and that installation is one of the other blocks, so the three clauses form a cycle. With the declaration present, the page gives the public-origin clients and the emulated BMC image that the installation needs only the mirror as their origin.

**Evidence.**

- `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:123-124`: "the controller block waits for the mirror's blocks, and every other block still waits for the controller block."
- `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:127-129`: "A mirror on a Machine whose operating system Bootwright installs waits for that installation, whose own media come from an artifact server elsewhere"
- `specs/state-reconciliation.md:1077-1079`: "When a plan contains a controller block, every other block in that plan depends on it, because the clients it installs are what the other ..."

**Consequence.** With a KubeVirt or vSphere provider, installing the mirror Machine needs `virtctl` or `govc`. Both are public-origin tools that only the mirror may serve, so the 'Mirror on its own Machine' row for a host Bootwright installs (D250 (14)) cannot be planned as written.

**Recommendation.** In 'Filling the mirror', limit the clause 'every other block still waits for the controller block' to blocks outside the mirror host's own realization chain. Add one sentence saying how that chain gets its artifacts and in what order. The chain is the provider clients for the mirror host, its BMC image, its installation, and the Registry and ArtifactServer images. Say that these are acquired directly, ordered after a first controller block that holds only the clients the chain selects.

**Acceptance.** specs/deferred/controlled-network.md 'Filling the mirror' names the mirror host's bootstrap set, its origin and an ordering with no cycle for a mirror on a Machine that Bootwright installs.

**Decisions and principles.** Decisions read by the judge: D163, D250, D251. Principles applied: none recorded.

**Verification.** refuter narrowed; judge narrowed at Medium; recommendation amended by the judge; extent arbitrated: a narrower claim at Medium.

<a id="new-03"></a>

#### NEW-03 An agent can write and commit its own vulnerability exception unreviewed

Medium; unsafe-rule; changes agent-guidance; effort S; source N02-6.

**Claim.** D250 (15) lets a coding agent write an exception and proceed, so agent authorship is decided. The defect is that 'reviewed' (design lines 153-155, B1244 outcome, D250 (9)/(15)) names no reviewer, no review record and no point where review is required. The finding procedure (lines 162-173) has no review step at all, so the 'reviewed exception' rule reads as a check that nothing performs.

**Evidence.**

- `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:153-155`: "A reviewed exception is the only way past, and it ships with the SBOM as a VEX statement."
- `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:168-170`: "add one exception naming the advisory, the component and release, why the build is not affected or why no fix exists, and an expiry"
- `specs/milestones/backlog.md:7867-7867`: "The vulnerability gate fails "with reviewed exception""

**Consequence.** An agent's reachability judgment ('Bootwright never reaches the affected code') becomes a shipped VEX statement 'not affected' without a second party, for up to 90 days. That is the bypass the gate exists to prevent. A downstream scanner then trusts a claim no human checked.

**Recommendation.** Give the exception record a review state, for example `{advisory, component, release, justification, expires, proposedBy, reviewedBy?}`. An agent writes it without `reviewedBy`. `make build` passes a proposed exception for development builds and prints it, while a release build and the VEX emission refuse one without `reviewedBy`. State in step 3 that the owner sets `reviewedBy` and that the agent never does.

**Acceptance.** The design and B1244 define who reviews and how the review is recorded. B1244's exit evidence adds a release build that refuses an unreviewed exception.

**Decisions and principles.** Decisions read by the judge: D250, D251. Principles applied: none recorded.

**Verification.** refuter narrowed; judge narrowed at Medium.

<a id="new-04"></a>

#### NEW-04 Pages give different rules for raising a client's minimum after an advisory

Medium; contradiction; changes spec-text; effort S; source N04-3, N03-2.

**Claim.** specs/controller.md 815-816 and specs/deferred/controlled-network.md 140-141 say that when an advisory reaches a default or a minimum, the build raises both to the first fixed release. docs/development.md 296-297 and the deferred finding procedure at controlled-network.md 166-167 raise the minimum only when the advisory reaches it, and the guide also says never above the default. Neither "raises both" sentence says the default stays when it is already above the fixed release.

**Evidence.**

- `specs/controller.md:815-816`: "when an advisory reaches a default or a minimum, that build raises both to the first fixed release"
- `docs/development.md:296-297`: "Raise a minimum only for an advisory that reaches the releases below it, and never above its default."
- `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:141-167`: "a new build raises both ... raise the default, and the minimum when the advisory reaches it, to the first fixed release"

**Consequence.** The rules agree only while a client's minimum equals its default, as in the first table (D251 (2)). Once a later refresh raises a default and leaves its minimum, the pages disagree. Take minimum 1.0.0, default 1.5.0, and an advisory on 1.3.0 to 1.5.0 fixed in 1.5.1.

**Recommendation.** Let specs/controller.md#the-tool-table own one rule: "When an advisory reaches the default, that build raises the default to at least the first fixed release. When it reaches the minimum, that build raises the minimum to the first fixed release, never above the default. No refresh lowers a default." Use it in place of the "raises both" sentences at specs/controller.md:815-816 and specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:140-141. Make docs/development.md:296-297 and procedure step 1 at controlled-network.md:166-167 link to that section instead of restating it.

**Acceptance.** A grep for "raises both" across specs/ and docs/ finds nothing. specs/controller.md#the-tool-table states, in one place, when the default and when the minimum move, and that no refresh lowers a default.

**Decisions and principles.** Decisions read by the judge: D152, D250, D251. Principles applied: none recorded.

**Verification.** refuter narrowed; judge confirmed at Medium; recommendation amended by the judge; extent arbitrated: a narrower claim at Medium; merged from 2 candidates (N04-3 Medium, N03-2 Medium).

**Merged candidates.** The entry states the defect as its clearest candidate put it; these raised the same defect, sometimes a further instance or aspect of it: N03-2: Three pages give different rules for raising a minimum after an advisory.

<a id="new-05"></a>

#### NEW-05 Guide says Red Hat catalogs need nothing, but default catalogs carry public images

Medium; contradiction; changes docs; effort S; source N02-4.

**Claim.** The guide's row exempts 'a Red Hat catalog' as a vendor origin, but the security spec classes an origin by the host serving the image, not by who serves the catalog. The default catalogs community-operators and certified-operators are served by Red Hat, yet the operator images they list are published by others, community-operators' often on quay.io or similar hosts. Under the security spec's rule those hosts are public origins. The row should class the catalog's image hosts, not the catalog's owner.

**Evidence.**

- `docs/operator-guide.md:213-213`: "Nothing to do for a Red Hat catalog or IBM's Data Foundation on 'icr.io', vendor origins"
- `specs/api/addons.md:539-540`: "The default catalogs are 'redhat-operators', 'certified-operators', 'community-operators' and 'redhat-marketplace'."
- `specs/security.md:801-801`: "A public origin | Any account, or a project other than those vendors"

**Consequence.** An operator who builds a controlled network from this table admits only the Red Hat and IBM hosts. An add-on subscribed from community-operators or certified-operators then fails to pull on the nodes, or the operator widens the firewall to quay.io or docker.io without knowing the rule calls for a mirror.

**Recommendation.** In docs/operator-guide.md's controlled-network row for a cluster's operators, replace 'a Red Hat catalog' with '`redhat-operators` and IBM's Data Foundation on `icr.io`, vendor origins'. Add that the images listed by another catalog, `community-operators` and `certified-operators` included, are classed by the host that serves each image. Where that host is public, imageDigestSources maps it when the cluster pulls by digest. Do not say where certified images live, since many sit on Red Hat-run hosts. Add the same note to the 'Left out' paragraph of specs/deferred/controlled-network.md.

**Acceptance.** The guide's row names `redhat-operators` rather than 'a Red Hat catalog' and classes the other default catalogs' images as public.

**Decisions and principles.** Decisions read by the judge: D250, D251. Principles applied: P5, P12, P40.

**Verification.** refuter narrowed; judge narrowed at Medium; recommendation amended by the judge.

<a id="new-06"></a>

#### NEW-06 Guide has operators fill the mirror from a developer make target

Medium; gap; changes docs; effort M; source N03-3, N01-4, N04-5; related [DOC-14](#doc-14).

**Claim.** The operator guide's new controlled-network step sends operators to `make tool-table`, a developer gate. It needs a checkout and publisher access, and it only re-proves the table. The guide's own build route already has the operator on a workstation with a checkout. The real defect is a different one. No operator-facing page names the default releases or the archive file names a mirror must hold.

**Evidence.**

- `docs/operator-guide.md:224-226`: "Fill the mirror with the default releases 'make tool-table' names, under the layout the download mirrors section states."
- `docs/operator-guide.md:43-44`: "A controller needs no checkout or Go toolchain"
- `docs/development.md:293-294`: "'make tool-table' reads each default's checksum and size from its publisher and fails on any difference"

**Consequence.** An operator on a controlled site holds only the executable and has no route to the publishers, which is the whole point of the mirror. They can't run the step the guide prescribes, and they can't learn the exact archive names (for example Helm's archive name under the base URL) that the stage will request.

**Recommendation.** In operator-guide.md, replace `make tool-table` with a link to controller.md#the-tool-table. Name the file `internal/controller/tooltable.json` as the source of each default release, size and SHA-256 until B1245's acquisition list replaces it. In environment.md#download-mirrors, state each tool's file name pattern, for example `helm-v<version>-linux-amd64.tar.gz` under the base URL and `<base>/v<version>/govc_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz`. Do not add a new command: B1245 owns the read-only listing.

**Acceptance.** The operator guide names a command or table that an operator holding only bin/bootwright can use to get each default release's exact mirror path, size and SHA-256. The download-mirrors section, or a section it links to, states each tool's file name pattern.

**Decisions and principles.** Decisions read by the judge: D250, D251. Principles applied: none recorded.

**Verification.** refuter narrowed; judge narrowed at Medium; recommendation amended by the judge; merged from 3 candidates (N03-3 Medium, N01-4 Medium, N04-5 Medium).

### 17.4 What the new text gets right

The lanes recorded what must survive any change to this text. These statements are the auditors' own and were not verified.

- The mirror rule says exactly what a mirror replaces. A default release comes with the table's size and SHA-256 and needs no publisher contact. Any other release takes its checksum from the publisher, even when the mirror serves the bytes. (specs/api/environment.md:362-365; lane N01)
- A per-tool table names where a non-default release resolves and where its SHA-256 comes from. It also names openly how far publisher authenticity is widened, because no signature is verified. (specs/controller.md:602-621; lane N01)
- Each refusal row carries a parameterized reason and remedy, and a named test binds the rows to the capability's Unsupported list. The remedy offers both 'declare the minimum or newer' and 'remove for this build's default'. (specs/api/environment.md:464-487; lane N01)
- Origins are classed by who may publish on the serving host, not by the content's author, which gives a reviewer a testable rule. It correctly puts the OpenShift payload on quay.io in the public class and records the icr.io override as an explicit owner choice with its cost ('admits that whole ... (specs/security.md:793-807; lane N02)
- The design states that the threat is the route, not the content: a digest protects the bytes, and only an absent route protects the Machine from exfiltration. That is the correct threat model for egress control. (specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:13-16; lane N02)
- The mirror is curated, never a pull-through cache or proxy, and consumers verify digests they held before asking, so a compromised mirror can only deny service. The one exception to that guarantee is named rather than hidden. (specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:60-71; lane N02)
- The controlled-network table gives, for each step, who connects, what it reaches by default and the Environment setting that moves it. This is the right shape for an egress-restricted operator. (docs/operator-guide.md:203-214; lane N03)
- Origins are classed by who may publish on the serving host rather than by content author, and the icr.io exception is recorded against the owner's decision instead of being hidden. (specs/security.md:791-807; lane N03)
- The tool-table authenticity model is stated plainly as a named widening: a default is pinned by size and SHA-256 and needs no publisher metadata, while any other release's checksum is read from its publisher and never from a mirror. (specs/controller.md:602-621; lane N03)
- The latest removal reached every live surface: the API grammar, the field defaults, the controller selection rule, the SHA-256 table header, the security widening and the KubeVirt examples. No live spec or example still offers `latest` for a client. (specs/api/environment.md:42-66; specs/controller.md:592-621; api/v1alpha1/lexical.go:21; lane N04)
- The new refusal rows give an exact cause, message and remedy for the minimum and for a release without MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and TestControllerRefusalTableMatchesUnsupported holds the table to the code. (specs/api/environment.md:484-485; lane N04)
- The security spec names the trust widening honestly: a publisher compromised at the table's refresh or at a declared release's first acquisition is trusted from then on. (specs/security.md:776-787; lane N04)
- A default release is fully pinned by size and SHA-256 frozen into the stage request, so a mirror serving other bytes fails integrity and the mirror is trusted for nothing on the default route. (specs/controller.md:602-608; lane N05)
- The tool table is self-checking: format-versioned, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH without v, default at or above the minimum, held by a named test, and re-proved against publishers only by make targets, never at use. (specs/controller.md:806-830; lane N05)
- Removing `latest` closes the last runtime release resolution: no stage resolves a newest release, so a frozen plan never moves under a publisher. (specs/controller.md:592-596; lane N05)

### 17.6 What this does to the roadmap

Section 15 orders the work for the audited commit. The three commits change it
in four places, and leave the order of packages 1 to 6 as it is.

- **Package 7, the completed-apply rule, gains [NEW-01](#new-01).** It answers the same
  question as the rest of that package: what a command does over a completed
  apply. The fix is spec text, which says that a settling apply and a removal
  run the release the completed apply proved. One decision is the owner's:
  whether a running environment should take a raised minimum without a
  destroy, and whether `status` or `diff` should report a proved client below
  the build's minimum. D250 (17) states the intent and does not address the
  settle rule. [NEW-15](#new-15) belongs with it: the X342 record says an earlier build's
  operation refuses to continue, and omits that its destroy refuses too.
- **Package 9, the stale restatements, shrinks and grows.** The Ceph coverage
  row of [DOC-02](#doc-02) is corrected, and its disconnected example still names the
  removed flags. [DOC-07](#doc-07) and [DOC-09](#doc-09) need no work. X342 added copies of its own
  rules that already disagree: [NEW-04](#new-04), [NEW-08](#new-08), [NEW-09](#new-09), [NEW-14](#new-14), [NEW-17](#new-17) and
  [NEW-19](#new-19), and the milestone records [NEW-16](#new-16) and [NEW-18](#new-18). Each is a small text
  edit, and they fit the same pass.
- **The controlled-network program needs three answers before its slices
  open.** [NEW-02](#new-02) (the mirror's ordering is cyclic for a mirror on a Machine
  that Bootwright installs) and [NEW-13](#new-13) (who issues the mirror's certificate
  and how each consumer comes to trust it) are open points for B1249's
  definition. [NEW-03](#new-03) is for the owner: D250 (15) lets a coding agent write a
  vulnerability exception, and nothing says who reviews it before it ships as
  a VEX statement. The gate itself landed in `7d6d205a8` while this pass ran
  (section 17.7), so [NEW-03](#new-03) is the first of these to read again. [NEW-11](#new-11) and
  [NEW-12](#new-12) are wording of the origin rule.
- **Operator documentation.** [NEW-05](#new-05) (the guide exempts every Red Hat catalog,
  though the default catalogs list images on public hosts) and [NEW-06](#new-06) (the
  guide sends an operator who holds only the executable to a developer make
  target) are Medium and cheap. [NEW-07](#new-07), [NEW-10](#new-10) and [NEW-20](#new-20) are one sentence
  each.

### 17.7 Limits of this pass

- **It is a pass over a change, not a second audit.** The lanes read the text
  the three commits added or changed and what that text depends on. The 150
  lanes of the audit proper were not run again, so the scores of section 2.4
  and the counts of sections 2 to 15 are those of the audited commit.
- **Findings that cite no changed text were not re-read.** A commit can settle
  or sharpen a finding without touching a line it cites. Only lane N04 looked
  for such effects, by searching for stale copies of each changed rule.
- **The deferred design is judged as a design.**
  `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md` describes work that items B1243 to
  B1251 park. That a rule in it is not implemented is not a finding. A finding
  there is a contradiction, an unsafe rule, a step two implementers would
  build differently, or a planned rule that reads as delivered.
- **Code was not reviewed.** Commit `aa46736e7` changes Go code and tests. The
  lanes opened declarations and the tool table as evidence of how the contract
  materializes, as the audit proper did.
- **Two more commits landed while this pass ran, and were not read.**
  `10705b925` adds a command that prints the executable's bill of materials,
  and `7d6d205a8` adds the build's vulnerability gate with its exception file.
  Every citation of the catalog and of this section was checked mechanically
  against `7d6d205a8`. No further finding of the catalog lost a quote. [NEW-03](#new-03)
  and [NEW-04](#new-04) each lost one, in `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md`, so both
  need a second look against the current text. [NEW-03](#new-03) is about who reviews a
  vulnerability exception, which is the subject of the second commit.

## Appendix A. Lane records

One record per lane: what it was assigned, its own assessment of its slice,
and what became of its candidates (a final id, or refuted, decided or
tracked). Where a section of the report gives only a condensed form of a
lane's working table, the table is printed here in full: the rule-by-rule
tables of the reconciliation lanes, the scenarios the attack lanes walked, the
per-kind tables with their proposed shapes, the friction logs, the extension
touch-point tables, the leak hunts, the retrieval paths and the examples
table. The working tables of the other lanes are condensed into sections 3 to
11 and are not repeated.

A working table is the auditor's own. Its rows were not verified one by one:
only the candidates a lane filed went through verification, so a row that
names a defect without a final id is an observation, not a finding. A lane's
assessment is likewise its own summary, written before verification. Link
targets inside a table are dropped, because they were relative to the page
the auditor read. The five lanes of the pass of section 17 come last; they
read the later commit, and their line numbers are that commit's.

### Reconciliation, safety and security rules, page by page

<a id="lane-l01"></a>

#### Lane L01: Lifecycle unit, mutation evidence, durable identities

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/state-reconciliation.md:1-558`.

Good: the slice is a strong crash-consistency contract. Evidence goes up before effects, finalization is ordered and re-proved under the lock, and the ABA case of evidence bytes is handled by proving claim directories. Registration outcomes are split by provability, IDs come from CSPRNG with exclusive reservation, and records are closed and bounded with plan-to-record digest binding. Idempotent settling with no authorization is a valuable operator property. Needs improvement: some sentences went stale as later decisions landed. The orphan acknowledgement still promises abandoned objects are unreachable, although B568's same-name adoption is documented elsewhere. The contexts.md update warning predates the additive apply. The index refusal keeps an earlier-build `qualification` rule that D241 retires. The block-ID rule refuses only hashed collisions. Remedies for unknown optional members cover only attempt records. Bad: nothing unsafe as written in my ranges. The main cost is density: the no-operation and housekeeping cases (lines 52-152 and 229-311) form a state machine in run-on prose with exceptions scattered across paragraphs. The settle rule's 'no transaction' already contradicts later destroy housekeeping. A decision table keyed by index, evidence, reservation, claims and verb would make two implementers converge.

Candidates after verification: L01-1 REC-23; L01-2 REC-03; L01-3 REC-88; L01-4 API-50; L01-5 REC-89; L01-6 REC-90; L01-7 REC-91. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

#### Lane L02: State machine and plan structure

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/state-reconciliation.md:559-1056`.

Good: the state machine in this slice is unusually rigorous. Every exit is named, including the orphan-acknowledged deletion as the last resort. Custody is ordered so material is never lost across a crash or a failed publication (D123/D124). Resolution is read-only and evidence-gated, and the fresh-destroy asymmetry (apply observation, then removal check) is explicit. Five spec tables are tied to code by a test. I found no unsafe transition and no state without an operator exit.\n\nNeeds improvement: the vocabulary and table claims have drifted from the prose and the code. `inconclusive` is missing from the effect-state list. `paused` has two definitions that disagree on a log fault, and the precedence preamble claims every row is block-derived when the `paused` row is not. The 'exact' block-transitions table omits stay-in-place outcomes. The D119 removal-check table is outside the mechanical guard although 609 implies otherwise.\n\nWeak: the inconclusive retry's own outcome and the scope of its one-retry budget are left to an implementer. managed-os.md answers 'stays unknown', which belongs in the owner. The D124 hand-over reads as engine-level kubeconfig logic rather than the generic Keeper port the code has, which taxes the extension goal. The prose is dense: single sentences carry four or five conditions, which raises agent reading cost. All findings have S-sized fixes.

Candidates after verification: L02-1 REC-24; L02-2 REC-92; L02-3 REC-25; L02-4 REC-93; L02-5 REC-94; L02-6 ARC-48. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l03"></a>

#### Lane L03: Stages, recovery safety, attempts and convergence

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/state-reconciliation.md:1057-1628`.

Good: this slice is the safety core, and it is mostly rigorous. An unknown outcome is never success and is never retried without a durable, logged, read-only resolution. Retry safety is grounded in one convergence rule that the capability owns, not in native-tool idempotence. Stage selection explicitly cannot weaken resolution or dependency order. Rebuild continuation is gated on re-planning identical blocks, with content digests computed from the declared contract rather than from automation bytes. Retries are bounded to one per block per invocation, and an inconclusive removal admits a single retry. Needs improvement: some passages restate rules owned elsewhere and have drifted. The controller stage row omits the container runtime that controller.md selects, and the pause definition duplicates the precedence table without its conditions. A few sentences make claims the surrounding rules falsify: admission independent of completion order, and a direct no-effect result counted as a typed failure. Bad: the generic runner's read-only allowlist names one concrete implementation (`substrate-host-kubevirt-v1`), which conflicts with the goal that general code never knows which implementation runs. Prose density is high: single sentences carry two refusals and their remedies, which raises the risk of divergence for agents.

Candidates after verification: L03-1 REC-26; L03-2 REC-95; L03-3 REC-27; L03-4 ARC-10; L03-5 REC-96. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l04"></a>

#### Lane L04: Continuation and removal

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/state-reconciliation.md:1629-1954`; `specs/deferred/reconciliation-scenarios.md:1-198`.

Good: the slice is unusually rigorous on the safety core. Ownership is every started block. Destroy is derived from frozen plans and requests rather than desired state. Self-contradicting records refuse before any effect or release. Nothing substitutes for a frozen Secret binding. Every transition re-proves the exact planned state under the exclusive lock. Cross-build continuation is bound to frozen blocks and the runtime closure, which is what lets an automation-only fix continue without a destroy. Needs improvement: the prose is very dense. Several paragraphs chain more than five conditions, which raises misreading risk for agents. One list claims to be complete and is not: the admission stops omit the cannot-start case. The lineage binding rule is ambiguous after a rebind. The deferred scenarios page has drifted: its seam, recipe and design rule 1 still prescribe a union plan and a lineage id that D211's predecessor lineage replaced or did not need. Bad: one removal-safety rule offers a false backstop. A loosened ownership observation moves only the content digest, but removals compare no digest and run under the build in hand. A destroy under the new build can therefore accept, and delete, objects the applying build would have read as foreign. Requiring a request-version move, as for fixed places, fixes it.

Candidates after verification: L04-1 REC-07; L04-2 REC-28; L04-3 REC-29; L04-4 REC-97; L04-5 refuted; L04-6 REC-98. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l05"></a>

#### Lane L05: Desired-versus-real comparison and GitOps readiness

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/state-reconciliation.md:1955-2296`; `specs/cli.md:839-1003`; `specs/add-ons.md:528-584`.

Good: the comparison contract is unusually rigorous. It is strictly read-only. Unknown never reads as absent. Projection stays generic through capability ports (Projector, Discoverer, NothingLive), backed by a table-to-code test. Secret material is guarded at every exit, re-proof under the lock prevents races, and --tool and --output-dir have sound privilege rules. The readiness predicate requires the input to match the frozen bytes and gives ordered reasons. Needs improvement: the exit-code contract does not match the spec's own drift definition. Partial realizations, which is how Argo CD co-management of add-on objects shows up, and changed input or plan all exit 0. The two pages also list different exit-3 sets. The taint rule is kind-specific text in the generic flow. Readiness is records-only and the output does not say so. Bad: the GitOps ownership boundary is defined only by add-on evidence. That makes other Bootwright-owned objects on a cluster (KubeVirt VMs and DataVolumes, cluster-network objects) eligible for GitOps control. And no command shows the operator the owned-object list they are required to exclude, so the central handoff rule cannot be followed from the contract.

Candidates after verification: L05-1 REC-30; L05-2 CLI-10; L05-3 CLI-21; L05-4 CLI-10; L05-5 CLI-10; L05-6 ARC-49; L05-7 REC-99. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l06"></a>

#### Lane L06: Mutation safety, confirmation and authorization

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/state-reconciliation.md:2297-2763`; `specs/cli.md:245-432`; `specs/cli/commands.md:342-530`.

Good: the mutation-safety core is strong and coherent. Unknown is never treated as absence. Authorization never selects a target or relaxes a check. Inapplicable tokens refuse. Unattended destruction is bound to a digest of the printed steps. The bare-metal proofs state their residual race honestly. The erase contract binds identity, coverage and custody to the original apply and never picks disks from discovery. Controller-host protection and the rebind's limit (it changes how an endpoint is reached, never what is owned) are well drawn. Needs improvement: the general rule 'revalidate quiescence before every effect' is weakened on continuation. Removal proves the stop once before registration, only Machine inverses recheck, and the plan output says a continuation is not re-gated, while power commands can restart Machines in between. The rebind validates a Secret version before the prompt but pins 'its current version' later, with no re-proof under the exclusive lock. Refusal codes for an unanswerable confirmation differ across cli.md and commands.md. The digest's 'someone reviewed' wording overstates what it guarantees. Nothing found is self-contradictory on the erase or physical-disk paths. The prose is dense and long-sentenced, so readers and agents pay a real cost to verify each rule.

Candidates after verification: L06-1 REC-31; L06-2 REC-100; L06-3 CLI-05; L06-4 REC-101. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l07"></a>

#### Lane L07: Contexts: identity, binding, frozen input, restore, deletion

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/contexts.md:1-227`; `specs/contexts.md:825-1080`; `specs/contexts/controller-record.md:1-311`; `specs/contexts/log-root.md:1-140`.

Good: the slice is unusually rigorous about the mechanics of durable state. These include atomic publication of host identity, bindings and reservations together, the deleting mark before removal, re-proof after confirmation, a deletion walk that never removes what it cannot verify, and a rebind that admits its clone limitation and keeps identity values out of output. Name identity and its reuse hazard are stated honestly, and the orphan confirmation warns precisely. Needs improvement: the restore boundary. The text names a matching backup as an exit while declaring it unsupported, gives it no recency condition, and so lets an image restored for one context silently roll back every context on the host. Device-number binding is used without saying it survives a reboot. Import does not copy payload referents, which conflicts with the project's copied-input rule. The log root is said to change no outcome, yet it refuses setup and deletion and has refusals with no repair. Bad: the fresh-start remedies in the controller record still instruct hand removal of the store, which bypasses `controller uninstall` and leaves the hosted and log roots for a same-name context to reuse. They also restate the setup-output contract that the log root owns, and the two copies have drifted.

Candidates after verification: L07-1 REC-32; L07-2 REC-05; L07-3 CON-02; L07-4 refuted; L07-5 REC-33; L07-6 REC-20. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l08"></a>

#### Lane L08: Contexts: storage, locking and publication

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/contexts.md:228-824`.

Good: the lock design is deadlock-free by construction, because no root holder waits for anything and every lease or stage lock is taken non-blocking. Staleness is left to kernel-released flock, never to takeover. A timeout records failed or unknown by whether an effect ran. Media acquisition is an example of a long effect handled correctly: it holds no root lock, its stage is flock-guarded and stat-proved, and a pinned stage is retained. The bounds table checked against code, the capacity diagnostics and the removal reserve are strong. Needs improvement: four rules are underspecified for a crash-consistency protocol. The general publication rule never requires fsync. Reader hold durations are unbounded even though mutators wait only one minute, so a preflight on one context can turn another context's running block unknown. The trust writer contradicts 'state/ writers hold the lease'. Stage collection reasons from lock exclusivity, but one operation writes concurrently under a single lease. The filesystem rule qualifies three types but refuses only two, so network filesystems are undefined. Bad: the operation-area admission prose (627-716) is very dense. It mixes a fixed 16 MiB figure with plan-derived reserves, and its guarantee cannot be checked from the text. A worked formula would help both agents and reviewers.

Candidates after verification: L08-1 ARC-11; L08-2 REC-35; L08-3 ARC-12; L08-4 ARC-13; L08-5 REC-34; L08-6 ARC-14; L08-7 REC-102. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l09"></a>

#### Lane L09: Security: trust model and boundaries

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/security.md:1-914`.

Good: security.md is one of the strongest pages in the corpus. It has an explicit attacker model with named trust widenings, a principal-scoped trust table, fail-closed treatment of unknowns, careful handling of ansible-core template trust, concrete privilege re-execution proofs, and a table mapping invariants to tests. Insecure TLS exceptions are narrow and visible, and trust in a target tool on first acquisition is stated honestly rather than hidden. Needs improvement: some rules are restated in several places, each slightly different. There are three SSH crypto-policy regimes. The sticky exemption sits in the privilege section but not in the attacker model. The no-shell exception covers only module workers. Some of the page is implementation mechanism rather than policy (the job-sweep locking paragraph), which is expensive for agents to read. Bad: the listener-exposure contract requires source restrictions that the bounded firewall inspection refuses, and Bootwright's own managed-OS firewall changes never add them. Operators therefore cannot comply with the rule and pass preflight. The page's list of where secret bytes may stay is narrower than what secrets.md, infrastructure-services.md and openshift-clusters.md sanction.

Candidates after verification: L09-1 ARC-15; L09-2 CON-08; L09-3 ARC-16; L09-4 ARC-17; L09-5 ARC-18; L09-6 ARC-09; L09-7 CLI-08. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-l10"></a>

#### Lane L10: Secrets: custody, binding, keyring and reveal

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/secrets.md:1-654`; `specs/api/secrets.md:1-213`; `specs/ceph.md:2128-2163`; `specs/add-ons.md:416-450`.

Good: the custody contract is unusually rigorous. Binding is immutable and whole-version, and the three binding classes give a principled answer to rotation during continuation. Produced material is cleanly separated from declarations, with one reveal command per output. Native-side retention is explicitly outside custody, and keyring durability and crash semantics (seal reservations, commit visibility, attributable recovery, reader-version skew) are thorough. Reveals are consistently raw exports with no implicit fallback. Needs improvement: `generate --renew` is the one current-version replacement that skips the confirmation every other secret mutator requires, and an unnamed renew replaces everything at once. Generated-certificate lifecycle has two holes that will make implementations diverge: how a CA renewal affects its leaves, and whether derived names enter the stale fingerprint. The access-credential rebind treats a kubeconfig as purely authenticating, although it also names the endpoint and embeds a trust anchor. Bad: the registry login's native copy (podman-auth.json) is listed as retained but has no writer, no refresh on rebind and no reserved path, and ceph.md still says guest delivery uses the original binding. Prose density is very high. Several paragraphs carry five or more normative clauses in one sentence chain, which is costly for agents to load and verify.

<a id="lane-l11"></a>

#### Lane L11: Controller: hosts, runtime, setup and uninstall

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/controller.md:1-556`.

Good: the controller contract is strong. Host and context prerequisites are split cleanly. Admission fails closed with no release-name rules. The runtime is built offline and hash-pinned from wheels the executable carries and is published only whole. Runtime use and retirement are coordinated by locks. dnf runs within the host's own configuration. Intent is recorded before any effect. Uninstall's state removal is crash-safe (rename aside, no link following, ownership and mount checks, rename back on change), and the owned-object proof fails closed and states its own limits. Needs improvement: the format-healing discard does not say what happens when a runtime is in use, and it erases package attribution, so after any format move Bootwright's own packages are reported as 'present before bootwright'. The prerequisite table assigns the host binding to the wrong owner. Bad: package ownership on uninstall is weaker than promised. Attribution covers only requirement providers. dnf's removal of unused dependencies can take pre-existing packages nobody checks, and the safeguard parses dnf text that the same page calls unparseable. `--discard-unreadable` also deletes guest disks, which the spec itself says need `data-loss`, under an ordinary `--yes` confirmation.

Candidates after verification: L11-1 REC-08; L11-2 REC-104; L11-3 REC-37; L11-4 REC-38; L11-5 CON-11. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l12"></a>

#### Lane L12: Controller: the controller stage, egress, host identity

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/controller.md:557-1212`.

Good: this slice is among the most rigorous in the corpus. Intent comes before every effect. Failed and unknown are split by whether an effect may have happened. Tool areas are content-addressed and sealed, and their retirement means one context cannot harm another's clients. Executables are located only through the proved closure, and no downloaded tool is ever executed. The context-free route has a closed grammar with no fallback. Host identity is stated honestly, limits included. Firewall inspection is conservative. Needs improvement: two cross-page drifts. The root-lock paragraph still says a busy lock refuses, while contexts.md (X341) makes mutators wait one minute. The identity section still sends relocation to B103, though D184's `controller rebind` shipped. The route-failure remedy argues continuation is the only path and so never names destroy, correct, apply for a misdeclared proxy. 'Sole route selection' overclaims against dnf's proxy=, and the digest's 'provider' input is undefined. Bad (design): the controller stage is generic in mechanism but special-cased in selection. libvirt, Anaconda and OpenShift predicates, and six closure names, are written out in the general spec and repeated in about five lists. That taxes the stated goal of low-impact extension to new substrates and cluster types; a contributed-closure port would fix it. The prose is very dense, which costs agents tokens, though it is precise.

Candidates after verification: L12-1 ARC-08; L12-2 REC-39; L12-3 CLI-23; L12-4 ARC-50; L12-5 CLI-54; L12-6 CON-12; L12-7 CON-13. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l13"></a>

#### Lane L13: Substrates: selection, provider hosts, machine realization

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/substrates.md:1-762`.

Good: the slice is unusually rigorous on the hard parts of physical-effect safety. It defines an answered observation (per driver, and a virsh lookup plus a complete listing), never reads silence as absence, refuses foreign objects on both apply and destroy, proves domains quiescent from the host before restarting or removing networks, and resolves removals separately from apply evidence. The frozen realized target and the single fail-closed dispatcher are the right extension seam, and the general flow depends only on them. Needs improvement: cross-context coordination on SSH-placed libvirt hosts. substrates.md still says the SSH arm relies on the lease alone, while the reservations page publishes SSH-qualified claims. Qualification also defeats the shared bmc: guard against a physical Machine addressing an emulated BMC. Capacity rules are split, circularly, with ceph.md. The provider-host removal completion omits two owned units. vSphere is written both as refused and as realized. Structure: the two libvirt-only sections carry generic titles, which misleads anyone adding an arm. History and code paths (X48, catalog.go, the ledger dates) leak into normative text. The slice's own rules are sound, and the defects sit at its boundaries with infrastructure-services, ceph and the deferred pages.

Candidates after verification: L13-1 REC-09; L13-2 REC-06; L13-3 REC-40; L13-4 ARC-19; L13-5 SCO-05; L13-6 REC-105; L13-7 REC-106. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-l14"></a>

#### Lane L14: Substrates: physical machines, firmware, KubeVirt

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/substrates.md:763-1396`.

Good: the physical target proof is rigorous and fails closed. It needs the complete MAC set together with the ComputerSystem identity, and it pins and re-proves that identity before media and power. The firmware sequence is unusually careful: pending-value comparison, a BiosSetup override, If-Match, an unconditional ForceOff and an honest note of the residual timing gaps. KubeVirt lends follow least privilege, with bound TokenRequests revoked by UID-preconditioned delete, and every write is guarded by the kube-system UID and the VM UID. Needs improvement: cross-context serialization of physical servers rests on claims that machine power commands never consult. A server with no UUID has no identity key, so two spellings of its BMC address are both admitted. The physical destroy-time pin wording was not updated when D234 extended the taken-back pin. Bad: `bootMode: UEFI` is implemented as the one-time override mode. It does not deliver the persistent UEFI mode D191 intends, so on real hardware a disk can be erased and the installed system then fail to boot, which emulation hides. A refused enforce also leaves BIOS changes staged while destroy reports no impact. Vendor specifics are well isolated behind verbatim attributes and BMC links, but the generic port's pin and credential names still carry Redfish vocabulary.

Candidates after verification: L14-1 REC-10; L14-2 REC-42; L14-3 API-51; L14-4 REC-43; L14-5 REC-41; L14-6 REC-107; L14-7 ARC-45; L14-8 ARC-51. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

<a id="lane-l15"></a>

#### Lane L15: Substrates: vSphere, identity and power operations, host-key trust

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/substrates.md:1397-1804`; `specs/cli.md:1471-1660`; `specs/deferred/machine-arms.md:1-122`.

The Redfish, power and trust rules in this slice are written to a high standard. Power requests are never treated as evidence, every outcome is polled within a bound, an unanswered read is unknown and never absent, references are bounded to the one endpoint, and virtual-media trust never falls back from one mode to another. Host-key enrollment refuses first-use trust that nobody reviewed, and power commands are guarded against the controller host. The vSphere realization adopts the right identity pattern: managed-object references plus a marker and two instanceUuids compared immediately before each act. The weaknesses sit at the edges. A physical pin holding two empty values compares nothing and is still treated as a pin. The pin's lifetime during a destroy is stated differently in two places. The resend rule hinges on 'reset', which is never defined. The lock guarantee overstates what it excludes, because the native effects of an unknown block keep running after the lease is released. Structurally, the general power contract names arms ('libvirt or KubeVirt', 'KubeVirt and vSphere') and BMC vocabulary instead of substrate facts, so vSphere already falls through the rule for removed Machines. That contradicts the one-dispatcher-row extension promise in Selection. The vSphere arm is a credible sketch, not a distortion, but it lacks vCenter trust bundles, derived-MAC collision refusal and an identity channel for the template-clone installer it is committed to.

Candidates after verification: L15-1 REC-108; L15-2 REC-42; L15-3 CLI-55; L15-4 REC-109; L15-5 CON-04; L15-6 refuted; L15-7 API-134; L15-8 refuted. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

<a id="lane-l16"></a>

#### Lane L16: Managed OS: media store and installation core

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/managed-os.md:1-714`.

Good: this slice is strong. Completion is proved through a substrate-bound identity channel plus a pinned SSH host key, never trust-on-first-use. The target proof is taken at effect time and fails closed. The installer powers itself off, so the disk boot is deliberate. Budgets are frozen and the deadline arithmetic is exact. Media custody holds no lock during acquisition but re-proves at publication and is frozen by shared reservations. The release identity of the image is checked against the declared version. Needs improvement: the durable before-state that prevents a false "no effect" is recorded too late, at the network restart instead of the first marker proof. Private material, the delivered host key and the LUKS recovery passphrase, survives a failed or cancelled attempt indefinitely while the BMC holds its URL, which contradicts the private-publication principle. Destroy leaves BMC state (inserted media, an imported certificate) and relies on a later apply that may never come. The Replay remedy is wrong for retained bare metal, and `foreign-installation` has no refusal-table row. The MaxDeadline sentence for physical installs is ambiguous. Bad: nothing self-contradictory on the destructive path itself. The two High findings are windows and lifetimes the text leaves open, not wrong core rules. The section is dense: 30 to 60-word normative sentences make cross-checks costly for agents.

Candidates after verification: L16-1 REC-11; L16-2 decided; L16-3 REC-44; L16-4 REC-45; L16-5 REC-111; L16-6 REC-46; L16-7 REC-110. Named and not pursued: 1 further point.

<a id="lane-l17"></a>

#### Lane L17: Managed OS: network, FIPS, registration, physical paths

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/managed-os.md:715-1468`; `specs/managed-os-satellite.md:1-42`.

Good: this slice is among the most rigorous in the corpus. Network convergence relies on NetworkManager's checkpoint rollback so that a declared network cannot permanently cut off the controller, and it states the next step at every interruption point. Root and data disks are named only by durable identities and proved twice, once by the controller and again inside the installer's %pre. The clear refuses ambiguous stacking and says plainly that it is not sanitization. FIPS claims only FIPS mode. Every physical arm admits that emulation qualifies nothing. Needs improvement: the subscription ownership record is under-specified. A `pending` record is written before any consumer exists, yet adoption and removal match by consumer. That produces divergent implementations, and a lost reply can leak an orphan consumer. The FIPS failure remedy names nothing to correct. The word "registration" carries two meanings on one page. Bad: a failed attempt leaves the private subtree (host key, LUKS recovery passphrase) served, with no time limit, while the BMC may still hold the tokenized URL. This contradicts the stated rule that one-boot material must not outlive its boot.

Candidates after verification: L17-1 REC-112; L17-2 decided; L17-3 REC-113. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-l18"></a>

#### Lane L18: Managed OS: encryption, updates, package tree, firewall, refusals

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/managed-os.md:1469-2064`.

Good: this slice is unusually rigorous. Every effect (recovery publication, package update, tree publication, firewall service) has a proof before its claim, closed evidence states, named refusals with remedies, bounded budgets and an ownership mark or record. Secrets stay on stdin and never reach argv. The update stays install-scoped, so it is not day-2 in disguise. The package tree sits inside the context's own content root, so ownership between contexts is not an issue. The adapter boundary matches architecture.md's contract. Needs improvement: custody of the recovery passphrase is stated as an invariant (\"never renewed\"), but secrets.md lets an unnamed `--renew` silently replace a generated recovery token, and the bound value can never be revealed. The update retry from `pending` can skip the reboot after a dnf run that succeeded but was never recorded, and still report `complete`. The PCR 4/8/9 remedy offers `none`, though the spec itself predicts those PCRs fail on the first boot. The firewall ownership mark includes an apply-operation id whose role in matching and digesting is undefined. Bad (minor): refusal-table precedence relies on groups the table never marks, and a one-time build-migration note sits in normative text.

Candidates after verification: L18-1 REC-12; L18-2 REC-47; L18-3 REC-114; L18-4 REC-115; L18-5 REC-116; L18-6 REC-117. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-l19"></a>

#### Lane L19: Infrastructure services: reservations, artifact serving, network services

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/infrastructure-services.md:1-711`.

Good: this is a rigorous page. Refusal is pure and backed by tests. Reservations form a real cross-context mutual-exclusion protocol: typed key classes, one conflict relation per class, root-locked publication before the first effect, holder-only release with listed proofs, and durable releasing markers. An interrupted or failed registration keeps its keys, and an abandoned context's keys drop only under orphan acknowledgement. The SSH trust path is strong: one parsed entry, rewritten, with no ambient configuration. Unknown resolution and the private-publication confidentiality argument are precise. Adding a network service kind is a table row in one shared capability. Needs improvement: the summary table and the Host reservations opening still describe the pre-D183 world, where SSH placements are coordinated by the context lease only and reservations cover only the controller. The page's own later rules contradict them. Two routes to the controller (loopback at port 22) are classified differently at planning and at publication. A multi-entry known-hosts remedy promises a rebind that secrets.md forbids. Bad: the managed DNS service spec writes OpenShift's name set inline instead of taking contributions through a port, as storage already does. That taxes adding other cluster distributions. A DNSServer field, additionalIngressHosts, is accepted and frozen, does nothing, and raises no warning. Prose density is very high: many rules are single long sentences, which raises the cost for agents.

Candidates after verification: L19-1 REC-06; L19-2 REC-22; L19-3 REC-48; L19-4 ARC-52; L19-5 API-21; L19-6 REC-118. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

<a id="lane-l20"></a>

#### Lane L20: Container clusters: selection, installer inputs, boot media

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/openshift-clusters.md:1-600`.

Good: the safety-critical machinery is precise and testable. The refusal table carries verbatim reason and remedy and is held by a test, rows lift with their items, the serial root proof fails closed, the booted mark protects the only admin credential, the receipt records the context incarnation, and the image-confidentiality exception is explicit and bounded. Installer-input determinism (canonical frozen bytes, quoted JSON-syntax YAML) is among the best rules in the corpus. Needs improvement: the page has grown by accretion. Pushed delivery was layered onto rules written for a published image (the booted mark, evidence and replay), so push-only continuation is ambiguous. The host-record and root-hint projections contradict their own detailed sections. The physical root-selector rules (lines 43, 63, 153) disagree on logical volumes. Bad: family-level contract (node binding, delivery kind, deadlines, work-area custody) and substrate preconditions (libvirt and BMC rows) live inside the OpenShift agent page and its refusal table. That taxes every new substrate and every new cluster implementation, against the stated goal and the substrates.md promise. Cross-page drift: specs/api.md still warns that labels and taints are inert after D199.

Candidates after verification: L20-1 API-52; L20-2 REC-49; L20-3 API-08; L20-4 API-53; L20-5 API-23; L20-6 ARC-20; L20-7 ARC-21; L20-8 ARC-53. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-l21"></a>

#### Lane L21: Container clusters: installation, placement, preflight, post-install network

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/openshift-clusters.md:601-1213`.

Good: installation is one of the most rigorously specified paths in the corpus. Completion is proved from the cluster's own ClusterVersion and bound to the build by a client-certificate identity. Waits have a strict diagnosis order. Budgets and deadlines are frozen and derived. Each BMC insert carries a secret per-insert token with a provable sweep. Re-entry after interrupted boots is safe. Custody survives a partial destroy. Placement is an add-only pinned patch. Needs improvement: the completion predicate is stated three ways (Completion, Replay, Unknown resolution) and has drifted. Placement, added later by D199, never reached Replay or Unknown resolution, so a resolution can record the block done without placement. The release gate refers to a predicate that includes its own effect. Preflight implies broader coverage than its two check families and names libvirt in a generic stage. Bad: the recovery message 'destroy and a fresh apply' is unconditional although it only works for virtual nodes while Q8 and Q12 are open. The per-node cluster-network objects silently cap the node count far below the cluster-size promise. The paragraphs are very dense: several rules run to 200-word sentences, which raises agent reading cost and hides drift like the placement omission.

Candidates after verification: L21-1 REC-50; L21-2 REC-119; L21-3 ARC-22; L21-4 REC-120; L21-5 CLI-56; L21-6 ARC-23. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.
