<a id="lane-a11"></a>

#### Lane A11: Ceph resource kinds, part 2

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/ceph-resources.md:924-1749`; `api/v1alpha1/storage_smb.go`; `api/v1alpha1/storage_nvmeof.go`; `specs/storage-api-review.md:1-436`.

Good: these resource kinds have a strong safety contract. Native documents keep their spelling (NFS export JSON, SMB manager resources) under closed member tables. Secrets never travel in native payloads. Credential custody survives lost replies. Ownership is proved before every effect, and an idempotent create never counts as ownership. CephConsumer is a well-bounded integration kind with an honest trust extent and a plan-time warning for a surviving consumer. The ordering section is precise about dependencies versus readiness. The M2a review's criteria were largely met by the resulting API. Needs improvement: CephNVMeoFSubsystem requires `listeners` though they are fully derived, and reuses "host" for two meanings. The NFS export's defaults are stated both as Bootwright constants and as release-resolved values. NVMe-oF and NFS lack the trust-extent statement CephConsumer has, so a host-NQN or IP allowlist reads like authentication. Small drift remains: the SMB remedy and example still author derived values, the families table contradicts the NFS default-realm effect, NFS uses `serviceID` where sibling kinds use `serviceRef`, and the history review uses pre-rename names. Bad: nothing unsafe or self-contradictory on a destructive path in this slice.

Candidates after verification: A11-1 API-88; A11-2 API-28; A11-3 API-29; A11-4 API-89; A11-5 API-90; A11-6 API-10; A11-7 refuted; A11-8 API-91. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-a12"></a>

#### Lane A12: Add-on kinds

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/api/addons.md:1-372`; `specs/api/addons.md:658-707`; `specs/add-ons.md:1-243`; `api/v1alpha1/addons.go`; `api/v1alpha1/addons_hub.go`; `api/v1alpha1/addons_storage.go`.

Good: the built-in package path is exemplary. It uses closed typed configuration, one instance capability shared by packages and authored add-ons, exact Manual OLM approval with a proved upgrade chain, create-only ownership with receipts, and a complete table of indexed diagnostics with remedies. The executable authored OLM shape is guarded by real execution-time checks, and the examples are honest. Needs improvement: the catalogSource block exists in two copies whose safety rules have already drifted, against the more privileged operator-managed path. Which defined capability tokens an authored add-on may claim is stated only for kubevirt, and in another page. Ordering lives at binding granularity, and the profile kind earns little. The pages' own definition of "add-on" contradicts the glossary. Bad: a large admitted surface with no consumer and no tracking item (inputs with effects, addonConfigs, steps) contradicts the compiler-boundary rule. The add-ons page wrongly says B90 tracks it, and one inert effect still changes Environment selection. Pre-1.0, removing it is cheap and cuts roughly a third of the ClusterAddon contract.

Candidates after verification: A12-1 API-30; A12-2 API-31; A12-3 API-92; A12-4 CON-07; A12-5 API-93; A12-6 decided. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

Schema-maximal and goldens tests | The catalogSource sub-block is a second hand copy of the authored one, with weaker priority and poll rules | Share one `ownedCatalogSourceSchema()` and one rule set |

<a id="lane-a13"></a>

#### Lane A13: Built-in packages and their coverage

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/api/addons.md:373-657`; `specs/add-on-coverage.md:1-468`.

Good: the package catalog has strict, uniform OLM discipline: exact approval, no version pairings and specializations only on evidence. Owner boundaries are clean: coverage owns objects, the API owns fields, m4 owns delivery. MetalLB admission and the GitLab value table can be reviewed line by line, and uncertain native facts are listed rather than asserted. Needs improvement: the coverage table repeats field rules that have already drifted. Built-in packages apply a looser catalog-priority rule than authored add-ons, and every shipped fdf example uses the hazardous value. The unowned-source refusal exists for fdf only. The gitlab-to-fdf requirement depends on a StorageClass name prefix, which works against the stated goal of low-impact extension to other storage. The ACM `mce` block re-types part of the Subscription block. Bad: the owned GitLab resource pins a chart version that any approved operator upgrade invalidates, and the spec gives no supported way to move it short of destroy, which loses the Rails secret. The coverage page and the M4c scope still say per-interface MetalLB forwarding is parked after D246 delivered it. D246's own boundary test has not been applied to the hub and GitLab operands.

Candidates after verification: A13-1 REC-14; A13-2 API-32; A13-3 API-31; A13-4 API-33; A13-5 SCO-04; A13-6 ARC-42; A13-7 API-94; A13-8 API-95. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-a14"></a>

#### Lane A14: Reserved and unrealized surface

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/api/custom-playbooks.md:1-47`; `specs/deferred/custom-playbooks.md:1-108`; `specs/deferred/native-procedure.md:1-129`; `specs/deferred/cli-access-and-rendering.md:1-139`; `specs/api.md:21-91`; `specs/api.md:601-622`; `api/v1alpha1/unrealized.go`; `api/v1alpha1/customplaybooks.go`; `specs/cli.md:44-93`; `specs/ceph-resources.md:1652-1678`; `specs/openshift-coverage.md:194-209`; `specs/add-on-coverage.md:436-468`; `specs/ceph-coverage.md:460-494`.

Good: the refusal architecture is principled and mostly testable. One default refusal point, a data-driven unrealized table bound by tests, and a clean split between api.deferred and api.unrealized. The unavailable-command gate is strict about effects. CustomPlaybook is fenced honestly. Coverage pages route every exclusion to an item, and the Ceph matrix makes refusals verifiable. Needs improvement: the unrealized table has three 'none tracked' rows, which contradicts its own warning contract and the compiler-boundary rule. Its warning is unconditional where plan refuses only conditionally, so operators will learn to ignore it. The CustomPlaybook contract is split, with enforced rules on a deferred page. The deferred CLI page carries stale stubs, an already-live diagnostic code and an orphan section with dead types. Bad: one fact, OpenShift sessions being unimplemented, gets two codes and two exit statuses (`not-implemented` in cluster info against `access.unavailable` exit 255 on invocation), and the second code's registered meaning sends operators hunting for credentials. The cost of carrying CustomPlaybook's legacy-anchor graph is real, but D183 settled it.

Candidates after verification: A14-1 CLI-02; A14-2 API-34; A14-3 API-35; A14-4 API-96; A14-5 REC-80; A14-6 API-97. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-a15"></a>

#### Lane A15: Cold read: libvirt lab with OpenShift, Ceph and Data Foundation

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `README.md`; `docs/operator-guide.md`; `examples/README.md`; `examples/add-ons/lab-compact-df (every file)`.

Good: lab-compact-df is a complete, internally consistent input. Its README gives exact capacity and BMC-port needs, and the examples index is candid about placeholders, license acceptance and what validate proves. Service endpoints reference Machine addresses by name, and roles are derived from references, which keeps several facts single-owned. Needs improvement: a cold reader has no operator-facing journey. The operator guide and the examples index each send procedure elsewhere, so `secret generate`, `secret set` and `media add` appear only in e2e runbooks. Many facts are restated: NIC name, gateway, NTP, pool sizes, MDS count, RGW host token, and the IBM registry key in two Secrets. cephadm internals leak into desired state (RGW TLS binding paths, OSD device letters that follow from the libvirt bus choice). Bad: the Ceph node FQDN default is guaranteed to disagree with the installed hostname and the managed DNS, and nothing is refused before effects. Every example dodges it by restating `fqdn`. The scenario's managed proxy cannot serve the RHEL hosts, for a stated reason that the placement rule makes moot, and the example deploys a proxy no object uses.

Candidates after verification: A15-1 API-06; A15-2 API-98; A15-3 API-36; A15-4 API-37; A15-5 DOC-04; A15-6 DOC-12. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-a16"></a>

#### Lane A16: Cold read: bare metal through vendor BMCs

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `README.md`; `docs/operator-guide.md`; `examples/README.md`; `examples/ceph-clusters/physical-3-nodes-ceph (every file)`; `examples/openshift-clusters/lab-physical (every file)`; `examples/machines/lab-baremetal (every file)`.

Good: the bare-metal contract is safety-first, and the safety rules hold together. There is one canonical BMC spelling, verified TLS on both legs, delivered host keys, in-installer re-proof, a firmware `prove` mode, and honest qualification limits in every README. Provider defaults keep per-Machine blocks small, and cluster preflight makes external DNS workable. Needs improvement: authoring cost. Each physical disk's identity is typed four or five times across rootDevice, eraseOnRemoval, clearOnInstall and Ceph OSD paths. The root selector's spelling depends on which installer consumes the Machine. Ceph node FQDNs must be overridden by hand. No command reads the exact WWN, serial, size and MAC values the API demands. There is no bare-metal runbook, and no example combines physical hosts with external services. Bad: the latest owner decisions (D239/X319/X320) were applied to some pages and not others. On the most destructive path, whether an omitted root refuses or erases the firmware boot disk, and whether the root must be erased on Ceph retirement, differ by page. Physical OpenShift nodes are described as both installing and refusing. A missing erase policy on a physical Ceph host refuses only at destroy, after it is frozen, which leaves no exit except orphaning.

Candidates after verification: A16-1 API-03; A16-2 REC-02; A16-3 DOC-01; A16-4 API-38; A16-5 REC-15; A16-6 API-99; A16-7 CLI-33; A16-8 API-06. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

<a id="lane-a17"></a>

#### Lane A17: Cold read: KubeVirt machines

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `README.md`; `docs/operator-guide.md`; `examples/README.md`; `examples/openshift-clusters/lab-kubevirt (every file)`; `examples/openshift-clusters/lab-kubevirt-external (every file)`; `examples/openshift-clusters/lab-kubevirt-nested (every file)`.

Good: the KubeVirt contract is rigorous where it matters most. The kubeconfig forms are narrow, hosted hosts get minted and revoked tokens, ownership is proved by UID and identity is pinned. MACs and hosted RBAC are derived rather than authored, and refusals carry remedies. The operator guide's KubeVirt section is short and actionable. Needs improvement: the operator-facing material contradicts or omits things a cold reader needs. It asks for DNS records that managed DNS already derives. It says virtctl is pinned while the example pins nothing. It never says that RHEL Machines cannot be Bootwright-installed on KubeVirt. It makes an RWX class a prerequisite on a host the same apply builds, with no staged step. Bad: the KubeVirt arm's field reference sits on the deferred \"Refused machine arms\" page that routing tells agents to skip. Platform derivation and hosted-segment carriage are special-cased per substrate, which taxes the generic flow. Several facts (gateway, NIC names, hosted network identity) must be stated two to four times, and one of them (the hosted segment's Network) has no agreement check.

<a id="lane-a18"></a>

#### Lane A18: Cold read: infrastructure services and networks

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `README.md`; `docs/operator-guide.md`; `examples/README.md`; `examples/infrastructure-services/lab-services (every file)`; `examples/machines/lab-rhel-external-services (every file)`; `examples/machines/libvirt-network-variants (every file)`; `examples/ceph-clusters/libvirt-3-nodes-ceph-disconnected (environment and service files)`.

Good: the services and networks contracts are unusually precise. Proxy choice is atomic, static addresses and name servers each have one owner, the Network cross-kind checks catch VLAN, gateway and carriage drift at admission, certificate SANs derive from their consumers, and refusal tables give exact remedies. The examples are small and honest about placeholders. Needs improvement: there is no operator-facing authoring path. A cold reader must go from examples to compiler-contract API pages, and nothing points to `render effective --origins` for derived values. Facts repeat across objects: the noProxy list, the gateway and the search domain. Inert or unprobed choices pass silently: a profile proxy with no repositories, a Network gateway with no route, wrong external addresses. A managed Proxy has no RHEL consumer and cannot chain to an egress proxy, and nothing says so. Download mirrors go unmentioned in the operator guide, and they do not remove publisher hosts. Bad: the disconnected example and the Ceph profile catalog still prescribe the `--download-only`/`--wheel-mirror` flags that D248 removed, so they give a false offline procedure on the one disconnected profile.

<a id="lane-a19"></a>

#### Lane A19: Benchmark: the grammar against reference API conventions

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/api.md:99-384`; `specs/api.md:467-622`; `api/v1alpha1/schema.go`; `api/v1alpha1/object.go`; `api/v1alpha1/value.go`; `api/v1alpha1/families.go`.

Good: the grammar in my slice is unusually rigorous for a pre-1.0 product. Decoding is strict, with credential-safe and remediating diagnostics; YAML lexical hardening is thorough; there is one test-enforced union rule; named sets follow Kubernetes list-map practice; defaults are derived rather than authored; effective output is canonical. The cluster family registry is a sound extension seam for new cluster and storage kinds. Most differences from Kubernetes conventions are deliberate and fit a file-based day-0 tool: no status, lowerCamel enums, plain-string Refs, no versions. Needs improvement: the reference-typing guarantee overstates what the schema does. Site, tiebreaker-node and NFS serviceID references are untyped strings that the suffix test cannot see, so the uniform resolution and suppression rules do not cover them. Union rule 4 contradicts the Secret source's kept-absent default. There is no common quantity rule, and `targetSizeBytes` breaks the unit-suffix convention its siblings follow. Minor: envelope labels have no grammar or stated effect; the diagnostic field-path syntax exists only as an example; graph validation repeats the cluster-name namespace rule with hard-coded kinds. Nothing in my slice is unsafe.

Candidates after verification: A19-1 API-10; A19-2 API-103; A19-3 API-104; A19-4 API-60; A19-5 API-105; A19-6 API-59. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-a20"></a>

#### Lane A20: Benchmark: domain shapes against the APIs operators know

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/api/machines.md:24-330`; `specs/api/openshift-clusters.md:20-192`; `specs/api/ceph.md:19-84`; `specs/api/infrastructure-services.md:12-75`; `specs/api/addons.md:30-60`; `api/v1alpha1/machines.go`; `api/v1alpha1/openshift_clusters.go`; `api/v1alpha1/storage.go`; `api/v1alpha1/addons.go`; `api/v1alpha1/secrets.go`.

Good: the slice is consistently more precise than the reference APIs where that precision protects destructive or security paths. These are the canonical BMC address, durable root-disk identity, typed Secrets, platform derivation that refuses ambiguous mixes, manual OLM approval pinned to startingCSV, and native cephadm documents kept as-is. Presence unions for substrates make extension cheap, and roles derived from references avoid label drift. Needs improvement: a few shapes rename or reshape concepts operators know without gain. OLM's subscription.name means the object here but the package in OLM. Native Ceph service references are spelled three ways. CephPool.application is redundant. Profile sizes default to an always-refused 0. Physical-disk identities are split between spec.hardware and the substrate arm against the page's own placement rule, and the field tables have drifted from the schema. Missing: a per-cluster baseDomain, which install-config and Hive both put on the cluster, and an authored-add-on Subscription config. Bad: nothing blocking. The largest shape issue, the os.provided boolean union, is already tracked as open Q120 and should be resolved in favour of a presence union.

### The CLI and its output contract

<a id="lane-c01"></a>

#### Lane C01: CLI: command tree, parsing, context and validation commands

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/cli.md:1-567`; `specs/cli/commands.md:1-198`; `internal/cli/catalog.go`.

Good: the command boundary is unusually rigorous. There is a fixed invocation precedence, no-effect unavailable stubs with stable envelopes, raw argument bounds, a single payload rule for exec-style commands, one ordinary-confirmation contract with digest-bound remedies, inherited-flag scope derived from dispatch, and closed, shell-safe completion. Many of these rules are held by named tests, which makes them durable.\n\nNeeds improvement: the operator language has drifted from its own selector rule. `-f`/`--input-dir` mean different inputs on different commands. `--dry-run` has three boundaries. `--trust-on-first-use` names the opposite of what it does. Structured output without `--yes` fails in three ways. The `--stage` safeguard paragraph contradicts preflight. The Effects column, which claims to be the sole owner of effects, omits privilege and misclassifies `plan`. Privilege is coupled with availability in code.\n\nBad: the comma-list section keeps seven per-command empty-value rules labelled 'compatibility' in a pre-1.0 project. One of them silently widens `machine trust --name=` to every Machine. These rules are dense, hard for agents to apply and contradict D241's intent.\n\nThe prose is also very dense: single paragraphs carry many conditions, as in the sudo relay and status steps. That costs agent context but is mostly correct.

Candidates after verification: C01-1 CLI-04; C01-2 CLI-07; C01-3 CLI-05; C01-4 CLI-06; C01-5 CLI-08; C01-6 CLI-34; C01-7 CLI-35; C01-8 CLI-36. Named and not pursued: 6 further points.

<a id="lane-c02"></a>

#### Lane C02: CLI: lifecycle commands and diff

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/cli.md:568-1003`; `specs/cli/commands.md:342-530`; `specs/cli/output.md:791-993`.

Good: the lifecycle contract is unusually rigorous on safety. Repeating a verb is safe, a preview is the verb's own decision with no effects, authorizations are bound to step digests, `--yes` never authorizes anything, the receipt is stable and survives interrupts, and stage selection gates without narrowing the plan or bending dependency order. diff is read-only, its Input header names the real way forward after an edit, and `--tool` is privilege-safe. Needs improvement: the operator cannot learn before any effect what happens after editing a completed context. `plan` is specified as a destroy preview on one page and an additive preview on others, and `status` offers nothing, shows no input change and skips additive readiness. The receipt's shared `next` rule contradicts itself for `plan` over a completed apply. Exit statuses for failed, unknown and paused-destroy results are unmapped. The diff exit table omits `unmanaged`, and status 3 is oversold as drift detection. Bad: drift has no route to action. diff sends the operator to status, status offers nothing, and diff's object labels run against its patch signs. The prose is dense, with exception-on-exception sentences (cli.md:741-815) that an agent must parse very carefully, which raises the chance of divergence even where the rules agree.

Candidates after verification: C02-1 CLI-01; C02-2 CLI-09; C02-3 CLI-37; C02-4 CLI-38; C02-5 CLI-10; C02-6 CLI-39; C02-7 CLI-40; C02-8 CLI-41. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

<a id="lane-c03"></a>

#### Lane C03: CLI: inspection, access, power and file copy

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/cli.md:1004-1660`; `specs/cli/machine-copy.md:1-66`; `specs/deferred/cli-access-and-rendering.md:1-139`.

Good: the slice is safety-first. Target and applicability are proved before any custody read, raw exports have exact stream contracts, SSH sessions prove host keys before credentials with pinned clients and no ambient configuration, power commands cannot touch the controller host, and the lifecycle and power facts are kept independent. Every utility here states that it registers no operation, and the text largely keeps that promise. Needs improvement: the disclosure surface has grown by accretion. The object-user S3 reveal is in cli.md and secrets.md but absent from the output contract, which still claims a single secret field. `machine cp` is missing from the scope's list of admitted utilities. Kind-by-kind refusal tables restate the applicability table and have already drifted on codes and remedies, which taxes the goal of adding cluster kinds cheaply. Bad: a few direct contradictions. Empty keyring flags give exit 1 against the usage rule. The borrowed `--ssh-user` credential differs between one and several Machines. The host-key path of an installed Machine whose evidence the context does not own is undefined, with a remedy that points at a command that skips it. The prose is very dense; single sentences carry four or five rules, which raises the risk that an agent misreads one.

Candidates after verification: C03-1 CLI-11; C03-2 SCO-03; C03-3 CLI-12; C03-4 CLI-13; C03-5 CLI-14; C03-6 ARC-43; C03-7 REC-81; C03-8 API-97. Named and not pursued: 6 further points.

<a id="lane-c04"></a>

#### Lane C04: CLI output: streams, human and JSON output, preflight, discovery

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/cli/output.md:1-790`.

Good: the output contract is unusually rigorous for a pre-1.0 CLI. It has one stream and exit table, an envelope with strict invariants (`ok` iff exit 0, one document, no partial success), single-pass escaping against terminal injection, a test-enforced diagnostic registry with context-carrying remediations, progress that reports only observed events, and structured modes that keep every fact whatever the presentation flags. Preflight and cluster info are honest about what they don't observe. Needs improvement: the 'stable result fields' table has drifted from the prose and the command catalog (`authorizations`, `controller uninstall` and `rebind`, `objectUsers`). Check rows use two shapes and vocabularies for one fact. Preflight's exit status for unknown or pending readiness is undefined. The power verbs' failure envelope changes with the number of Machines named. The human failure stdout rule is a closed list that other passages break. Bad: whether `controller install` accepts JSON without `--dry-run` gets opposite answers on three pages. The output version is pinned at `v1alpha1`, the spec promises stable shapes, and no rule says when the version moves. That contradicts the pre-1.0 policy and leaves machine consumers unable to detect reshapes. The section mixes contract with long test-name lists, which is useful for traceability but makes the rules harder to scan.

Candidates after verification: C04-1 CLI-15; C04-2 CLI-18; C04-3 CLI-16; C04-4 CLI-11; C04-5 CLI-42; C04-6 CLI-43; C04-7 CLI-17; C04-8 CLI-44. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-c05"></a>

#### Lane C05: CLI output: results, diagnostics, logs, compatibility

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/cli/output.md:791-1426`; `specs/contexts/log-root.md:1-140`.

Good: the slice is unusually precise and deterministic. Diagnostic order is total, the registry is closed and test-enforced, `status` performs no probe and reads only records, and logs are firmly troubleshooting material, never evidence. The operator always gets a `Logs` and `Follow` pair before effects and after the result, and the log reader is safe by construction (escaping, no-follow descent, non-blocking locks). Needs improvement: the registry gives meanings only. Severity is implicit and worded three ways, default remedies live only in code, and generic codes (`context.state`, `lifecycle.state`, `secret.store`) are reused beyond their registered meaning. Log bounds are partly missing from the bounds table, and retention counting is ambiguous. Status tokens collide with progress tokens. Bad: the retained raw adapter output relies entirely on `no_log`, and the spec requires `no_log` only for tasks that read bound material. Produced credentials (kubeconfig, dashboard password) and secrets printed by native tools have no stated masking mechanism, despite the security invariant. The Compatibility section promises post-1.0 stability through an undefined review and ignores the project's pre-1.0 policy.

Candidates after verification: C05-1 ARC-05; C05-2 CLI-18; C05-3 CLI-45; C05-4 CLI-46; C05-5 CLI-47; C05-6 CLI-48. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

<a id="lane-c06"></a>

#### Lane C06: Operator journey as documented

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/cli/commands.md:199-341`; `docs/operator-guide.md:1-811`; `README.md`; `examples/README.md`.

The good: host preparation, privilege and sudo, network exposure, logs and following, the write-roots table and uninstall are precise, honest about effects, and agree flag for flag with specs/cli/commands.md. Help, version and completion contracts are exemplary: closed, test-named and implementable without divergence. Needs improvement: the guide is a set of excellent reference sections around a missing spine. There is no generic first-run sequence (context init, secret generate/set, media add, the controller stage, preflight, plan, apply, status, access, destroy, context delete). The operator is sent to lab runbooks that each repeat that sequence. Recovery after a failed apply is buried under a build-change heading. Unattended apply omits the digest-bound authorization rule. Bad: the guide's `cluster exec` default (first node) contradicts the spec after B1090, and its multi-Machine and cluster examples name a context that declares neither. The guide and the examples README disagree about who owns a journey; the real-hardware journey row points at a README with no commands, and one runbook lives under examples/. The guide also carries milestone gate status and developer gate commands that other pages own, which will drift.

### Objectives, scope, concepts and names

<a id="lane-s01"></a>

#### Lane S01: Objectives, scope and non-goals

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/project.md:1-184`; `specs/glossary.md:1-110`; `specs/index.md:1-58`; `specs/milestones.md:1-139`; `README.md`; `specs/deferred/add-ons-design.md`; `specs/deferred/ceph-api.md`; `specs/deferred/cli-access-and-rendering.md`; `specs/deferred/custom-playbooks.md`; `specs/deferred/machine-arms.md`; `specs/deferred/native-procedure.md`; `specs/deferred/reconciliation-scenarios.md`; `specs/milestones/m5.md`; `specs/milestones/m6.md`.

Good: project.md is compact and mostly principled. The portfolio and envelope split names who may widen scope. The handoff rule (no transfer of ownership; change = destroy + apply) is precise. The verify-only fabric boundary and the no-external-location rule are testable. Where day-2-looking features are defined (update within release, upgrade-chain tolerance, additive apply), each is bounded. Deferred pages state honestly what is enforced and which item revives them. Needs improvement: scope is often stated as hand-copied lists (portfolio bullets, utility commands) that have already drifted (M7 missing, machine cp missing). The rule for admitting future day-2 operations is 'when requested', not a criterion. Scope vocabulary (owner, operator, day-2, owned) is not in the glossary. Bad: two scope statements contradict live contract. The non-goal against running operator-authored code conflicts with the reserved CustomPlaybook and steps shapes that B102 and the unrealized table keep alive, and those shapes also break the no-external-location rule. The D246 sentence 'only what GitOps cannot do' is broader than the decision and fails the committed add-on portfolio and the MetalLB-pool exception. Also, three admitted declarations carry 'none tracked', outside every stated scope list.

#### Lane S02: Immediate portfolio, family scope and qualification truthfulness

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/openshift-coverage.md:1-209`; `specs/ceph-coverage.md:1-322`; `specs/add-on-coverage.md:1-37`; `specs/add-on-coverage.md:366-468`; `specs/substrates.md:20-133`; `docs/acceptance.md`; `specs/project.md:18-62`; `specs/milestones.md:1-40`; `specs/milestones/m1.md:1-80`; `specs/milestones/m2.md:1-80`; `specs/milestones/m3.md:1-80`; `specs/milestones/m4.md:1-80`.

Good: the coverage pages share one strong release rule (operator pins, native tool judges, specializations never approve). They state that profiles are samples, not limits, and keep a clear tier vocabulary (in-tree, emulated, real hardware). Undelivered rows refuse before effects. The substrate port and dispatcher design keeps arms behind one seam, so carrying refused arms does not leak into general code. Needs improvement: whether something is qualified is spread over four places (coverage cells, the substrates table, item sections, the ledger), and they have drifted. D235 and D224 changes did not reach the coverage pages. B776 still sits parked beside B1231, which delivered it. The Ceph page has no Qualified column and still treats OD21 as open. <a id="lane-s03"></a>

#### Lane S03: Concepts: lifecycle terms

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/glossary.md:1-110`.

Good: the glossary has the right governance rule (one meaning, one owner, a qualified marker). Its existing entries (block and step, controller, implementation, arm, variant and case, binding, profile, evidence) are precise and largely respected; controller in particular is used with discipline. The state owner defines wave, attempt, resolution and stage crisply and binds them to tests. Needs improvement: the glossary covers peripheral words but omits the core lifecycle vocabulary it relies on (operation, plan, stage, attempt, resolution, wave, lifecycle unit, environment). 'Operation' and 'plan' each carry three or four senses that no qualifier separates. 'Step' has a third sense, status next commands with `nextSteps`, that open Q125 does not consider. 'Stage' also names staging directories and controller-block runs inside the very page that owns the controller stage. Bad: the lifecycle unit is defined two ways. The owning section roots it in an environment directory, while the CLI spec, the path table and the contexts contract make it the context and say directories are never identity. All findings are cheap text fixes; one (`nextSteps`) touches a JSON name, which pre-1.0 makes cheap now.

Candidates after verification: S03-1 CON-15; S03-2 CON-16; S03-3 CON-17; S03-4 CON-18; S03-5 CON-19; S03-6 CON-20. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

#### Lane S04: Concepts: infrastructure terms

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/glossary.md:1-110`.

Good: the glossary enforces one meaning per term with an owner link, and its qualified entries (segment versus Network, arm versus variant versus implementation, add-on versus package) are sharp and match D240 and the architecture. The substrate seam itself is well designed: the arm selects, the realized target is frozen once, and consumers never name an arm. Needs improvement: the glossary covers fewer than half of the infrastructure terms this lane checked. Machine, node, host, provider host, site, placement and claim have no entry, and 'host' and 'placement' each carry five or six senses. A Ceph node's site can be authored on two objects, with an agreement rule that only code states. Each fix is cheap pre-1.0: a field table, three glossary rows, and dropping or constraining one API field.

### Architecture, extension and language responsibility

<a id="lane-r01"></a>

#### Lane R01: Architecture: boundaries, bounded contexts, package structure

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:1-503`.

What is good: the architecture is principled. Contexts are defined by domain, not by vendor. Families keep their implementations behind selection seams. Ports are consumer-owned. The general flow is guarded against implementation names. Exceptions are a closed, symbol-precise list, and procedures name real fitness tests. The on-disk directory map matches the context table at directory level. What needs improvement: the package-kind table does not cover several packages, including two technical packages with network and filesystem effects that domain code may import. 'Adding a lifecycle capability' omits the contract-suite row. A skill still says architecture lacks the touch set it now has. The 'Finding code' step for family kinds points to a nonexistent path. What is bad: the composition root is where generality leaks. It makes domain decisions and writes operator remedies, and it hard-binds specific arms and installers (libvirt, baremetal, agentinstall) in translators. The spec forbids this ('no domain decision'), the named exceptions do not cover it, and the 'touches only this list / no consumer changes' promise for new implementations is false. A new substrate arm or installer would pass every test and silently lose firewall preflight, storage dependency proofs or install status. The registry's ClusterInstallsByAgent accessor carries the same leak into Controller.

Candidates after verification: R01-1 ARC-26; R01-2 ARC-28; R01-3 ARC-27; R01-4 ARC-58; R01-5 ARC-55; R01-6 ARC-56; R01-7 ARC-06; R01-8 ARC-57. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

<a id="lane-r02"></a>

#### Lane R02: Architecture: lifecycle ports and the composition root

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:504-716`.

Good: one uniform Capability port covers every domain, with removal, quiescence and removal-observation mandatory. The resolver is an immutable allowlist keyed by (kind, implementation), and frozen blocks resolve exactly. Playbooks are bound as data in composition. Multi-implementation policies are aggregated as lists. Stage-specific work travels in a stage-scoped value, the engine never decodes evidence, and admission and compilation are cleanly separated. The general lifecycle learns of block types only through the resolver's Bindings, so the flow is generic. Needs improvement: the real port surface is Capability plus 27 type-asserted optional interfaces, and the spec documents two of them. architecture.md's description of Execution ("the one widening is Proved") contradicts state-reconciliation.md and the code. The resolver's "API kind" key admits a synthetic, OpenShift-named kind. Bad: cross-capability evidence decoding is wired per consumer to a single producer. Ceph's DataDisk proof goes to libvirt only and PhysicalMachine to bare metal only, so a new substrate arm forces an edit inside the storage domain, which is the edit the extension checklist promises never happens. The composition root also holds add-on and network ordering policy, which the wiring rules forbid.

Candidates after verification: R02-1 ARC-29; R02-2 ARC-30; R02-3 ARC-31; R02-4 ARC-26; R02-5 ARC-59. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-r03"></a>

#### Lane R03: Architecture: implementations, version variation, verification

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:1102-1408`; `.agents/knowledge/version-specializations.md`; `.agents/skills/extend-implementation/SKILL.md`; `.agents/skills/architecture-best-practices/SKILL.md`.

Good: the version-specialization contract is unusually rigorous. Unknown facts fall back to the general variant, seams stay out of trust code, intents and digests are untouched, there are no version pairings, and registries are found by marker. The Python registry tests hold most of these clauses, and the catalog rows cite artifact-level evidence. Selection rules (exactly one match, failure before effects, no fallback) and the exact shrinking allowlists are sound and must survive. Needs improvement: whether to use a typed variant, an implementation or a specialization can be decided from the spec but not from the skill agents follow. 'Proved coordinate' and 'version move' are undefined. Implementation selection by artifact facts has no timing rule. The catalog test ignores the condition and justification columns. The extend-implementation skill duplicates, and contradicts, the spec's touch list. The domain selection template exists in two incompatible forms, and the pages follow neither. Bad: the generic-flow guard is narrower than the spec claims. It knows substrate arms, `*Implementation` constants and the word "ceph", but not OpenShift distribution or install arms, not service implementation values, and not field paths. Yet the spec says the guard rejects 'any other arm … or arm field path'. For the owner's extension goals (other cluster types, other infrastructure components), the promise that general code never names an implementation is held by tests only for substrates and Ceph.

Candidates after verification: R03-1 ARC-32; R03-2 ARC-02; R03-3 ARC-33; R03-4 ARC-60; R03-5 ARC-61; R03-6 ARC-06; R03-7 ARC-62; R03-8 ARC-63. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-r04"></a>

#### Lane R04: Architecture: the Go and Ansible boundary and the collection structure

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:717-1101`.

Good: the adapter result protocol is the strongest contract in the slice. It is one channel, one decoder and one runner core for every domain, with closed phases, bounds, acknowledgement-before-effect, value-free refusals, and breach semantics that fail toward `unknown`. It is test-enforced on both sides. The language table and its single-site Python rules are concrete and mechanically held, and the substrate dispatcher is a sound extension seam. Needs improvement: naming is only partly specified and drifts from the code. The implementation token is placed only for substrate. Playbook and role capability tokens differ in five places. The enforcing test hardcodes domain and implementation lists that refuse the correct infrastructureservices rename and miss `agent`. Module and module-utility names follow no scheme. The read-only allowlist covers `observe` and misses `read`. Bad: the arm touch set is stated three incompatible ways, and the checklist an agent follows breaks a test. The postcondition is judged in Python and again in Go, against D11 and row 774. The first-row placement rule sends any sequenced native procedure to Go while the Python row keeps it. With no definition of 'spec-owned procedure', about 1.19 MB of Ceph Python sits inside the boundary with nothing to review it against.

Candidates after verification: R04-1 ARC-07; R04-2 ARC-64; R04-3 ARC-65; R04-4 ARC-34; R04-5 LNG-02; R04-6 ARC-66; R04-7 ARC-67; R04-8 ARC-47. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

#### Lane R06: Generic-flow leak hunt in the general code

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `test/architecture/family_neutral_test.go`; `internal/reconciliation (by grep)`; `internal/cli (by grep)`; `internal/desiredstate (by grep)`; `internal/environment (by grep)`; `internal/workspace (by grep)`; `internal/diagnostics (by grep)`; `internal/machine (by grep)`; `cmd/bootwright/wiring.go and wiring_*.go (declarations)`.

Good: reconciliation, desired state and diagnostics are close to implementation-free. The family registry and the substrate capability predicates (RealizesPhysicalNICs, VirtualArm, TaggedCarriage, MachineBoundsFor) are the right seams. The guards are mechanical, exact and only shrink: implementation identities are derived from constants, and the family-kind allowlist ceiling is 0. Needs improvement: the guard's literal net is narrow (exact "ceph", "/ceph/", arm values, identity values), and it skips internal/workspace and diagnostics entirely. As a result, Ceph-shaped types (ManagedCeph, IssuerCephadm "cephadm"), libvirt image roots, the Anaconda installer, Redfish, vSphere MAC rules and arm field paths sit in general or neutral packages with no test catching them. Bad: two of the spec's promises are false as written. The 'neutral StorageEvidence port' carries Ceph's FSID, monitors and admin command into the public cluster info shape. The identity test is said to reject arm field paths and does not. Composition binds a single storage inspector and a single storage preflight with no per-kind registry, so the first second storage implementation will need general-flow edits that architecture.md:500 calls a missing seam.

- The implementation-literal check matches exact arm values, implementation identity values, the exact literal "ceph" and the substring "/ceph/". It misses "cephadm", "redfish", "anaconda", "openshift", OLM and service product names (chrony, squid, dnsmasq, nginx), add-on package names, OS families, Go identifiers, struct tags, and arm field paths. Note that architecture.md:1201-1203 claims arm field paths are rejected.
- There is no import-level rule that stops general-flow packages from importing an implementation-specific package, such as internal/storage/preflight, which is in practice Ceph's.

<a id="lane-r07"></a>

#### Lane R07: Extension dry run: a new substrate

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:435-503`; `specs/architecture.md:1102-1235`; `.agents/skills/extend-implementation/SKILL.md`; `specs/api.md:385-466`; `specs/substrates.md:20-133`; `specs/substrates.md:1397-1438`; `specs/substrates.md:1697-1804`; `specs/api/machines.md:34-211`.

Good: selection is explicit, deterministic and fail-closed. Arm-blindness is enforced by an exact, shrink-only test. The Ansible dispatcher keeps consumers arm-blind. The 'seam is missing' rule is the right discipline. The vSphere realization contract is safety-complete on identity and removal. Needs improvement: the architecture's 'touches only this list' is false for a substrate arm, and the skill says the set is unnamed. Step 5 contradicts the dispatcher rule on argument choices. Per-arm facts live in central switches in the general substrate package and in composition helpers outside the listed touch points, and one of them defaults an unknown arm to fetch delivery. The common profile table and the OpenShift platform derivation enumerate arms. The admitted vSphere shape disagrees with its own realization contract. Bad: the machine port and both installation contracts assume an image is inserted (fetch or push). A public-cloud substrate that boots from a provider image with user data cannot be added as an implementation of the existing capability. It forces general-flow edits in cluster and managed-OS installation, which taxes the owner's stated cloud goal. The only image-plus-seed path, templateClone, is bound to vSphere by name.

Candidates after verification: R07-1 refuted; R07-2 ARC-28; R07-3 ARC-73; R07-4 ARC-07; R07-5 API-18; R07-6 API-136; R07-7 refuted; R07-8 API-16. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

**vSphere (declared, unrealized).** It touches everything above except the API arm, which exists. In addition: correct the admitted shape (MAC required where the spec derives it, `segmentRef` "not realized" where the spec says it picks the portgroup). **Is this the minimum?** No. The inherent minimum for a new substrate is: the API arm and its tables, one arm-descriptor row, the arm's package, role and playbooks, the dispatcher row and power-role choices, its bindings, contract-suite rows, goldens and spec sections. Edits that should not be needed are:
- the central `armFacts`/`MachineBoundsFor`/`Arms`/`Realized` switches in the general substrate package (they should be facets of the arm's binding, with no fail-open default);
- the composition helpers `realizationOf`, `pinnedIdentity`, `WithHostAccess(kubevirt...)` and the Ceph `DataDisk` binding (they should dispatch over the bound machine family);
- the OpenShift platform-derivation switch and its spec bullets (they should read a substrate fact);
- the shared machine-profile table and its variant switch;
- the libvirt-hosted family refusal test.

For a public cloud, the decisive blocker is the media-only machine port and the "one installation contract" built on media insertion. Without a declared seed or image delivery kind, the cluster and managed-OS installations, which are general consumers, must change.

#### Lane R08: Extension dry run: a new cluster type

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:435-503`; `specs/architecture.md:1102-1235`; `.agents/skills/extend-implementation/SKILL.md`; `specs/api.md:385-466`; `api/v1alpha1/families.go`; `specs/openshift-clusters.md:25-126`; `specs/openshift-clusters.md:1183-1213`; `specs/api/openshift-clusters.md:20-63`; `specs/add-ons.md:51-139`.

Good: the extension machinery is sound in principle. The cluster family registry with categories and roles, strict fail-closed implementation selection, the specialization-versus-implementation boundary, the seam rule in the implementation recipe, kind-neutral stages and test-held refusal tables are what a multi-implementation product needs. Needs improvement: the recipes cover a new capability and a second implementation of an existing kind, but not a new kind in an existing family, which D183 makes the normal path for kubeadm or managed Kubernetes. Several spec tables (environment closure, unclaimed objects, CLI applicability, add-on clusterRef and messages, controller packages) are written per kind while the registry is per category. The skill duplicates and contradicts architecture's touch list. Bad: method- and kind-specific knowledge sits in general places and is described as neutral: ClusterInstallsByAgent in the API registry driving controller packages, cluster access hard-wired to the agent install block, add-on instances freezing Kind OpenShiftCluster, and container-cluster port types aliased from the openshift package. The family-neutral test does not scan internal/addons, internal/substrate or the container-cluster root, so these escape it. The managed control plane, a cluster with no Machines, has no contract seam at all.

Candidates after verification: R08-1 API-137; R08-2 ARC-58; R08-3 ARC-75; R08-4 ARC-74; R08-5 refuted; R08-6 ARC-65; R08-7 API-138; R08-8 ARC-06. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

**Is this the minimum?** No. The additive part is the kind schema, catalog and registry rows, the implementation package, its bindings, roles, refusal table and contract-suite rows. It matches the architecture's promise, and stages, the engine and the adapter protocol need no edit. On top of that, today's contract and code force about a dozen edits to general places. These should not be needed: the container-cluster domain root (`effect.go`, `members.go`, `facts.go`) and the add-on instance kind literals; access wiring fixed to the agent install block; `ClusterInstallsByAgent` and the controller's agent-specific package rows; `openshift.AddonFacts` called directly in composition; playbook names without an implementation token; and spec tables written per kind (clusterRef row, environment closure, unclaimed row, CLI applicability). Each would disappear if the container category published its facts (access, host packages, platform tokens, provider edge) through `containercluster.Facts`, if specs stated rows per category, and if the neutrality test covered add-ons and substrate roots. The managed control plane adds one real gap with no seam at all: a cluster bound to an InfraProvider with no Machines. Nothing in the closure, claims or substrate contracts describes it.

<a id="lane-r09"></a>

#### Lane R09: Extension dry run: a new storage type

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:435-503`; `specs/architecture.md:1102-1235`; `.agents/skills/extend-implementation/SKILL.md`; `specs/api.md:385-466`; `api/v1alpha1/families.go`; `specs/ceph.md:20-77`; `specs/api/ceph.md:19-84`; `specs/ceph-resources.md:1350-1420`; `specs/api/environment.md:149-217`; `api/v1alpha1/addons_storage.go`.

Good: the selection contract (exactly one claim per object, allowlisted resolver, frozen identities), the version-specialization discipline and the cluster family registry with layout accessors are well designed. They are mostly enforced by named tests, and node layouts are already kind-neutral. Ceph's capability families have neutral names, so an alternative implementation can bind beside it. Needs improvement: the procedure for adding an implementation assumes the selector already distinguishes the newcomer, but Ceph's selector omits `spec.distribution`. A second distribution therefore edits Ceph's own refusal row and claims, and agents will split between an arm inside the implementation and a new implementation. Playbook naming has no implementation slot outside substrates. The skill and architecture disagree about whether a touch set exists, and about its file names. Bad: roles are registered per category, not per kind. The Environment closure and the add-on effect vocabulary are written in Ceph kinds. The cluster discovery output contract closes the kind set and has a Ceph-shaped type in general Environment inspection that the family-neutral test cannot see. Together these turn 'a new storage type is additive' into edits across api, environment, add-ons, the CLI and output, and scenario (b), an external array, has no specified home at all.

Candidates after verification: R09-1 API-139; R09-2 CLI-25; R09-3 ARC-76; R09-4 decided; R09-5 ARC-75; R09-6 ARC-65; R09-7 ARC-77. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

**Is this the minimum?** For (a), the floor is the new package, its composition rows, its roles and its domain-table rows. The procedure promises exactly that, but today it also forces edits to the existing Ceph implementation: its refusal row, its claims, and possibly its playbook names. It also forces edits to the general selector sentence in architecture.md, because the Ceph selector omits `spec.distribution`. None of those should be needed once the selector names the arm and each implementation's refusals derive from what it claims. For (b), the floor is a new kind, its registry entry, its domain and a consuming add-on package. Beyond that floor, today's contracts force edits to general code and general specs that should not be needed: the family registry's role shape, the Environment selection closure, the add-on effect vocabulary and the fdf schema's `CephConsumer` reference, the cluster discovery and status output schema with its general-flow `ManagedCeph` inspection type, and the CLI not-applicable tables. All of these move onto per-kind role registration and a domain-published inspection detail. The edits to fitness lists and wiring in the composition root are the expected cost of an allowlisted registry, and they are acceptable.

</details>

<a id="lane-r10"></a>

#### Lane R10: Extension dry run: a new infrastructure component type

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:435-503`; `specs/architecture.md:1102-1235`; `.agents/skills/extend-implementation/SKILL.md`; `specs/api.md:385-466`; `specs/infrastructure-services.md:1-117`; `specs/infrastructure-services.md:581-711`; `specs/api/infrastructure-services.md:12-144`.

Good: the selection and claiming contract is strong. It is deterministic, allowlisted and fails closed, every effect-bearing object is claimed once or refused by a named table, and the 'missing seam lands as its own step' rule is sound. The cluster family registry shows the right extension pattern. Managed services derive their configuration from the graph and share one role across both placement arms, so trust and SSH rules carry over to new kinds at no cost. Needs improvement: there is no extension procedure for a new kind or capability definition, and the procedures that exist do not state the fit criterion for the shared capability. The infrastructure-services selection section lacks the Implementations, Supported shape and Test subsections that architecture says it has. Service kinds have no registry, so Environment, compilation and controller code restate them, and per-kind transports and probes live outside the Definition, in Go composition and Python. Bad: one shared request shape and version for every managed network service means that adding a kind moves the digests of the existing kinds and forces operators to destroy contexts. That breaks the 'additions are additive' goal on the exact scenario the owner plans (more infrastructure component types).

Candidates after verification: R10-1 decided; R10-2 ARC-78; R10-3 refuted; R10-4 ARC-79; R10-5 ARC-02; R10-6 ARC-80; R10-7 ARC-06. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

Is this the minimum? No. The irreducible set is: the kind's API schema, catalog row, order and page row; one Definition package; its templates, playbooks and probe; its derived-configuration and security rows; its edge row; its contract-suite and recipe rows; and an example. Several edits should not be needed. Environment selection's `rootKinds`, compilation's `normalizationOrder`, the domain's `IsService` and the controller's `conflictKinds` restate the service-kind list that a `ServiceKinds()` registry, like the cluster `Families()`, should own. Composition repeats the definition list three times, and tests repeat it six more times. The firewall wiring, `layout.go` and the Python `TRANSPORTS`/`answer_for` branch on the kind for facts (transports, fixed port, probe) that the Definition should declare. The most costly edit is the shared `managedservice.Request` and its one `RequestVersion`. Adding a kind changes the Go request schema of proxy, DNS and NTP, forces a version and digest move, and by the spec's own rule makes every context with a managed proxy, DNS or NTP service refuse until it is destroyed. That is a non-additive change to unrelated implementations. The spec's procedures also say nothing about this scenario: neither 'Adding a lifecycle capability' nor 'Adding an implementation' covers a new kind built as a capability definition, and nothing says when a kind (DHCP with lease state, a CA with produced material) is outside the shared single-socket capability and needs its own capability, as ArtifactServer has.

<a id="lane-r11"></a>

#### Lane R11: Language responsibility: the stated rules

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/architecture.md:717-831`; `specs/project.md:111-135`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/go.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/ansible.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/python.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/formatting.md`; `.claude/rules/go.md`; `.claude/rules/ansible.md`; `.claude/rules/guidance.md`; `test/architecture/language_rows_test.go`; `Makefile`; `docs/development.md`.

Good: the slice is unusually explicit. A table gives a Holds and a Never per language. The Go and Ansible ownership bullets are crisp. Python execution sites are defined by where the code runs, with single owners for process start, JSON and quoting, enforced by an AST test with exception lists that only shrink. A fitness test ties the source map to the spec's row names, and shell exceptions are tracked (B967). Needs improvement: the table is not decidable as written. The first-match rule plus a broad Go question routes allowed adapter sequencing and repository tooling to Go. Nothing decides between YAML tasks, filters and modules for remote effects, parsing native output or rendering native documents, and the role YAML shows that split in practice. The Go row's Never cell contradicts the Go local probes the same section requires. Bad: coverage has holes the test cannot see. A remote-run Python worker in internal/ has a stated 3.9 floor but no row, floor test or sites test. Make recipes, the Dockerfile and four completion shims have no row. The formatting reference demands POSIX sh for scripts the spec makes bash. Path-scoped agent rules skip scripts/, e2e/ and the Makefile entirely.

Candidates after verification: R11-1 LNG-02; R11-2 LNG-03; R11-3 LNG-04; R11-4 LNG-01; R11-5 LNG-05; R11-6 LNG-06; R11-7 LNG-07; R11-8 LNG-08. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

<a id="lane-r12"></a>

#### Lane R12: Language responsibility: where logic lives

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `AIDS/snapshot-files.tsv (grep plugins, scripts, Makefile, completion)`; `scripts (every wrapper; they are short)`; `scripts/hooks/stop-check`; `e2e/render.sh`; `Dockerfile`; `specs/architecture.md:717-831`.

Good: the language boundary is one of the strongest parts of the contract. It gives a first-yes placement table, single-owner modules per Python site enforced through the syntax tree, named exceptions that only shrink, and a fitness test that holds every source to a row. Go's own reach is narrow and named. Ansible YAML has no shell tasks. Wrappers are pinned, and the case renderer has sound limits. Needs improvement: the vocabulary at the Go/Python seam. Python demonstrably runs spec-owned step readbacks, convergence comparisons and step machines (Ceph stretch stages, Redfish firmware, network convergence), while the table and D11 say Python never judges a postcondition. Cross-language twins (protocol constants, erase regions, request shapes, semantic admission rules) are held by ad hoc tests with no contract. The term 'canonical JSON' covers two byte encodings. The site rule omits module utilities and filters. Bad: the Shell row states an absolute rule that three tracked scripts break. Its exceptions live in agent guidance, the hook's exception is untracked, and the fitness test checks shebangs, not logic. Proportion: Python is 47k non-test lines against 153k of Go, almost half of it Ceph. That is consistent with 'specifics behind adapters', but it makes the seam definitions important.

Candidates after verification: R12-1 LNG-09; R12-2 LNG-10; R12-3 LNG-11; R12-4 LNG-12; R12-5 LNG-13. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

### The spec corpus as an agent harness

<a id="lane-h01"></a>

#### Lane H01: Routing layer: entrypoints, indexes and conventions

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `AGENTS.md`; `CLAUDE.md`; `specs/index.md:1-58`; `specs/milestones.md:1-139`; `.agents/skills/index.md`; `.agents/knowledge/index.md`; `.claude/rules/ansible.md`; `.claude/rules/go.md`; `.claude/rules/guidance.md`.

Good: the routing layer is small, has byte budgets and is held by ratcheting tests: reachability, section and leaf budgets, history allowances, Not-yet-met lines, links and anchors, skill-wrapper parity, and an ask list derived from the catalog. Every index anchor I checked (about 30) resolves to the heading that holds the rule, and the authorization rules agree between AGENTS.md and milestones.md. Needs improvement: the index mostly routes whole pages of 70 to 186KB while AGENTS.md demands section-only reads. It has no route for the generic extension contract, which is the owner's main goal. The milestone reading rule is stated four times and has drifted. The section budget exceptions are parked indefinitely. One convention lives only in a Claude-only rule file. docs/ has no owner in the routing layer. Bad: the agent effect ban is an inline partial list. The tracked ask exemptions let an agent run `context delete --purge --allow-orphans` with no prompt, which abandons live resources and their credential custody. Codex has no tracked policy at all, so the AGENTS.md prose is its only guard. One owner per fact is held by discipline, not by a check. The drift in the reading rule shows the cost.

Candidates after verification: H01-1 COR-01; H01-2 COR-24; H01-3 COR-26; H01-4 COR-27; H01-5 COR-28; H01-6 SKL-12; H01-7 COR-29; H01-8 SKL-19. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.

<a id="lane-h02"></a>

#### Lane H02: Retrieval path, quantified

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `AGENTS.md`; `specs/index.md:1-58`; `specs/milestones.md:1-139`; `.agents/skills/index.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/SKILL.md`; `AIDS/sizes.tsv`; `AIDS/sections.tsv`; `AIDS/outline.txt`.

Good: the retrieval design is unusually deliberate. AGENTS.md is a small router, budgets only fall and are enforced, milestone openings are bounded, and anchored section routing for the large domains keeps a typical task at 25-38k tokens in a corpus of about 3 MB. Needs improvement: the read rule for milestones is stated in four places that already disagree. The index's section table misses six of the largest pages, and one index link sends agents to a 29 KB section when a 1.3 KB leaf exists. The leaf budget measures a smaller unit than the one an anchor link loads. The per-edit stack of procedure files (about 9k tokens for Go work) costs more than the owning content on small edits, and three of its files have no budget. Bad: \"and what they link\" in AGENTS.md has no bound and contradicts \"never read them whole\". Followed literally, it turns a 2 KB item read into a load of more than 1 MB. The exception tables owned by a parked B965 have become the standing rule for the largest sections, and B965's count has drifted. Nothing records where a delivered record goes, and recent records sit under an M3 heading that does not describe them.

Candidates after verification: H02-1 COR-30; H02-2 COR-24; H02-3 COR-31; H02-4 COR-28; H02-5 COR-26; H02-6 COR-27; H02-7 COR-32; H02-8 COR-25. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

<a id="lane-h03"></a>

#### Lane H03: The Not-yet-met convention

Auditor model: sonnet. Assigned: `AIDS/not-yet-met.txt`; `specs/index.md:49-58`; `.agents/skills/milestones-and-knowledge/SKILL.md`; `specs/api.md:39-83`.

What is good: the convention is simple, owned in one place, and backed by a precise self-tested matcher. The skill adds a useful rule against delivered-record links, and the items resolve. The unrealized table is data-backed, and the history ratchet is a sound way to shrink debt. What needs improvement: the matcher proves only that an item exists and is not 'completed', so lines outlive in-tree delivery (B721, B67, B760), point at items that were split (B79), or track gaps no open item states (B1104). Markers that are mid-line, bold or unlinked escape the check (six sites, one unlinked). Several checked paragraphs also run on into live rules. What is bad: unmet state is restated across five channels with no declared owner, so an agent cannot answer "is this implemented" from one lookup, and the observed drift is real contradiction on a physical-install path and a proxy path. Three unrealized fields have no item, and two parked non-goals are written as unmet rules. All fixes are cheap now (no compatibility), mostly sentences plus two test cases.

Candidates after verification: H03-1 COR-02; H03-2 COR-05; H03-3 COR-06; H03-4 COR-33; H03-5 API-34; H03-6 COR-34. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

#### Lane D01a: Schema-to-page parity: environment, secrets, machines, networks

Auditor model: sonnet. Every lexical grammar the pages state matches api/v1alpha1/lexical.go. What needs improvement is the prose around the fields. Four rules are owned by two or three pages that drift: root-disk listing in erase (the one contradiction on a destructive path), the serial-number grammar, SSH credential separation, and the install-gateway check. The realized KubeVirt arm lives in a page titled 'Refused'. Nothing in the lane is unsafe as written except the stale erase sentence, which is a page defect (the code follows the safer reading).

Assigned: `.agents/skills/index.md`; `.agents/skills/architecture-best-practices/SKILL.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/SKILL.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/agent-operation.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/ansible.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/formatting.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/git-integration.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/go.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/python.md`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/verification.md`; `.agents/skills/extend-implementation/SKILL.md`; `.agents/skills/milestones-and-knowledge/SKILL.md`; `.agents/skills/security-safety/SKILL.md`; `.agents/skills/ux-and-apis/SKILL.md`.

Good: every command, test name, script and path cited by the skills, references, wrappers and rules exists in the snapshot. Wrapper parity, byte budgets and ask-rule coverage are held by tests. The verification tiers, the Contract/breaking-change discipline and the add-on recipe are precise and executable. The guidance is lean, and agent operation stays vendor-neutral and quality-first. Needs improvement: some skills restate spec rules or inventories in their own words, and those copies have started to drift. The selection-heading rule contradicts architecture.md's template. The extend-implementation touch set is stale now that architecture names it. git-integration copies the contract_paths list. The read-narrowly rule exists in three versions. There is no procedure for gate failures and flakes the task did not cause, and verification.md contradicts AGENTS.md on whether to fix them. The ask list's git rebase entry taxes the D168 no-ask integration, and it falsifies the index's description of the list. Bad: nothing unsafe was found. The defects are drift, in exactly the places the corpus's own one-owner rule exists to prevent; the fixes are mostly one-sentence links.

Candidates after verification: G01-1 ARC-02; G01-2 ARC-06; G01-3 SKL-06; G01-4 SKL-07; G01-5 COR-24; G01-6 SKL-08; G01-7 DOC-20; G01-8 SKL-05. Named and not pursued: 8 further points.

<a id="lane-g02"></a>

#### Lane G02: Runtime discoverability and parity: Claude Code and Codex

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `.claude/settings.json`; `.claude/skills (the six wrappers)`; `.claude/rules (the three files)`; `CLAUDE.md`; `AGENTS.md`; `.codex/hooks.json`; `scripts/hooks/stop-check`; `.agents/skills/index.md:25-36`; `.agents/skills/code-implementation/references/verification.md:65-80`.

Good: the instruction layout is minimal and correct for both runtimes. CLAUDE.md imports AGENTS.md, skills are canonical in Codex's discovery path, and the wrappers' frontmatter is gate-checked. The Stop hook script meets both runtimes' documented exit and stdout contracts, has a thorough test, and dedups failures for runtimes without stop_hook_active. The Bootwright ask globs are well shaped (leading wildcard) and tied to the command catalog by a test, an unusually strong practice. Needs improvement: both the hook and the path-scoped rules depend on the session's working directory, while the mandated workflow edits a separate worktree, so in a common setup both silently do nothing. The 300 s hook bound is shorter than focus's own lane bound. The git and Ansible patterns miss `git -C`, trailing force flags and ad-hoc `ansible`. One convention lives only in a Claude rule file. Bad: the hardware-safety rule of AGENTS.md has machine enforcement in Claude Code only. Codex supports project rules and a deny-capable PreToolUse hook, and the repository tracks neither, so one shared guard script would serve both runtimes.

Candidates after verification: G02-1 SKL-01; G02-2 SKL-09; G02-3 SKL-10; G02-4 SKL-02; G02-5 SKL-11; G02-6 SKL-12; G02-7 refuted; G02-8 SKL-13. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-g03"></a>

#### Lane G03: Skill portfolio and token cost

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `.agents/skills/index.md`; `.agents/skills (every SKILL.md and reference; sizes in AIDS/sizes.tsv)`; `AGENTS.md`; `specs/index.md:1-58`; `AIDS/sizes.tsv`.

Good: the portfolio is small, with six skills, about 1.4 KB of always-loaded descriptions and a 2.5 KB AGENTS.md. Procedure is separated cleanly from specs and history. Wrappers are held by a test, always-read files carry ratcheted byte budgets, and the verification tiers are measured. The 'broken once' rule lists and the add-on recipe are high-value and specific. Needs improvement: the content-digest procedure is scattered across seven files and owned by the Go reference, so Ansible work pays for go.md. formatting.md and the guidance rule pull large, mostly irrelevant files into common tasks. Of the per-edit files, only code-implementation is budgeted. The index's 'provisional' rule cannot be measured and no item tracks it. The skill and specs/architecture.md disagree on where a domain names its selector, and six domains use four layouts. Bad or missing: the repository's most frequent slice type, audits and reviews (25+ audit-lane slices), has no skill. Slice planning, defined as in-sequence work, has no procedure. Live-run triage, where a knowledge page records an unnecessary destroy, has none either. Codex sessions have only prose against effectful commands, while Claude has tested ask rules.

### The tracked examples

<a id="lane-e01"></a>

#### Lane E01: Examples: coverage of the API surface and composition

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `examples/README.md`; `AIDS/examples-stats.txt`; `specs/api/input.md:1-196`; `specs/api.md:385-405`; `examples/full-platforms/multidc-platform (every file)`; `examples/infrastructure-services/lab-services (every file)`; `two examples of your choice from each of examples/add-ons, examples/ceph-clusters, examples/openshift-clusters and examples/machines (every file)`.

Good: the examples are honest. They separate 'Install' scenarios from 'Prepare' profiles, flag placeholders inline, hold no secret bytes, keep every scenario self-sufficient, and the refused multidc reference has pinned diagnostics. Service endpoints use addressRef, so the controller IP is stated once. Kind defaults are a sound mechanism for stating fleet facts once. Needs improvement: examples restate many values that normalization derives (fqdns, SANs, sites, defaults), so adapting one means many edits with no stated minimal set. The layout convention is unstated. Several kinds and Environment fields have no example. ClusterAddonProfile's description promises configuration it cannot hold. Bad: two KubeVirt READMEs and a runbook promise a virtctl pin that no Environment declares. The spec has no supported way for two environments to share objects: import takes one directory, links are refused, and the 'Environment's directory is the scope' wording conflicts with multi-source validate. As a result 59% of example YAML files are byte-identical copies, and READMEs describe scenarios as 'X plus' a few files.

Candidates after verification: E01-1 DOC-07; E01-2 API-131; E01-3 API-57; E01-4 API-132; E01-5 DOC-26; E01-6 DOC-27; E01-7 DOC-23; E01-8 DOC-28. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.
