### Second round: findings named and not pursued, and gaps the critics found

<a id="lane-z01"></a>

#### Lane Z01: Overflow promotion: reconciliation, safety and security rules

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `AIDS/overflow-rules.md`.

Good: the reconciliation and safety contract fails closed nearly everywhere. Removal proofs are read-only before any effect, unknown is never read as absent, and refusals name exits pinned by tests. Many overflow items were judged Low on inspection because a later re-verification (erase worker, %pre, apply-time media check) catches the hazard. Needs improvement: the promised exits, and the retention and classification rules at the edges of durable state. An update path can collect the revision a completed apply still depends on. An I/O error is classified as a foreign format and leads to an irreversible discard. A named deletion exit cannot run on the store it is offered for. Bad: two Ceph removal rules can leave an environment undestroyable (a shared provided tiebreaker) or destroy data the operator was told is protected (pools created after handoff inside a retired VM cluster). Neither has an admission guard or a plan-time disclosure. The provided-host package rule also contradicts the 'never upgrades a host' promise on the same page.

Candidates after verification: Z01-1 REC-70; Z01-2 REC-71; Z01-3 REC-72; Z01-4 REC-136; Z01-5 REC-137; Z01-6 REC-138. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

<a id="lane-z02"></a>

#### Lane Z02: Overflow promotion: API, CLI and concepts

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `AIDS/overflow-api-cli.md`.

Most overflow items in the API, CLI and concepts lanes are Low: restatements that drifted, fields with one legal value, or naming taste. Several apparent contradictions dissolve once the owning section is read. Paused destroy is in the state machine table, `storage.not-ready` comes only from observations, and the `next:` token is explicitly not a command. Two items earned promotion. First, the cluster discovery contract promises fields (OpenShift endpoints and artifact metadata) and a node list (in the session remedies) that neither the spec defines nor the code emits. Second, the Network API admits a VLAN tag on a managed libvirt Network that its own arm always carries untagged. What is good: the managed Ceph inspection entry is a model field contract; the unrealized table is code-backed and tested; the Network provided/arm union is clean; and the state machine table is complete. What needs work: prose summaries (Kinds rows, catalog cells, remedies) are written separately from the field tables, and that is where both promoted defects came from. Deriving summaries from the tables, or linking to them, would prevent this class of defect.

Candidates after verification: Z02-1 CLI-30; Z02-2 refuted. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-z03"></a>

#### Lane Z03: Overflow promotion: architecture, extension, language and skills

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `AIDS/overflow-architecture-harness.md (the lanes whose key starts with R, G, H or E)`.

Good: most overflow items are minor, and the corpus has strong general principles to judge them against: the missing-seam rule, fail-closed proofs, refusal rows that lift with their delivering item, and version-specialization discipline. Most of the R, G, H and E overflow is Low drift or repeats filed candidates, especially in the G and H lanes, where the Codex guard, effect lists and milestone routing are already filed. Needs improvement: the general flow still leaks libvirt in places an extension would hit first. Capacity admission is owned by the Ceph page and wired through a storage package and a single libvirt admission closure. The uninstall proof and its image root are a fixed libvirt/podman enumeration. Substrate target refusals live on the OpenShift page. In each case the 'touches only this list' promise of architecture.md is false for the next arm. Bad: the storage-node FQDN default breaks the Ceph host-identity rule for every Bootwright-installed node. The examples hide this with 45 hand-written overrides, and preflight checks the Machine name, not the registered name, so the failure surfaces only once cephadm runs. Also, 'installer-provisioned' names a Machine lifecycle with the opposite of its OpenShift meaning.

Candidates after verification: Z03-1 API-06; Z03-2 ARC-19; Z03-3 ARC-83; Z03-4 ARC-21; Z03-5 ARC-84. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

<a id="lane-z04"></a>

#### Lane Z04: Overflow promotion: drift sweeps and the milestone corpus

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `AIDS/overflow-architecture-harness.md (the lanes whose key starts with D or M)`.

Good: the overflow lists were honest. Most items are Low, and several Medium-sounding ones fail on refutation. The log-fault coupling is stated in log-root.md. The WIP-limit complaint, which nine lanes repeated, is exactly what D183 Q63 decided. The M2c pause contradiction is already an open question (Q119). The spec corpus generally says the hard thing out loud: refusal rows name defaults and remedies, and log-fault restoration is closed and test-held. Needs improvement: some normative facts still escape their owners. A Ceph refusal precondition lives only in a delivered record. The milestone corpus keeps a parked item and a scope exclusion for a feature D246 shipped, because the decision retired B1124 but not B776. A decision that delivers an outcome should sweep parked items with the same outcome. Bad: one Ceph page states the default replica pair three ways, and the code follows the minority rule for derived pools. That is a real contract-and-implementation split on a storage sizing path. The Ceph distribution default selects an arm that is always refused, which costs every operator a failed plan and leaves a misleading effective state.

Candidates after verification: Z04-1 COR-04; Z04-2 COR-84; Z04-3 API-142; Z04-4 API-32. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-z05"></a>

#### Lane Z05: Gap: where the decisions D235 to D249 reached and where they did not

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/milestones/backlog.md:7129-7635`.

Good: decisions D235 to D249 are well formed. Each one separates the owner's words from the session's clauses, links to the spec that owns each rule, and names exactly which earlier clause it supersedes. The large CLI, storage-layout, packaging and network-API moves (D240, D243, D244, D247, D248, D249) reached the specs, the operator guide and the skills almost completely. Needs improvement: one decision fixes the rule in its own page but leaves restatements elsewhere unchanged. Three small stale copies are operator-visible: the wheel flags in the disconnected example, the default node in cluster exec, and the human Lifecycle `Next` row. Ceph's '6h every adapter run' refusal text is false since X313, and its not-yet-met line names the wrong item. Bad: D239 is the one decision that did not propagate. The logical-volume root and the omitted-root default live only in api/machines.md. managed-os.md, which owns the Kickstart erase target and %pre, the disk-safety invariant in state-reconciliation.md and the security-safety skill all still teach 'exactly two forms; empty refuses'. state-reconciliation.md also still requires the root in every erase policy, which contradicts X320. These are destructive-path contracts, the place where divergent implementations cost the most. A delivery check should grep for the retired fact on every decision that touches a destructive path.

Candidates after verification: Z05-1 REC-02; Z05-2 API-03; Z05-3 REC-139; Z05-4 DOC-02; Z05-5 CLI-59; Z05-6 DOC-03; Z05-7 DOC-25. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-z06"></a>

#### Lane Z06: Gap: every observation and completion predicate against one durable before-state rule

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/state-reconciliation.md:613-722`; `specs/openshift-clusters.md:960-1036`; `specs/managed-os.md:551-700`; `specs/substrates.md:430-470`; `specs/substrates.md:610-690`; `specs/substrates.md:860-880`; `specs/infrastructure-services.md:440-470`; `specs/add-ons.md:451-527`; `specs/ceph.md:770-966`.

Good: the engine's core rule is precise and safe. Silence, a refused read and an inconclusive read never become no effect. A canceled attempt stays unknown. Removal predicates read only what the removal takes back. Managed OS and Ceph keep real durable before-states: the Q66 disk-boot intent, and Ceph's intent records and fences. Needs improvement: there is no single definition of the proof that an effect never began. The engine offers only an optional `preparation`. Capabilities express the proof five ways (a recorded before-state, a claim never published, a host fence called an 'attempt record', positively unstarted, plain absence), and two of them cite a record that is never written. Several blocks (libvirt host, KubeVirt machine, cluster media, Ceph host and cluster) state no apply-side no-effect or partial rows at all, although a fresh destroy depends on that observation first. Bad: the libvirt machine and managed-service no-effect predicates can be read two ways, one unsafe and one that never resolves. A short engine rule naming the allowed never-began proofs, plus one sentence per block, would close the lane.

Candidates after verification: Z06-1 REC-140; Z06-2 REC-73; Z06-3 REC-141; Z06-4 refuted. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-z07"></a>

#### Lane Z07: Gap: cross-context exclusivity across every entry point that acts on a shared resource

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/infrastructure-services.md:118-323`; `specs/contexts.md:228-420`; `specs/cli.md:1539-1660`; `specs/substrates.md:820-892`; `specs/substrates.md:1439-1560`; `specs/security.md:340-360`.

Good: the host-reservation contract is unusually rigorous for the resources it names. Each key class has one conflict relation and closed release paths. bridge-use re-proves under the root lock with a durable releasing mark. SSH claims are qualified by both address and pinned host key, and the claim is consistently kept apart from ownership and from live proof. The lock matrix in contexts.md is exhaustive by command. Needs improvement: exclusivity is still defined per mechanism, not per resource. A physical server is protected only within BMC key space, and a consumed resource is protected only for bridges. The KubeVirt per-VM key cannot fire because names already embed the context. The foreign-listener probe names two service classes, although its opening sentence covers every socket. Bad: the 'two contexts never drive one server' promise is stated twice as absolute, yet power commands (already reported) and SSH placements on a BMC-driven server (new here) sit outside it. On the physical path, the only remaining guard is the 'machine must be off' precondition, which the driving context's own power command can satisfy. One mechanism-independent identity key and one generic use-claim family would close both gaps with small text changes.

Candidates after verification: Z07-1 REC-74; Z07-2 REC-142; Z07-3 REC-143. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

<a id="lane-z08"></a>

#### Lane Z08: Gap: a closed inventory of produced and natively retained secret material

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/secrets.md:348-460`; `specs/state-reconciliation.md:723-833`; `specs/add-ons.md:416-450`; `specs/ceph.md:2128-2163`; `specs/managed-os.md:1469-1560`; `specs/security.md:786-835`; `specs/cli/output.md:1126-1200`.

Good: custody of produced material is specified with unusual rigor. It is captured before done, a failed publication records unknown, the D124 hand-over is crash-ordered, the identity-preserving recapture is backed by named tests, and the placement sources form a closed set. Native-side retention is cleanly separated from custody. Needs improvement: there is still no single inventory. Material produced natively and never captured falls between the pages. The kubeadmin password has one sentence and no reveal, retention or masking rule, and the no_log trigger is keyed to bound inputs rather than to confidential native output. Bad: secrets.md asserts a closed route into clusters ('only as an owned Secret') that the installer's own placement of the pull secret and vCenter credentials contradicts. The orphan deletion warns about produced access but not about declared effect material, such as a generated recovery passphrase, that abandoned machines still need. Most other empty cells in my table (the registry login on hosts, Ceph outputs in retained output, renew of effect material, the object-user output contract, the Ceph unproved states) were already filed by L10, L18, X06, D04 and C03/C05, so I did not repeat them.

Candidates after verification: Z08-1 REC-75; Z08-2 ARC-05; Z08-3 REC-76. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

<a id="lane-z09"></a>

#### Lane Z09: Gap: the owner map and precedence for cross-cutting rule classes

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/index.md:1-58`; `specs/glossary.md:1-110`; `specs/substrates.md:689-762`; `specs/contexts.md:825-885`; `specs/infrastructure-services.md:64-117`; `the first 14 lines of every page under specs, specs/api, specs/cli and specs/contexts (their ownership paragraphs)`.

Good: the one-owner rule is stated plainly in the index, the glossary and AGENTS.md. Most page openings name what they own and link what they defer. Diagnostic codes and host packages have one test-backed or table-backed owner. Completion is layered correctly: the engine owns the outcome model and each domain owns its predicate. The realized-target and dispatcher contract states its extension rule. Needs improvement: of the twelve rule classes, seven have two owners or circular owners (capacity, bypass grammar, setup output, the root disk, produced material, reservations, listeners). Most were filed pairwise in the first round, which shows the cause is structural rather than local. Nine page openings state no ownership, and several openings name owners by bounded-context name ("Workspace") rather than by page. Bad: no rule anywhere says which text governs when two passages disagree, so every contradiction must be settled by hand. In addition, a cross-domain registry (host reservations) sits on one domain's page, which will tax every new substrate.

Candidates after verification: Z09-1 COR-85; Z09-2 ARC-85; Z09-3 COR-86; Z09-4 COR-87. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

<a id="lane-z10"></a>

#### Lane Z10: Gap: do the named guards prove the invariants the specs say they hold

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/security.md:890-914`; `specs/architecture.md:1255-1408`; `specs/state-reconciliation.md:834-893`; `specs/infrastructure-services.md:38-63`.

Good: the corpus ties invariants to executable guards on purpose. Every test name the security proof table cites exists. The refusal, transition and precedence tables are parsed by tests and compared exactly with the code. The docs-check list, the walker list and the plan-handle check are self-verifying, and exemption lists can only shrink. Needs improvement: the register has decayed against the milestones. One row says 'none yet' although B86 and B760 claim in-tree completion and tests exist, and three Gap cells cite delivered items, so a reader cannot tell open proof gaps from closed ones. Several guards are narrower than the sentences that cite them. The read-only-command row is proved at the store layer, not for catalog commands. The no-bypass row has no adapter or trust-check case. The planner/executor partition walks curated lists while its file classes assert nothing. The 'every check walks sourceTree' claim has two counterexamples. Bad: nothing keeps the register in step with item status, and no rule requires a guard to enumerate the set its invariant quantifies over ('every command', 'every bound'). A docs check that refuses Gap links to delivered items, plus a rule that 'every X' rows need a table-driven guard, would fix both.

#### Lane Z11: Gap: agent-facing procedures outside the skills: knowledge pages and the e2e runbook

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `.agents/knowledge/redfish-physical-bmc.md`; `.agents/knowledge/sudo-pty-terminal-handoff.md`; `.agents/knowledge/sudo-command-line-environment.md`; `.agents/knowledge/ssh-session-boundary.md`; `.agents/knowledge/ibm-ceph-cleanup.md`; `.agents/knowledge/operation-store-entry-confirmation.md`; `.agents/knowledge/controller-runtime-isolation.md`; `.agents/knowledge/ceph-native-pull-boundaries.md`; `.agents/knowledge/kubernetes-object-ownership-with-oc.md`; `.agents/knowledge/firewalld-reads-need-root.md`; `e2e/README.md`; `AGENTS.md`; `.claude/settings.json`.

Good: the knowledge pages are evidence-grade. Firmware facts cite dated captures, UNVERIFIED items carry concrete checks, upstream claims cite exact versions and lines, and most pages link their owning spec. The e2e README is careful operator procedure: strict success criteria, reversible host changes, acceptance kept with the owner, and evidence archived with checksums before purge. Its log paths match the post-D244/D249 layout. Needs improvement: several pages have gone stale against later decisions. The sudo pages still say re-execution goes only through /proc/&lt;pid>/exe, the Redfish page names a 3.13 runtime (D248) and an emulator rehearsal (D224), the operation-store page describes a writer race D244 removed, and the firewalld page names a removed preflight subcommand. <a id="lane-z12"></a>

#### Lane Z12: Gap: refusal tables and diagnostics as one closed registry with remedies that lead somewhere

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/cli/output.md:994-1125`; `specs/managed-os.md:1956-2026`; `specs/substrates.md:99-119`; `specs/openshift-clusters.md:126-186`; `specs/ceph.md:546-569`; `specs/ceph.md:1129-1143`; `specs/infrastructure-services.md:38-63`; `specs/add-ons.md:585-611`; `specs/cli/commands.md:342-530`.

Good: every domain refusal table is a closed, test-held list with exact reason and remedy strings. The diagnostic registry is mechanically closed, and every error code has a tested default remedy. Managed-OS is the model: placeholders are defined, precedence is explicit and remedies name the operator's own fields. Most remedies, walked one step, reach a plan that can succeed, and CLI flag-conflict refusals are early, safe and specific. Needs improvement: four of six tables leave the code implicit. Precedence is stated per page in three different ways, while two pages promise one diagnostic per object. Placeholders are undefined in substrates and OpenShift, and one in managed-OS points at the wrong Secret. Several OpenShift and Ceph remedies say only 'correct'. Bad: attempt-time named refusals, whose code decides whether a block ends failed or unknown, have no spec registry. Ceph tokens and codes live in Go maps with only a partial prose list, five emitted tokens have no spec text, and Ceph spends lifecycle.unsupported on observed disk state, contradicting the registry's 'an existing code keeps its meaning'. A single template in architecture.md (code column, precedence rule, placeholder block, named-refusal table) would close the whole lane.

<a id="lane-z13"></a>

#### Lane Z13: Gap: field traceability for DNSServer and CephPool, from authored field to diff

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `api/v1alpha1/infrastructure_services.go`; `api/v1alpha1/storage.go`; `specs/api/infrastructure-services.md:23-144`; `specs/api/infrastructure-services.md:246-257`; `specs/infrastructure-services.md:581-711`; `specs/ceph-resources.md:33-91`; `specs/ceph-resources.md:306-411`; `specs/ceph.md:295-420`; `specs/state-reconciliation.md:159-209`; `specs/state-reconciliation.md:2237-2251`; `specs/cli/output.md:791-993`.

Good: every authored DNSServer and CephPool field except one reaches a named request member. The service domain separates derived from authored configuration, and storage-to-DNS composition stays package-free. Pool readiness compares every frozen attribute, and drift is refused, never rewritten. The diff projection contract is closed and honest about what it does not compare. The change rule is uniform: any changed value over a completed apply refuses, in both domains. Needs improvement: diff observes only six pool fields although the pool observation already reads rule, profile, compression, bulk and PG count. Drift that blocks the next readiness is therefore invisible to `diff --observe`. CephPool's never-realized values (warn, parameters, crushRoot, clay/lrc/shec, the technique) refuse at different stages, outside the api.unrealized contract, and the technique refusal is not stated in the spec. A few sentences contradict or blur each other: nativeName versus the shared metadata.name rule, 'changed intent', and the autoscale.mode wording. Bad: DNSServer.additionalIngressHosts is admitted in both management modes, frozen into the DNS request digest and does nothing. No api.deferred warning or tracking item covers it, so changing it forces a destroy.

Candidates after verification: Z13-1 API-21; Z13-2 REC-77; Z13-3 API-55; Z13-4 API-87; Z13-5 API-80; Z13-6 API-143. Named and not pursued: 2 further points.

<a id="lane-z14"></a>

#### Lane Z14: Gap: time, deadlines and bounds across domains

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/contexts/controller-record.md:129-176`; `specs/contexts/log-root.md:41-140`; `specs/controller.md:87-126`; `specs/contexts.md:228-320`; `specs/managed-os.md:504-550`; `specs/ceph.md:967-1128`; `specs/openshift-clusters.md:601-760`; `specs/substrates.md:1439-1560`; `specs/state-reconciliation.md:1426-1474`; `specs/cli/output.md:1226-1306`.

Good: time is treated as data. Each long wait is a frozen request budget, each deadline is derived from those budgets with arithmetic that recomputes exactly (managed-OS, OpenShift, Ceph, KubeVirt power runs), and a single runner rule (kill, then unknown) governs expiry, backed by a test that checks how each constant is applied. Interrupts and deadlines interact uniformly through the attempt-outcome table. Needs improvement: the deadline policy is scattered across seven pages with no registry. After D235, MaxDeadline is a self-check that each family applies differently or not at all (Ceph refuses at planning, add-ons at admission with a bare 5h50m, physical managed-OS runs past it, OpenShift ignores it), and Ceph text and diagnostics still claim that every adapter run is held to six hours (tracked as B1183). Bad: the Redfish-arm power runs and readings state no deadline, so the shared lease that blocks apply is bounded only by the two-hour default. The controller record's byte bound pre-empts its counted bound with a remedy-less error. A physical cluster's round margin lives in a milestone item rather than a spec. The boot-budget expiry outcome (unknown versus failed) and the reader-hold bound are already filed by other lanes.

Candidates after verification: Z14-1 REC-111; Z14-2 REC-145; Z14-3 REC-78; Z14-4 REC-146; Z14-5 REC-79. Named and not pursued: 3 further points.

<a id="lane-z15"></a>

#### Lane Z15: Gap: site topology end to end

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/api/environment.md:1-60`; `specs/api/environment.md:136-160`; `specs/api/networks.md:1-149`; `specs/api/machines.md:212-260`; `specs/api/machines.md:400-420`; `specs/api/ceph.md:300-494`; `specs/ceph.md:570-769`; `specs/substrates.md:134-230`; `api/v1alpha1/environment.go`; `api/v1alpha1/networks.go`; `api/v1alpha1/machines.go`.

Good: one registry on the root kind, which every consumer resolves against. Ceph service sites are derived from native placement instead of a second field. Network scope has a clear default. Stretch realization is staged, read back and frozen. Ceph keeps all site-specific behavior on its own pages, so the general flow carries no Ceph logic apart from one wording slip. Needs improvement: 'site' is never defined. Networks treat it as one 802.1Q domain and Ceph as a routed CRUSH failure domain of any type. Nothing says whether a site is an asserted label or a fact checked against the substrate, so the libvirt provider host and the vSphere region and zone stand unrelated to it. That is the main extension risk for new substrates and cluster types. The registry's consumer list has drifted: it names a removed service field and omits Network. The Machine field names neither its consumers nor its stretch freeze. Bad (cost): one host's site can be written in five places (Machine, node, location, dataSites, tiebreaker.site). Three of them only restate a derived value, and the reference example authors them all. Already filed by other lanes and not repeated here: untyped site references (A19-1), node site against Machine site (S04-4), and Machines with no site against scoped Networks (A04-4).

Candidates after verification: Z15-1 CON-33; Z15-2 API-144; Z15-3 API-145; Z15-4 API-146. Named and not pursued: 4 further points.

#### Lane N01: Client releases after X342: the Environment API and the controller stage

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/api/environment.md:1-112`; `specs/api/environment.md:340-372`; `specs/api/environment.md:464-512`; `specs/controller.md:557-830`; `api/v1alpha1/environment.go`; `api/v1alpha1/lexical.go`; `internal/controller/tooltable.json`; `internal/controller/tooltable.go`; `internal/controller/tools.go`; `internal/controller/versions.go`; `specs/milestones/backlog.md:7796-7901`.

Good: X342 makes the client model mostly predictable. An omitted release takes the build's default, fetched by the pinned size and SHA-256 with no publisher contact, through a mirror or directly. A declared release keeps the publisher-checksum route, and the mirror text now states this exactly. The two new refusal rows are complete and test-bound. The table parser is strict, and the spec names the Go constant rather than the format literal. A newer build's different default works safely through the generic rule that a continuation must freeze the same blocks. Needs improvement: the ordering rule stops at 'a prerelease suffix', and the code's suffix handling and v-normalization are unstated. One stale sentence still admits every prerelease. The sentence saying the default 'replaces' latest misdescribes an admission refusal. Six names cover one concept. Bad: a standalone kubectl is pinned, minimum-checked, listed as an egress destination and counted among the 'four pinned clients' with 'a mirror route' (D251 (3)), yet nothing selects it and it has neither a field nor a mirror. The operator also has no product surface to learn the minimum or the default: the guide sends them to a developer make target that contacts every publisher.

#### Lane N02: Acquisition origins and the controlled-network design

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/security.md:746-848`; `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md`; `specs/milestones/backlog.md:7796-7901`; `specs/milestones/backlog.md:3296-3461`; `specs/milestones/backlog.md:285-315`; `specs/controller.md:806-952`.

Good: the origin rule (class by who may publish on the serving host) can be applied by a reviewer and is used consistently for quay.io and icr.io across security.md, the design, the guide and D250 (11). Assigned: `docs/operator-guide.md:10-280`; `docs/operator-guide.md:657-700`; `docs/development.md:233-339`; `examples/openshift-clusters/lab-kubevirt/README.md`; `examples/openshift-clusters/lab-kubevirt/runbook.md`; `examples/openshift-clusters/lab-kubevirt/environment.yaml`; `examples/openshift-clusters/lab-kubevirt-external/README.md`; `specs/security.md:791-848`; `specs/controller.md:589-625`; `specs/controller.md:806-830`; `specs/api/environment.md:40-112`; `specs/api/environment.md:340-372`.

Good: the new controlled-network section is the right instrument. It gives a per-step table of who connects, the default origin and the moving setting. The origin classing in security.md is principled and records the icr.io exception against D250 (11). The tool-table authenticity rule is stated consistently in controller.md, environment.md and security.md, and the KubeVirt examples now match their Environment, which closes DOC-07. No tracked example still declares `latest` or a release below the minimum. Needs improvement: the documentation trails X342 in two places. The guide's closing paragraph and the deferred page still present the build-pinned tools as designed and parked, and the deferred page counts three mirror fields. The advisory rule for minimums is stated three different ways. The development guide doesn't say what a weekly verify failure means. The standalone kubectl is pinned with a minimum that no field can reach, has no mirror, has no stated selector, and is missing from the controlled-network table. So the egress-restricted operator can't derive every destination and how to move it.

<a id="lane-n05"></a>

#### Lane N05: Attack: the pinned client table over time and under failure

Auditor model: opus. Assigned: `specs/controller.md:557-1022`; `specs/api/environment.md:40-112`; `specs/api/environment.md:340-372`; `specs/state-reconciliation.md:1629-1800`; `specs/project.md:137-184`; `specs/deferred/controlled-network.md:131-175`; `specs/milestones/backlog.md:7796-7901`.

Good: the tool table makes a default client as tightly pinned as the runtime lock. The frozen size and SHA-256 travel in the request, mirrors are trusted for nothing on that route, `latest` and runtime release discovery are gone, and the refusal rows give clean exits. Interruption, shared-host and retirement behaviour stays sound. Needs improvement: the comparison grammar (v prefix, build metadata, a fourth part) is underspecified. The checksum route for a declared release is worded differently in controller.md, the X342 record and the deferred design, and the deferred trust exception does not cover a release between the minimum and the default. Bad: the headline promise of the minimum, that the next apply under a build that raised it replaces the retained client, contradicts the lifecycle unit. A completed apply over unchanged input settles, an earlier build's continuation refuses, and destroy runs the old client. Only a destroy followed by a fresh apply moves the release, nothing reports the gap, and the operator is told the opposite. Separately, the X342 record understates its breaking change: earlier-build contexts lose destroy under the new build too, not only continuation.

Candidates after verification: N05-1 NEW-01; N05-2 NEW-14; N05-3 NEW-15; N05-4 NEW-10. Named and not pursued: 5 further points.
